chunks.name: Antique
chunks.text: Antique is a province on the island of Panay in the Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Antique got its tagline "Where the mountains meet the sea" because of the relatively short distance between its mountains and its coast, which lies parallel to it. Just like its highland attractions, there's absolutely a lot to explore in Antique's long coastal area aside from providing an unobstructed view of the sunset. On the southernmost tip of Antique is Nogas Island, an uninhabited 26-hectare marine and bird sanctuary.

According to oral history, related as the legend of Maragtas, Antique is believed to be the landing site of ten Bornean Datus who escaped persecution from Sri-Vishaya, a Hindu-Malay empire that existed from the 7th to the 14th century in Borneo and Sumatra. There they met the Negrito/Ati (earliest settlers of Panay) chieftain Marikudo. They bought the island from the chieftain for a golden saduk (headpiece or helmet), and a golden necklace, among other gifts, the event is known as the "Barter of Panay". The Negritos then retreated to the mountains, while the Borneans settled in the lowlands. Today, the landing is commemorated every year in Antique in the Binirayan festival on the month of April with highlights on April 27 to 29.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: The Antiqueños are noted for their industry. They are renowned weavers throughout the Visayas. The Bugasong patadyong, a tube cotton fabric of plaid design, is highly valued because of its fineness of weaving. Piña cloth is also produced in looms throughout the province. Wine manufactured from the sap of the coconut is a cottage industry. Muscovado sugar production is also a big industry in Antique, which has become an attraction of sorts because of Antique's native delicacies derived from muscovado sugar.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Iloilo and Aklan are the gateways to Antique by land. It is also accessible from Palawan, Manila, Romblon, and Mindoro by sea. Buses and Vans bound for San Jose and Libertad are stationed at the terminal in Molo District, Iloilo City. Transportation time from Iloilo City to the capital San Jose is 2-3 hours.

The provinces only airport is at San Jose (), served by PAL Express.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: It is possible to get around Antique by Jeepney, trike (motorbike with sidecar) or hired cars. Foreigners may be a little daunted at first by the Jeepney or trike but the drivers are experienced and charge very reasonable fares.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text:
The Batbat and Punta coral reef in Barbaza and Seco Island in Tibiao feature unparalleled wonders of marine life. Antique's best kept secret though is the Caluya group of islands, with natural beauty and resources that can easily compete with what the world famous Boracay can offer. Tourists that can bear the 3 hour travel to Caluya are rewarded with white, powdery sand beaches surrounded with pristine waters and diverse species of marine life that have not yet been touched with commercialism.

Another attraction in Antique is its historical sights. The Catholic Church holds a very strong influence on Antiqueños. For centuries, the churches were the physical vanguards of the people. Being a coastal province, and having been vulnerable to attacks by Moro raiders, Antique was guarded by a series of watchtowers, like the 'Old Watchtower' in Libertad and Estaca Hill in Bugasong all of which were built under the direction of the Spanish friars. A lot of these heritage structures still stand as a reminder of Antique's history and culture.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: For the more adventurous, climbing Mt. Nangtud, considered as the highest peak in Panay, offers a great view and the experience of discovering unexplored sights. The rugged and varied land of Antique offers visitors a variety of exciting outdoor activities from white water kayaking and white river rafting in the northern town of Tibiao to relaxing in Sira-an Hot Springs of Anini-y, Antique's southernmost town.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text: People in Antique eat most dishes common to the rest of the Philippines however visitors should try 'Batchoy' which is a local noodle dish in a pork broth.

chunks.name: Apalit
chunks.text: Apalit is a municipality in the province of Pampanga, Philippines. It is a primarily commercial town at the crossroads between the Pampanga River delta, Bulacan, and the rest of Pampanga.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Apalit is one of the oldest towns in Pampanga, having been established by the Spanish in 1582. For much of its history, Apalit has prospered thanks to its location at the southern edge of the Candaba Swamp and the Pampanga River, then a vital trade artery that also sustains its agricultural and fishing industries while at the same time providing chronic headaches through flooding during the rainy season.

Since the shift to motorized transportation beginning in the 20th century, Apalit has further prospered, first due to its location along a now-defunct railroad (now being revived), its position along the MacArthur Highway and it being at the junction leading to the towns of Macabebe and Masantol further downstream along the Pampanga River.

chunks.name: Victory Liner Bus Terminal
chunks.text: address: MacArthur Highway, Sampaloc

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Apalit lies along MacArthur Highway, the main thoroughfare of Pampanga. To avoid chronic traffic congestion, most travelers from Metro Manila take instead the Pulilan or San Simon Exits of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) before entering Apalit from either Calumpit or San Simon via MacArthur Highway. NLEX itself passes through town, including near Apalit Church, but has no dedicated exit within its territory.

From Trinoma in Quezon City, passenger vans link Apalit with Metro Manila from 4AM to 12MN, but will involve waiting for the vehicle to fill up before leaving. There are also passenger vans in the adjacent SM North EDSA mall.

Victory Liner also offers limited bus services from Apalit to Metro Manila. It is also a stopover on some buses along the San Fernando-Metro Manila route, especially if the bus signages indicate “Inner Cities”. These buses enter MacArthur Highway at NLEX Tabang Exit in Guiguinto, Bulacan, and pass through Malolos and Calumpit before reaching Apalit.

Apalit is the terminus of a minibus route running south from Dau in Mabalacat, ideal for those commuting from Clark and Angeles. It is also along the jeepney and minibus route from Malolos in Bulacan to San Fernando, the capital of Pampanga, as well as the ones running between San Fernando and Macabebe and Masantol. All four routes traverse MacArthur Highway.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
A secondary road also connects Apalit with Pulilan in Bulacan. A road built over the Arnedo Dike leads to other towns of eastern Pampanga such as San Simon, San Luis, Candaba and Arayat.

There are no trains to Apalit since the main line to La Union closed in 1988. There is ongoing construction of an electrified standard-gauge railway running from Metro Manila to Clark International Airport in Angeles and New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac. As of 2026, the line is still under construction, with a station serving Apalit being built near Apalit-Macabebe-Masantol Road in Barangay San Vicente.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of transportation between barangays, especially as Apalit Church and the Municipal Hall are bypassed by MacArthur Highway, 500 m away. The tricycle terminal leading to these sites is along Gonzalez Avenue, a few meters from the junction with MacArthur Highway. Fares start at P20.

chunks.name: Aparri
chunks.text: Aparri is a town in northern Cagayan. It lies at the mouth of the Cagayan River which drains into the Babuyan Channel. This article covers only the mainland portion; Fuga Island, while administratively part of the town, is considered a separate destination.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Aparri had been an important trading post for its location north of Luzon. It was also the first area in Cagayan Valley that was conquered by the Spanish in 1581 following a battle with Japanese pirates. While its port remained operational as a critical link to Calayan despite being largely destroyed by frequent typhoons, the town is still a major commercial center for northern Cagayan as it houses large tobacco plantations that account for much of its local income.

. The original inhabitants of Aparri are the Ibanag, an ethnic group which have inhabited the area long before the Spaniards arrived. Ilocanos and Filipino Chinese also have settled here since colonial times.

chunks.name: Understand / Orientation
chunks.text: Aparri is bisected by the Cagayan River into western and eastern halves. Town proper is at the eastern side, while the western barangays are more rural in character.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text:
Aparri has a monsoon-influenced climate, with a short dry season between February and April, and rain for the rest of the year.

The town is at the typhoon belt, and is also an important location for typhoon tracking by the national weather agency, PAGASA, which has a meteorological station at the port.

Western Aparri is served by AH26, where a junction in Barangay Bangag leads to the Camalaniugan Bridge over the Cagayan River and a junction with Cagayan Valley Road at the boundary with eastern Aparri and the town of Camalaniugan.

chunks.name: Get in / By van

chunks.name: Apayao
chunks.text: Apayao is a province in the Cordillera region of Luzon in the Philippines. One of the country's least-known provinces and the Cordillera's "Last Frontier", it has underrated natural and cultural attractions such as indigenous villages and unspoiled, jungle-covered mountains.

chunks.name: Understand / Geography
chunks.text:
Apayao occupies of land area, mostly mountainous and forested terrain. The capital in theory is Kabugao, but due to its isolated state, the provincial administration is in Luna, along the boundary with Cagayan province to the north. The province occupies some of the last remaining jungles of the Cordillera Mountains, and hosts some endemic species such as the national bird, the Philippine eagle.

The province is bounded on the south by Abra and Kalinga, on the west by Ilocos Norte, and to the north and east by Cagayan, which has a narrow coastal strip blocking access to the Babuyan Channel. It is bisected by the Apayao or Abulug River, which runs in a U-shaped loop around the province south from Calanasan before making a northeastward bend towards the Babuyan Channel in Cagayan, passing through an extension of the coastal plain that reaches into Luna, Santa Marcela, Pudtol and Flora.

chunks.name: Understand / People
chunks.text:
Apayao has around 126,000 inhabitants. It is the least densely populated province in the Philippines, with only 29 people per square kilometer, mostly squeezed into the Apayao River valley in the northeast of the province in the minor conurbation formed by Luna, Flora, Santa Marcela and Pudtol. It is predominantly inhabited by the Isneg or the Itneg, an Igorot subgroup closely related to the Tingguians of neighboring Abra. They are then divided into various tribes and clans. There are also some Aeta tribes related to those in the Sierra Madre and Zambales mountains.

Long seen through the colonial era and much of the post-independence years as a “no-go zone” due to its reputation for being a hotbed of tribal warfare, headhunters and communist rebels, since the late 20th century, Apayao has seen an influx of predominantly Ilocano migrants who have mostly settled in Luna and other lowland areas in the northeastern part of the province.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text:
Apayao's climate varies extensively. While the northeastern valleys can be hot in summer, the interior has a more temperate climate due to its altitude, but the dense jungle makes things more humid than in the rest of the Cordilleras.

Many visit the province during the dry season between March and May, where temperatures are at its highest but rainfall at its lowest. The rainy season is rather the same as with the rest of Luzon, but precipitation is somewhat higher, with the cool season from November to February also bringing in torrential rains. Heavy rain, especially those brought by typhoons, can cause seasonal road closures due to landslides and rockfalls.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
Archeological evidence suggests that Apayao has long been settled as early as the prehistoric era. Throughout the 17th to 19th centuries, the Spaniards based in Cagayan Valley tried to subjugate Apayao with limited success. In retaliation, Isneg tribes raided lowland villages and beheaded residents in headhunting raids.

In the early 1900s, the Americans occupied Apayao and turned it into a subdistrict of the Mountain Province encompassing much of the Cordillera region in 1908.

In 1966, Apayao was merged with Kalinga subdistrict to became the province of Kalinga-Apayao. In the 1970s and 1980s, the area became a hotbed of rebellions led by the communist New People's Army and a Cordilleran separatist splinter group, the Cordillera People's Liberation Army (CPLA). At the same time, cronies of the Marcos dictatorship entered Apayao and were awarded logging concessions before proceeding to ravage large swathes of the province's forest until the 1990s, when they were finally driven out by the NPA and a belated effort by the government to stop large-scale deforestation.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
After Marcos was overthrown in 1986, the government of president Corazon Aquino reached a peace agreement with the CPLA, leading to Kalinga-Apayao's transfer from the Cagayan Valley Region to the Cordillera Administrative Region in 1988. In 1990, Apayao rejected autonomy for the Cordilleras in a referendum. Amid complaints by residents of Apayao that the provincial government in Tabuk was too distant, Kalinga-Apayao was dissolved into two separate provinces comprising its constituent halves following a referendum in 1995. Kabugao was proclaimed the capital of Apayao, though for logistical reasons, administrative offices were instead placed in Luna, an already thriving commercial hub. A second autonomy referendum for the Cordilleras in 1998 led to a pro-autonomy victory in the province, which was disregarded by the rest of the region rejecting the proposal.

In 2024, the entirety of Apayao was recognized by UNESCO as a Biosphere Reserve for its overwhelming concentration of wild plants and animals.

chunks.name: Understand / Economy
chunks.text: Historically an agricultural society, Apayao's economy was interrupted with the entry of commercial logging in the 1970s that introduced consumerism in the province but not much else and left deep scars on the environment after the loggers were driven out by the NPA and government restrictions. Even today, Apayao is ranked as one of the country's poorest provinces. Since the 21st century, Apayao has began to open up to tourism, although the province's geography, poor infrastructure and bouts of political instability make it challenging for large-scale tourist enterprises to take hold unlike in Baguio.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Apayao is mainly accessed through roads from Cagayan and Kalinga. The nearest airport is in Tuguegarao, from where there are passenger vans towards various towns in Apayao, while bus services from Metro Manila and Laoag usually stop just outside of Apayao, in towns of Cagayan bordering the province such as Claveria, Tuao, Allacapan, Pamplona and Abulug, where a road in Junction Luna aka Junction Libertad leads towards Kabugao-Junction Luna Road, the main highway in Apayao leading to Luna, Pudtol and Kabugao. There are jeepneys to these towns from Junction Luna.

There are no road connections to Abra, while a road connects Calanasan with Solsona and onwards to Laoag in Ilocos Norte.

Public transportation to Apayao operates at an infrequent pace, which usually involves waiting for an indefinite period for your vehicle to fill up before it leaves the terminal.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
The Kabugao-Junction Luna Road is the main thoroughfare in Apayao, connecting much of the province with Cagayan. One can get around the province by public transportation such as jeepney, bus, and passenger van. Tricycles and tuktuks are used within towns.

Due to infrequent services, it is better to take a 4WD or any vehicle suitable for mountain roads. Many attractions are accessible following extended hikes.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text: Tourism is still in its early stages in Apayao, with many waterfalls, mountains and caves still waiting to be discovered and identified even by the locals themselves. Nonetheless, there are already established landmarks such as Mount Sicapoo, a 2361 m peak in Calanasan bordering Ilocos Norte, caving and swimming in the Marag Valley of Luna, rafting and canoeing along the Apayao River and its tributary, the Ngagan River, and the Mataguisi Spanish church ruins in Pudtol. There is also a growing interest for cultural tourism.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: Partake in cultural activities such as pounding rice, community dances and listening to the chants of the indigenous songs and epics.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text:
Like the rest of the Cordilleras, Apayao cuisine is comprised of highland rice, starch vegetables, game, and smoked meats. There are more fish dishes than usual thanks to the Apayao River. A unique dish in the province is sinursur, in which freshwater fish is pounded into a vomit-looking mush and cooked with spices inside a bamboo tube over an open fire.

There are many fruit farms in Conner offering offering tourists the chance to harvest various fruits such as durian, rambutan and lanzones.

chunks.name: Drink
chunks.text: Rice and sugarcane wines are the native drink.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text: The bulk of tourist accommodation, including small and mid-size hotels, is in Luna and Pudtol. Most accommodation elsewhere consists of small inns, hostels or homestays.

chunks.name: Apo Island
chunks.text: Apo Island is in the province of Negros Oriental, in the Central Visayas region of the Philippines, about 30 km (20 miles) south of the provincial capital of Dumaguete. Administratively, the island is a barangay of the town of Dauin; population is about a thousand.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
It is common to use Dumaguete as a stop-over en route to the island. Any travel agent or dive shop in Dumaguete can arrange transport; most offer both day trips and transport for longer stays. See the Dumaguete article for details.

Nearby towns also have resorts that offer day trips to the island. Zamboanguita has Thalatta Beach Dive Resort and Wellbeach Dive Resort, while Dauin has Liquid Dive Resort; see the articles for those towns.

From the Malatapay barangay of Zamboanguita to Apo Island a two-way boat rental is:
₱2000 - small boat max 5 passengers
₱3000 - big boat max 10 passengers
Solo travelers may also join other boats for ₱300. It doesn't matter if you stay in the island for a day or a week; the rates are the same.

You must arrange for transport from one of the local boats to come and retrieve you for a fee. It is a several mile trip in an outrigger canoe with outboard motor over open water, swells can be large and you can expect to be sprayed with saltwater throughout the trip (wear sunglasses). The boats will generally meet you at Zamboanguita where the Malatapay Wednesday market is held. Take a jeepney from Dumaguete, just ask the driver or conductor to warn you when it is your stop.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: The island is only 3 km around and 120 m high at the top of the hill; walking will get you anywhere you need to go.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text: One of the Philippines' famous diving sites, Apo Island has one of the world's best known community-organised marine sanctuaries. It's home to over 650 documented species of fish and estimated to have over 400 species of corals. There are also many sea turtles.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text:
Diving and snorkeling are the main activities around the island. Resorts on and off the island typically hold diving programs for different skill levels. Instructors are commonly PADI-certified. The diving is excellent, plenty of reefs, tons of fish and turtles, and amazing visibility. Keep an eye out for the Giant Trevally (largest of the jackfish family) which is known in these waters.

There are two dive shops in Apo Island:
Apo Island resort - USD25 inclusive of complete gear, boat and divemaster; USD20 exclusive of gear, inclusive of tank & weights, boat and divemaster. Less USD2 for shore dives.
Paul's diveshop - ₱1150 for one dive, ₱2200 for 2 dives exclusive of gear. For complete gear, add ₱280 per dive.

Conservation tax of ₱300 is charged if diving within the sanctuary and ₱200 if diving outside of the sanctuary. These rates are as of June 2009.

chunks.name: Buy
chunks.text:
There isn't much in the way of retail on Apo Island. It's advisable to bring anything that you may need with you because it is a long trip back to Dumaguete. The local women will try to sell you t-shirts and sarongs when you arrive and when you leave.

Both resorts have Apo Island t-shirts and hats which are little more than the words Apo Island and the symbol for divers.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text: Both hotels have restaurants; Liberty's has particularly good chocolate/banana shakes. Menus are limited, but what is available is pretty good. At Liberty's, the dive master will go table to table during dinner and help you arrange the next day's dives.

chunks.name: Liberty Community Lodge
chunks.text: Liberty Community Lodge is the larger of the two with a very nice restaurant and both private and dorm type rooms. The private rooms are situated in what appears to be a large expensive private house, the showers use barely desalinated water and the island is always on restricted water use

chunks.name: Apo Island Beach Resort
chunks.text: Apo Island Beach Resort is on the opposite side of the boulder from Liberty Community Lodge. 5 min walk from Liberty and in a more secluded cove. The cottages here are made of earth / concrete mix (as compared to Liberty which has a lot of bamboo/nipa). The company that owns this place also owns the Coco Grande hotel in Dumaguete; bookings and transport can be arranged through the hotel.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text:
Several beach resorts at nearby towns offer trips to the island; see #Get in above.

There are two publicised resorts on the island, Liberty Community lodge and Apo Island Beach Resort.

chunks.name: Go next
chunks.text:
Dumaguete is the main transport hub of the region; most travellers will reach Apo from there and return there after the island trip.

It is also possible to spend time on the coast near Apo (in Zamboanguita or Dauin) or to continue south (away from Dumaguete) after visiting the island, but these are much less common choices. The highway south follows the coast all the way to Bacolod; resort areas along it include Siaton and Sipalay.

chunks.name: Arayat
chunks.text: Arayat is a town in northern Pampanga, Philippines. It is named after the eponymous inactive volcano that looms over it.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Arayat is known to have existed before the Spanish era. It was conquered by the Spanish in 1579. A predominantly agrarian town along the banks of the Pampanga River, its main draw is Mount Arayat, a massive 1026 m dormant volcano that looms over the Central Luzon plain and was regarded as sacred by the animist natives during the precolonial era.

chunks.name: Arayat Central Terminal
chunks.text:
The main transport terminal in Arayat, servicing the jeepney and minibus route to San Fernando. There are segregated spaces for tricycles heading to various barangays of Arayat.
address: J.M. Espino Street, Mangga-Cacutud

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
From Manila, take the San Fernando exit along the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) leading to the Gapan-Olongapo Road, also known as Jose Abad Santos Avenue (JASA), then turn left towards Arayat, passing through Mexico and Santa Ana. An alternate route is to take a right turn at NLEX Angeles Exit and continue towards Magalang, then turn south towards Arayat. Arayat is also the northern terminus of the Arnedo Dike Road, which connects the eastern municipalities of Pampanga such as San Simon, San Luis, Candaba and Apalit.

From San Fernando and Magalang, there are jeepneys servicing Arayat, although the Magalang route only runs in the morning. It is also traversed by the jeepney and minibus routes running between San Fernando and Gapan in Nueva Ecija via JASA. Buses running from Metro Manila to San Isidro in Nueva Ecija also pass by Arayat via JASA.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Downtown Arayat is at a junction between JASA on one side, and the road leading to Magalang and Angeles City on the other, which in turn has a junction west of town with bypass roads leading separately to Mexico and Santa Ana. Tricycles are the main form of transportation between barangays.

chunks.name: Mount Arayat
chunks.text: A looming inactive volcano that also contains the largest stretch of forested jungle between the Zambales and Sierra Madre Mountains. The mountain is part of a protected reserve known as Mount Arayat National Park. However, access to the area is partially restricted due to rudimentary facilities and landslides that have disrupted the usual hiking trails.

chunks.name: Argao
chunks.text: Argao is a town on Cebu Island, south of Metro Cebu.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Argao is the name both of a town and of the municipality which includes it; municipal population was 78,000 as of the 2020 census, mostly in the town. The municipality extends into the island's mountainous interior, but most of the population and most places of interest to visitors are along the coast.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
It is on the highway that rings the island and on the busy bus route between Cebu City and Dumaguete. In Cebu, these buses depart from the South Bus Station.

Lite Ferries runs two boats a day between Argao and Tagbilaran on Bohol. These are "roro" boats, cars can roll on and roll off.

Nearly all visitors who fly arrive via Cebu Airport and take a bus to Argao, as for any town in the province. One might also fly to Dumaguete and take a bus or to Bohol and take a ferry. Argao has no airport; there is an airstrip in nearby Dalaguete, but that serves only general aviation and has no scheduled passenger flights.

chunks.name: See / Argao Church and Plaza Complex
chunks.text:
San Miguel Arcangel Parish Church is one of the oldest churches in southern Cebu. Built during the Spanish colonial period, it remains the visual and cultural center of the town.

The surrounding plaza area still functions as an actual community gathering space rather than a decorative Instagram backdrop.

chunks.name: See / Argao Hall of Justice Ruins
chunks.text: Argao Hall of Justice Ruins preserves remnants of older Spanish-era structures and gives insight into the town’s colonial history.

chunks.name: See / Balay sa Agta
chunks.text:
Balay sa Agta is a heritage-style structure tied to local folklore about a giant (“agta”) said to have once terrorized the area.

Whether historically accurate or not, every old Philippine town seems contractually obligated to have at least one giant story.

chunks.name: See / Linut-od Falls
chunks.text: Linut-od Falls is among the tallest waterfalls in Cebu. The trek can be challenging during wet weather, but the scenery is worth it for travelers comfortable with rougher terrain.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: The Archangel Michael is the town's patron, and there is a Torta Festival (see #Eat) on his feast days, 28th/29th September.

chunks.name: Do / Eat torta and sikwate
chunks.text:
Argao is famous throughout Cebu for its torta, a rich traditional sponge cake usually paired with hot chocolate (sikwate).

The best torta is usually found in local bakeries rather than aggressively branded “heritage cafés” charging city prices.

chunks.name: Do / River trekking and mountain tours
chunks.text:
river systems,
caves,
waterfalls,
and mountain viewpoints.

chunks.name: Do / Visit during festivals
chunks.text: The town fiesta and cultural celebrations showcase traditional dances, food, and religious processions.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text:
The town is well-known for baking, in particular for the torta, a local type of sponge cake. The original recipe was Spanish; the local variant uses palm wine instead of yeast as the rising agent.

The region also has cacao plants and produces chocolate. The Cebuano version of hot chocolate, sikwate, is easily found and goes nicely with torta.

chunks.name: Eat / Local specialties
chunks.text:
torta
sikwate
tablea chocolate
fresh seafood
puso meals and lechon during fiesta

chunks.name: Eat / Recommended local spots
chunks.text: Popular torta makers include family-run bakeries around the public market and town center. Ask locals where they personally buy torta instead of relying purely on online rankings. Cebuano food recommendations become dramatically more accurate once an auntie starts pointing directions with her lips.

chunks.name: Drink
chunks.text: Argao is relatively quiet at night. Expect local eateries, videoke spots, roadside barbecue stands, and small cafés. This is not a nightlife town.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text:
There are beach resorts along the coast and some hotels in the town. Accommodation options include:

pension houses,
beach resorts,
homestays,
and small boutique stays.

Some travelers use Argao as an overnight stop before continuing farther south toward Oslob or Santander.

chunks.name: Go next
chunks.text: Moalboal — with many diving resorts, restaurants with international menus, and lively nightlife — borders Argao to the west.

chunks.name: Aringay
chunks.text: Aringay (pronounced uh-ring-guy) is a town in La Union.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Aringay is one of the oldest settlements in La Union, having existed in the precolonial era as a coastal trading post for Cordilleran traders selling their gold at the mouth of the Aringay River. It was conquered by the Spanish in 1572 and became a municipality in 1741 after it was separated from Agoo to the south. The town was rebuilt after World War II, when it was the site of amphibious landings along Lingayen Gulf by Japanese and then American forces in the battle to control Luzon.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Aringay is along Route 2 (Manila North Road), the main thoroughfare in La Union. Buses heading to San Fernando and other locations further north in the Ilocos Region also ply this highway.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of transportation in town.

chunks.name: Samara Beach
chunks.text:
The main coastal promenade in Aringay, with grayish sand stretching from the boundary with Caba to the north down to the Aringay River estuary.

chunks.name: Santa Lucia Parish Church
chunks.text:
Aringay's main Roman Catholic church, built during the Spanish era in 1736 and extensively repaired following World War II damage. The plaza in front of the church was a battleground during the Philippine Revolution against the Spanish in 1898.
address: Marcos Avenue, Poblacion

chunks.name: Centennial Tunnel
chunks.text:
An 4.5 m long unfinished tunnel built by the Philippine National Railways as part of a planned extension the railway line from Manila towards San Fernando, which was abandoned at the outbreak of World War II and was instead used as a bomb shelter by the Japanese.
address: San Juan-Aringay Road, Poblacion

chunks.name: Bubon Posi
chunks.text:
The highest point in Aringay, it is a 325 m peak of a mountain ridge bisected by the Aringay River. Its conical summit looms over the town and is a designated forest reserve and hiking spot.
address: San Eugenio

chunks.text: address: Macabato

chunks.name: Dulao Lagoon
chunks.text:
An estuarine lagoon lined with mangrove forests on the boundary with Agoo.
address: Dulao

chunks.name: Gallano Rice Terraces
chunks.text:
A terraced rice farm on the slopes of the Cordillera Mountain Range overlooking the boundary with Tuba in Benguet province.
address: Gallano

chunks.text:
The administrative building of the town's main primary school is an American-era bungalow (commonly known as the Gabaldon) dating from between 1907 to 1912.

chunks.text: Aringay is a leading producer of milkfish (bangus), with many fish farms along the Aringay River and its estuary.

chunks.name: Atimonan
chunks.text: Atimonan is a rural municipality, the gateway to eastern Quezon.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Atimonan serves as the gateway to eastern Quezon, which is very rural, and has a rainier climate. The town center is along the coast, at the mouth of a river, and the municipality relies on fishing and agriculture. Further inland, the terrain is mountainous, and forested, though many have gave way to coconut plantations.

Atimonan residents are called Atimonains (ah-tee-moh-nah-EENS). They speak the Tayabas dialect of Tagalog, but has some peculiarities that are bewildering to standard Tagalog and even Tayabas Tagalog speakers

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
Atimonan's name is somewhat shrouded by legends. One legend have the town named after a "Ate Monang", a daughter of a local town chief, while others say it is from Tagalog atin muna, an expression of the sentiment the locals have to their enemies, especially onto the Muslim pirates, or atimon, an extinct species of tree.

The town dates back to 1608. Old Atimonan was established on the mouth of a river, but due to the constant threat from pirates, it has been relocated multiple times. It lost some of its residents following the establishment of the municipality of Padre Burgos to the south along the Bondoc Peninsula.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
By car and by bus, one travels the beaten-path Manila South Road or Maharlika Highway (Route 1/AH26) which leads to Bicol. Atimonan is about from Manila, and from Lucena.

There are two possible routes through the southern Sierra Madre mountain range that separate Atimonan from western Quezon. The shortest is a winding highway through the middle of the Quezon National Park, the Old Zigzag Road aka Bitukang Manok (Chicken Intestine), which is open only to cars. There is also a longer route, the New Diversion Road, that carries the Route 1/AH26 designation through another winding alignment a few kilometers to the north of Old Zigzag Road and is used by buses and heavy trucks. If you drive, you'll usually go through the Old Zigzag Road for the scenic but hazardous route, but if you take a bus, you'll be traveling on the Diversion Road. Both routes are however, dangerous, especially at night or during rainstorms.

There is a pier which serves boats to and from the island of Alabat, across from Lamon Bay.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: The town proper is walkable, but you can also catch a tricycle. From downtown to the national park, you generally need a car, as buses cannot take the zigzag road and tricycles cannot travel there either.

chunks.name: Our Lady of the Angels Parish
chunks.text: It was first built in 1643, but was repeatedly destroyed by a fire and an earthquake. The present church was built between 1687 and 1700. The church's ceiling and interior dome have paintings of archangels, the Virgin Mary, and symbols of heavenly authority.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text: Atimonan has a small town center with a Spanish-era church, but nothing much. Most of the municipality's sights are related to nature.

chunks.name: Quezon Protected Landscape
chunks.text: It is a protected landscape on the southern end of the mighty Sierra Madre range, which straddles the boundary with Pagbilao. It was founded in 1934 as a national park until it was elevated into a protected area in 2003. It covers of tropical rainforests, home to endemic species of birds, reptiles, mammals, and trees. Inside the park is Mount Pinagbanderahan, where a Philippine revolutionary flag was raised, and is reachable through an hour of hiking. There are also caves and waterfalls within the park, and some campsites.

chunks.name: Do / Festivals
chunks.text: Tagultol Festival — Atimonan town's major fiesta, it is held every August 1 and 2, and is a feast of the town's patron, Our Lady of the Angels. The festival's main attraction is the Karakol, a fluvial parade held at the bay. The festivities end at the old church at downtown.

chunks.name: Atimonan Public Market
chunks.text: address: Juez Andres Street, Zone IV

chunks.name: Atok
chunks.text: Atok is a municipality in the province of Benguet, Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Located in the geographical center of Benguet, Atok is one of the highest towns in the Philippines, thus experiences relatively colder weather than the rest of the country. The average temperatures in Atok is colder than the more popular tourist destination city of Baguio which is also dubbed as the Summer Capital of the Philippines, due to being popular with Filipinos from the lowlands seeking relief from hot temperatures of summer in the country.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: The way to get into Atok is by bus, van or jeepney bound to Halsema Highway from Baguio. Drop off at Kilometer 55 of Halsema Highway.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There are tricycles in town, but a 4WD or any vehicle suitable for mountain roads is best used. Most attractions in town are accessible following extended hikes.

chunks.name: Highest Point View
chunks.text:
Located at 7400 ft above sea level, this attraction used to be the highest point in the Philippine Highway System until it was surpassed by another spot in Tinoc, Ifugao in 2019. The location also provides a view of the mountains of Atok and surrounding municipalities including Mt. Pulag.
address: Kilometer 53, Halsema Highway

chunks.name: Haight's Place
chunks.text:
Located at 7937 ft above sea level, it provides a panoramic view of Atok's vegetable terraces which includes the Naguey Rice Terraces in the west. Frost occurs in the area from December to February. The place was named after an American soldier who fought during the Spanish-American war who brought the first vegetable seedlings for the area which has a temperate climate who also married a local and settled in Atok.
address: Barangay Paoay

chunks.name: Benguet-Kochi Sisterhood Park
chunks.text:
A park commemorating the 40th sisterhood ties between the province of Benguet and Kochi prefecture of Japan located within Haight's Place. At least 34 cherry blossom trees were planted in the area in mid-2016. A future tourist destination especially among the locals after the trees' first bloom expected to occur in 2019.
address: Barangay Paoay

chunks.name: Sayangan New Public Market
chunks.text: address: Halsema Highway, Paoay

chunks.name: Buy
chunks.text: Atok is where one can buy vegetables directly from farms before their prices get jacked up in the market due to transportation costs.

chunks.name: Aurora (province)
chunks.text: Aurora is a coastal province of Central Luzon region in the Philippines. Little is known about the province due to its remoteness, but its capital is known for its surfing scene, and the province has one of the largest expanses of rainforest spared from development, and also has hidden beaches and mountains.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Named after the wife of the second president of the Philippines, Manuel L. Quezon, Aurora used to be part of a larger Quezon province until it was made a sub-province in 1951, and finally made a province through a law passed in 1975. One obvious reason for creating Aurora is due to the area's isolation from the rest of Quezon province: there are no direct links to the rest of the province and much of the terrain is mountainous and heavily forested, which makes the area relatively isolated. It was separated officially in 1979, it was transferred from Southern Tagalog to Central Luzon in 2002 after Southern Tagalog was divided into Calabarzon and Mimaropa.

Aurora houses one of the final swaths of lowland tropical rainforest in Luzon, and much of the province is off the beaten track. The towering Sierra Madre mountain range separates Aurora from the central plains of Luzon, and most of the province faces the Pacific Ocean.

Aurora's population is about 215,000 as of 2015, and is the least populated province of Central Luzon. Aurora's population is approximately 50% Tagalog, 30% Ilocano, and the remainder indigenous peoples (Kankana-ey, Casiguran, Bugkalot, Dumagat), Bicolano, Visayan, Kapampangan, and Pangasinan. Southern and central Aurora are generally Tagalog, and the northern part mostly Ilocano. The Dumagat, a Negrito group believed to be a cross of Austronesian and Melanesian features, inhabit the hillsides and mountains of the province.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text:
Being largely covered by rainforest, Aurora has a rainforest climate, which means it frequently rains at almost every day, especially in the afternoon, though it can rain at any time of day. Except for occasional above-average highs or lows, there is not much variation in temperature, with highs between and lows between , but the amount of rainfall varies by month. It rains at Aurora for almost half a year.

Facing the Pacific Ocean, Aurora often faces the havoc wreaked by typhoons, and the province is also at the heart of the typhoon belt.

The high season for travel to Aurora is generally from March to October. Surfing season is generally from May to October, where it rains frequently and winds are perfect for surfing.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text:
Genesis Transport operates air-conditioned provincial bus routes from Cubao in Quezon City and Bocaue to Baler, with stops at Angeles, Tarlac City and Cabanatuan bus stations.

UV Express vans run from Cabanatuan to Baler, but are slower than the bus, and take the longer route via Bongabon.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text:
Being separated from the central plains by the Sierra Madre, driving to Aurora involves mountain roads with many sharp curves.

Aurora is connected to the rest of Central Luzon by two highways from Nueva Ecija. The most commonly traveled route runs from the town to Rizal to Maria Aurora via Pantabangan and Alfonso Castañeda. The other less traveled route (Nueva Ecija-Aurora Road, Route 111) runs from the town of Bongabon directly to Baler; it is paved but has one one-lane bridge upon leaving the Sierra Madre and one ford due to a bridge being replaced.

From Cagayan Valley, Cordon-Aurora Road (Route 108) runs from the town of Cordon (near Santiago City) in Isabela, passing through Quirino province.

Dingalan is reachable by a lone road link (Route 114) from Nueva Ecija. Construction is ongoing for a coastal route from northern Quezon Province.

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text: There are two airports, Dr. Juan C. Angara Airport () and Casiguran Airport (), but only Baler airport has flights, on Air Juan, which operates amphibious aircraft from Manila.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
The Baler-Casiguran Road is the main transport artery of the province. It is a two-lane road that is vulnerable to road closures caused by storm surges, landslides and erosion during the typhoon season.

There is at least one bus everyday at 7AM from Baler going up the coast until Dilasag.

The province sees less cars, and there are more motorcycles on the roads; you can rent a motorcycle from most dealers around Baler.

There is no direct road connection between Dingalan and the rest of Aurora, and to get there means passing through Nueva Ecija.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text: Aurora is primarily a destination for nature lovers on account of its location squeezed between the forested mountains of the Sierra Madre and the Pacific Ocean. Fans of culture will appreciate experiences with indigenous Dumagat and Bugkalot tribespeople, while history buffs while find plenty in the historical monuments and museums of Baler.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text: Aurora's local cuisine is a crossroad of Tagalog and Ilocano cultures.

chunks.name: Baao
chunks.text: Baao is a municipality in Rinconada District of Camarines Sur.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Baao is 15 kilometres (9.3 mi) from Pili and 465 kilometres (289 mi) from Manila.

chunks.name: Get in / By train
chunks.text: Commuter rail services are provided by PNR serving from Naga City as its terminus and stops at Baao Station up to Ligao City in Albay then back again northward to Naga. As of 2026, rail service to Manila remains suspended due severe damages brought by Typhoon Reming in 2006.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: From Naga City, the easiest way to go to Baao is to ride a bus going to Iriga City from the Naga City Central Bus Terminal and disembark at Baao bus stop.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Jeepneys and tricycles are available in downtown.

chunks.name: Tinawagan Hills Campsite and L-Farm
chunks.text:
Popular elevated getaway for camping, cool mountain air, and 360-degree views of surrounding volcanoes and peaks like Mount Isarog and Mount Mayon.
hours: Open 24 hours; address: Sitio Pagluwas, Lourdes

chunks.name: 158 Food Street
chunks.text: hours: Opens Tue 5PM; address: 158 San Pedro Street, Zone 4, San Nicolas

chunks.name: Babatngon
chunks.text: Babatngon is a town of 29,000 people (2020) in the northern part of the island of Leyte, Philippines, along the shore of Carigara Bay. Babatngon is known for Busay Falls, a three-tiered cataract which is an attraction for picnickers who flock to Babatngon during the summer months. A massive bowl of solid, moss-covered rock catches the cool waters of the third fall.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: It is situated on a small plain set in a semicircle of mountain ranges and nestles in the northern mouth of the San Juanico Strait, which separates Samar from Leyte. Boats coming in or going out of Tacloban City have to pass by it through the pilot station of Canaway, one of the islets along the strait. Small coconut covered islets fringe its coast along San Juanico Strait, the most important of which are Rizal, Magsaigad, Tabigue, almost all of which extend from east to west.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: It is 33 km (21 mi) north-west of Tacloban City and about 10 km (6.2 mi) north of the town of San Miguel.

chunks.name: Busay Falls
chunks.text: address: Brgy. District 3

chunks.text:
a farm resort located in North part of tacloban, Offer a native and organic food.
hours: 10AM-8PM; address: Brgy. Villa Magsaysay

chunks.name: Babuyan and Calayan Islands
chunks.text: The Babuyan and Calayan Islands are a volcanic archipelago in the Babuyan Channel between northern Luzon and Batanes that belong to the province of Cagayan in northern Philippines. It it is comprised of five major islands, four of which (Babuyan, Calayan, Dalupiri, and Camiguin) are administered by the municipality of Calayan, while the island of Fuga is administratively part of Aparri.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The islands are mostly of volcanic origin, and contain some of the country's active volcanoes. They have a rich history of human settlement even before the Spanish conquest, as seen by multiple archaeological excavations across the islands. Its inhabitants were repeatedly relocated to mainland Luzon due to difficulties in accessing them on account of the rough waters of the Babuyan Channel and its position along the Philippines' typhoon belt, only to return when the opportunity came. Even today, the islands are incredibly difficult to access, and facilities remain rudimentary compared to the mainland or even in the Batanes archipelago further north, but the islands' natural wonders are appreciated by those who prefer to see a minimal amount of fellow tourists.

The islands' residents are a mix of Ibanags, Ilocanos and Ivatans. They subsist on agriculture, with Calayan's name originating from a Ibanag term for a place to grow ginger while Babuyan literally means piggery, as well as fishing and catering to the occasional tourist brave enough to endure frequent power outages, expensive fuel imported from the mainland, and getting stranded when the seas are too rough seas for sailing. The area has also seen a lot of emigration, especially as there are no universities or college and mundane health conditions frequently become medical emergencies due to the lack of resources.

chunks.name: Calayan Airport
chunks.text:
Serves light and turboprop aircraft only.
address: Dadao, Calayan Island

chunks.name: Calayan Seaport
chunks.text:
The main maritime terminal for Calayan Island.
address: Magsidel, Calayan Island

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Transportation to the islands is incredibly disorganized. While there are airfields and airstrips on Calayan and Fuga Islands, due to low population and demand, these are restricted to military and charter flights, with the one in Fuga exclusively used by the company which bought the island in the 1970s. There are seasonal flights from Tuguegarao Airport to Calayan Airport operated by SkyPasada.

The only viable option is to join the residents in taking boats known as lampitaw in the mainland Cagayan port towns of Santa Ana (for Camiguin and Babuyan Islands), Aparri, and Claveria (the last two ports for the other main islands). Travel times take a minimum of 3 hours in fair weather, but can reach 12 hours in rough waters. Note that this journey is not for the faint-hearted; expect to see a rickety wooden boat rather than a leisurely cruise and share space with bulky cargo and even livestock. Be sure to take enough safety gear and identification with you in the event of an emergency. Always notify authorities in Calayan as well as in your port of entry of your travel plans.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There is no public transport in the islands and very little to no cars or any larger vehicle. Expect to ride motorcycles, tuktuks or the buggy known locally as kuliglig instead. To travel between islands, you will need to hire boats again; there is no organized boat transport. Expect the same conditions as getting into the islands. Even some destinations in the same island are only accessible by boat due to the lack of roads. Expect to pay thousands of pesos when renting a boat.

chunks.name: Smith Volcano
chunks.text: An almost cylindrical active volcano with a height of 688 m that last erupted in 1917.

chunks.name: Babuyan Claro
chunks.text: The other active volcano in Babuyan Island, it is an 843 m massif that last erupted in 1924 and has two craters each measuring between 300-400 m.

chunks.name: See / Babuyan Island
chunks.text: The furthest among the islands from mainland Luzon. It is a quiet place mostly subsisting on agriculture and fishing, and dominated by the Babuyan Claro Volcano at its center, with black sand beaches.

chunks.name: Kannaway Cave
chunks.text:
A coastal grotto with a natural pool, accessible only during low tide.
address: Dilam

chunks.name: Bangaan Viewpoint
chunks.text:
An elevated lookout with views over the Babuyan Channel into neighboring islands. Nearby is a memorial the Philippine Navy vessel BRP Datu Kalantiaw which ran aground on the island during a typhoon in 1981 with the loss of 79 crew.
address: Dadao

chunks.name: Nagudungan Hills
chunks.text:
A hilly promontory jutting southwards and ringed by high and rocky cliffs. There is a lighthouse on the site.

A white-sand beach.

The main Roman Catholic church in Calayan.
address: Poblacion

chunks.name: See / Calayan Island
chunks.text: This is the islands' most populated and is also the political and economic hub. The most developed tourist attractions and infrastructure can be found here.

chunks.name: Didicas Volcano
chunks.text: A small volcanic island with an elevation of 228 m that repeatedly erupted out of the ocean and sunk before definitively emerging into dry land since an eruption in 1952. It is the most active of the islands' volcanoes and there are tight restrictions on approaching the island, although some who have managed to step on its shores describe the ground as being hot enough to cook a fish on.

chunks.name: Camiguin de Babuyanes
chunks.text:
An active 712 m volcano on the southern tip of Camiguin Island that last erupted in 1857.
address: Naguilian

chunks.name: Naguilian Beach
chunks.text:
A stretch of white-sand beach around a sheltered cove at the western side of the island.
address: Naguilian

chunks.name: Pamoctan Island
chunks.text:
An islet facing Naguilian Beach with its own white-sand beach.
address: Balatubat

chunks.name: See / Camiguin Island
chunks.text: The nearest island from Santa Ana, and the most visible from mainland Luzon. This should not be confused with the equally volcanic island province of Camiguin in the southern Philippines.

chunks.name: Banua Beach
chunks.text: A white-sand stretch on the southwestern side of the island.

chunks.name: See / Dalupiri Island
chunks.text: Probably the least known of the islands, it is an elongated stretch of land with white-sand beaches on its eastern side and rocky coastlines to the west.

chunks.name: Mount Nanguringan
chunks.text: The highest peak in the island at 191 m.

chunks.name: Saint Ursula Church Ruins
chunks.text:
The ruins of a Spanish-era church.
address: Sitio Naguilian

chunks.name: Musa Beach
chunks.text:
A stretch of white-sand beach on the western side of Fuga Island.
address: Sitio Mudoc

chunks.name: See / Fuga Island
chunks.text: Administratively part of Aparri, it is visible from the coast of northwestern Cagayan. Since the 1970s, it has been the property of Fuga Island Holdings Inc. and is also part of the Cagayan Economic Zone Authority (CEZA) based in Santa Ana, which has been trying to develop the island into a luxury holiday destination without much success, with the resident population trying to get by in between.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: While on a boat, expect to see the islands' vibrant marine life, including dolphins and humpback whales. On land, try to find endemic birds such as the Calayan rail (Garillalus calayanensis, locally known as piding) as well as migratory ones while hiking. Dalupiri has some rare reptiles such as the Philippine crocodile and the endemic Ross's wolf snake.

chunks.name: Buy
chunks.text: Prices of most goods tend to be higher as they have to be imported from the mainland, especially fuel. These can skyrocket when bad weather prevents deliveries from the mainland. Due to erratic phone signals and the absence of banks and ATMs, always pay in cash. As there are no malls, grocery stores or markets to speak of, make sure to bring enough food, water, batteries and other necessary supplies whenever you travel in the area.

chunks.name: Olen's Miki House
chunks.text:
A restaurant serving rice noodle soup (miki).
address: Poblacion, Calayan Island

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text: Apart from the usual seafood, a popular souvenir from the islands is the honey gathered from the forests and banayuyu wine, which is made from an endemic species of berry.

chunks.name: Cafe Flora

A coffee shop that also serves rice meals.

chunks.name: Nomad Eco Resort

A homestay.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text: There are no large-scale hotels to speak of, just some homestays and inns.

chunks.name: Bacacay
chunks.text: Bacacay is a municipality in the east coast of Albay accessible via Legazpi-Tiwi coastal road and has a shoreline facing both Lagonoy Gulf and Albay Gulf. Separates the municipalities of Santo Domingo and Malilipot, it is a fishing town with beaches, islands and caves.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Bacacay is perhaps known for its beaches, and is nicknamed the "Beach City". It is composed of the mainland and island barangays, with black sand beaches on the mainland and white sand beaches on the island. The residents of the neighboring landlocked municipalities visit them during the summer seasons. Cagraray Island is known to the locals as ibong, a Bikol word which means the other side.

The numbered barangays 1 to 14 on the mainland is the town proper (Poblacion). The main highway is Magsaysay Avenue where you can find the public market and other business establishments, the Catholic Church and some government buildings and it leads to the municipal pier. Schools are just walking distance away from the public market.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text:
There are buses from Manila to Bacacay, stopping also at other towns and cities along the way, and there are also UV Express vans from Legazpi and jeepneys from Tabaco.

Barangay Bonga is the only barangay located along the Legazpi-Tiwi coastal road where two seaward roads are leading to the town center. Jeepneys from the city of Tabaco traverse the Sogod-San Jose road while UV Express coming from the city of Legazpi traverse the Bonga-Hindi road. Barangays Hindi and Sogod are both coastal barangays.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Around the town center there are pedicabs while tricycles are available heading to the outlying barangays. Boats going to Cagraray island are found at the town's pier.

Island Hopping – Discover the white-sand beaches of Misibis Bay and nearby islands.
Karagumoy Festival - a vibrant annual celebration highlighting the town’s rich culture, heritage, and the, Karagumoy plant (Pandanus simplex) used for traditional weaving. Held from August 19 to 31, 2025, the festival features cultural shows, street dancing, sports events, food stalls at the municipal plaza, and the Mutya ng Karagumoy coronation night, celebrating local unity, tradition, and environmental awareness.

All rooms are equipped with wireless internet access, air conditioning, daily newspaper, desk, hairdryer, minibar, coffee/tea maker, LCD TV with cable channels, private toilet and bath. Some of its facilities and services are bars, business center, cafe, conference room, fitness room/gym, jacuzzi, restaurant, shops, swimming pool, aerial tours, airport transfer, babysitting service, massage service, private beach access and water sports (motorized and non-motorized).

chunks.name: Bacarra
chunks.text: Bacarra is a town in Ilocos Norte. It is famous for its leaning, albeit partially ruined belltower.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Bacarra is one of the oldest settlements in Ilocos Norte, having been founded by the Spanish in 1593.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Bacarra is along Route 2 (Manila North Road), which skirts the eastern and northern edges of downtown. It is served by buses running the Manila-Pagudpud and Laoag-Tuguegarao route. Some bus companies operate limited direct services from Metro Manila.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of transportation in town, particularly as downtown Bacarra is further inland from the coast.

chunks.name: Bacarra Church
chunks.text:
Bacarra's main Roman Catholic church, built during the Spanish era and repaired to its current state following heavy damage from an earthquake in 1983. There is an ecclesiastical and local history museum in the convent.
address: M. Castro Street, Santa Rita

chunks.name: Bacarra Belltower
chunks.text:
Bacarra church's belltower was built during the Spanish era. Over the years it gradually tilted on its side due to earthquakes and its location on an alluvial plain with soft ground. In 1983, the church's dome collapsed in an earthquake, giving its current decapitated-like appearance. Despite this, the tower was declared a national cultural treasure in 1973.
address: Rizal Boulevard, Santa Rita

chunks.name: Vijia Watchtower

Bacarra's main beach, named after its silver sand.
