chunks.name: Isabela (city)
chunks.text: Isabela is a city in Basilan, an island on the Sulu Archipelago in southern Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
While administratively part of Zamboanga Peninsula, this guide treat Isabela as a part of Basilan.

The city is both dominated by Christian Chavacano speakers and the Muslim Tausug people. It serves as the economic center of Basilan, though it has been separated from Basilan after the rest of Basilan voted for inclusion into the Bangsamoro. The surrounding area remains volatile due to the ongoing Islamic insurgency, and the tourism industry has stagnated.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
There is regular ferry service from Zamboanga port to Isabela City. See the Basilan page for details.

There are no flights to Isabela City; the nearest one is in Zamboanga.

chunks.name: Cathedral of Santa Isabel de Portugal
chunks.text: The seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Basilan and Prelature of Isabela, built in 1960s modern-art style with a distinctively Classical Roman mosaic for an altar wall.

chunks.name: Kaumpurnah Mosque
chunks.text: Historic seat of Islamic faith and teaching in Basilan, can be seen as you enter the Isabela Channel.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text: Constructed with elegant Middle-Eastern architectural lines reflecting the majority Muslim population (70%) of the Island Province

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text:
Annual Cocowayan Festival - Anniversary of the Cityhood of Isabela, April 25
Fiesta Santa Isabel - Annual Feast of St. Elizabeth of Portugal, July 8
Alano White Beach Resort - located on the northern part of scenic Malamawi Island, features white sand beaches, day cottages and basic amenities for a day of fun with family and friends
Barandino Farm - located on the eastern part of city, it is 12 kilometers from the main city and has hectares coconut and fruit trees
Sumagdang Beach Resort - a publicly owned beach resort
Isawad Resort - an inland pool and water park located in Cabunbata Barangay
Yakan Crafts - showcasing authentic Yakan cloth designs and souvenir products, located at J.S.Alano (Zenith) Bldg.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text:
A number of hotels, resorts and hostels dot the City of Isabela.

The Farmland Resort (Lanote),
Basilan Hostel (Eastside),
Buwalan Beach Resort (Sumagdang),
Sofia Hotel (Port Area).

chunks.name: Isabela (province)
chunks.text:
For other places by the name, see Isabela.
Isabela is the second largest province in the Philippines in land area. It is in the Cagayan Valley.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Isabela is considered among the richest and most progressive provinces in the Philippines.

The province has three geographic areas. The eastern area, straddled by the Sierra Madre mountain range, is rugged and thickly forested. A substantial portion is uncharted. These unexplored hinterlands are home to a rich variety of flora and fauna, and some are under government reservations. It is home to one of the world's largest remaining low-altitude rainforests, with numerous unknown endemic species of flora and fauna and biological diversity in the protected area known as the Northern Sierra Madre Natural Park.

This primarily agricultural province is the rice and corn granary of Luzon due to its plain and rolling terrain.

Major languages spoken are Ilocano followed by Ibanag, Yogad, and Gaddang.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
Isabela was colonized by the Spanish in the late 16th century. But due to indigenous resistance, only the towns along the Cagayan River basin and the route leading to Nueva Vizcaya were occupied by the Spanish, leaving a string of heritage churches in their wake. Nevertheless, Ilocano migration has upended the ethnic balance and turned indigenous peoples into minorities. The province was established in 1856 from the southernmost towns of Cagayan and what used to be the northern and central portions of Nueva Vizcaya. It was named after Queen Isabella II of Spain. Like the rest of Cagayan Valley, Isabela was turned into the main production hub of tobacco during this time.

Isabela, particularly Palanan, was the site of the last capital of the First Philippine Republic, which ceased to exist after President Emilio Aguinaldo was captured in Palanan in a daring American raid in 1901.

The province was one of the first epicenters of the New People’s Army rebellion in the 1970s but gradually subsided by the 21st century.

chunks.name: Get in / By road
chunks.text:
Almost of the Asian Highway 26 pass through the different towns and cities of the province. Several bus companies offer daily trips to different routes like Manila, Dagupan, Baguio, Ilocos, and vice versa. Public utility vans and small-time bus operators ply daily trips from Tuguegarao in Cagayan to Santiago City vice versa, while jeepneys and tricycles are commonly used as the basic mode of transportation within the province's jurisdiction.

Dinapigue is accessible only through Aurora province.

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text:
There are three airports in the province. Cauayan Airport () is the primary airport in the province serving a trip to Manila, Palanan, and Maconacon. The other two are Palanan Airport in Palanan and Maconacon Airport in Maconacon. The country's leading passenger airlines Cebu Pacific and Philippine Airlines service the Cauayan-Manila-Cauayan Route. Light planes operated by Cyclone Airways and WCC Aviation's Sky Pasada have flights from Cauayan Domestic Airport to the community airports in Palanan and Maconacon.

The northernmost parts of Isabela, including Cabagan, Tumauini, San Pablo, Delfin Albano, Santa Maria, Santo Tomas, and Quezon, are serviced by Tuguegarao Airport in Cagayan, which is nearer.

chunks.name: Get in / By boat
chunks.text: The Pacific coastal towns of Divilacan, Maconacon and Palanan are also accessed from Santa Ana in Cagayan or from Dinapigue using irregular ferry boats that involve a 9-hour journey across choppy waters.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
The main backbones of road travel in the province are the AH-26, which services the main cities of Isabela, and the parallel Santiago-Roxas-Tuguegarao Road, which services the Mallig Plains. Capillary roads connect the two thoroughfares.

Vans and buses are the main forms of transportation between towns. A jeepney service operates between Cauayan and Ilagan. For travel within towns, a tricycle is the best option. Calesas (horse-drawn carriages) exist in Cabagan.

In the rainy season, some bridges over the Cagayan River may be submerged. You may need to take a ferry, basically a small motor banca or a barge consisting of at least two motorized bancas tied together with a plank installed to accommodate vehicles.

Since 2025, the Ipil Bridge along the Maharlika Highway in Echague has been closed to buses due to structural issues. Hence, passengers going to Alicia, Echague, and neighboring towns may need to change vehicles in Santiago, San Mateo, or Cauayan.

Since 2019, construction is ongoing on a road to connect the coastal towns of Divilacan, Maconacon and Palanan.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: It is common practice for farmers to dry their rice and corn on the surface of provincial roads and even on the shoulders of major highways. Although officially outlawed, this is an often tolerated practice, with farmers even encouraging motorists to drive over their grains as it somehow helps grind them without much need for mills and threshers and separates the chaff and other impurities. However, motorcycles are not encouraged to do this, as they tend to slip often, causing fatal accidents.

chunks.name: Alicia Church
chunks.text:
An 18th century heritage church.
address: Maharlika Highway, Barangay Magsaysay, Alicia

chunks.name: Northern Sierra Madre Natural Park
chunks.text: An extensive protected area covering a large swathe of the Sierra Madre Mountains from the boundary with Cagayan to San Mariano town. Home to the indigenous Agta/Dumagat tribes, endemic species such as the Philippine crocodile, the Philippine eagle, the Isabela oriole, pitcher plants and virgin forests, in addition to 2000 m peaks that have never been named or climbed by humans.

chunks.name: Dunoy Lake
chunks.text:
An isolated lake reachable only by a four-hour hike or by motorcycling on a single-lane trail, it is home to the endemic Philippine crocodile, which was rediscovered in the area in 1999. An observation tower provides sightseeing opportunities for the reptile as well as endemic birds.
address: Barangay Dibuluan, San Mariano

chunks.name: Magat Dam
chunks.text:
Opened in 1983, it was deemed the largest dam in Southeast Asia at the time and created a reservoir that displaced numerous communities in neighboring Ifugao. Since then it is one of the main sources of irrigation and electricity in the Cagayan Valley Region. The complex and its surroundings have become a favorite recreation spot for residents as well as day-trippers from Santiago. Fishing activities are also available at the reservoir.
address: Burgos-General Aguinaldo Road, Barangay General Aguinaldo, Ramon

chunks.name: Bambanti Festival
chunks.text:
An annual festival celebrating Isabela's culture. Most major events are held at the amphitheater at Queen Isabela Park.
hours: latter half of January

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text:
Rice and corn-based delicacies and sweets are a staple here, including inatata, tupig and binalay. During corn harvest season, expect to see roadside vendors selling boiled or roasted corn cobs.

Pancit Cabagan is a local noodle dish named after the town.

Ilocano dishes such as pinakbet and igado, derived from liver, are common.

chunks.name: Isulan
chunks.text: Isulan is a town of almost 100,000 people (2022). It is also the capital of the province of Sultan Kudarat.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Isulan houses a large oil palm plantation to the east of the town.

Most of the locals are Hiligaynon-speaking migrants, who settled here in the 1930s, but there are still the native Maguindanao people who originally resided here.

chunks.name: Isulan Public Transport Terminal
chunks.text:
Buses and UV Express (minivans) all pick up and drop off passengers here. There are nothing much inside the terminal, except for noisy vendors.
address: Isulan-Tacurong Road

chunks.name: Get in / By bus or minivan
chunks.text:
Yellow Bus Lines has trips from Kiamba via General Santos, Koronadal and Tacurong.
Husky Transport makes a stop at Isulan on their Cotabato-General Santos route. A trip from Cotabato is risky, as it passes through war-torn Maguindanao, though there are rarely any attacks on buses plying the highways there.

There are plenty of UV Express leaving the terminal to serve other points in Sultan Kudarat, and even into Maguindanao and Cotabato.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: Himugaya Festival - Every August 30, the municipality of Isulan conducts the Hamungaya Festival to celebrate its foundation. The festival showcases skills and talents in literary, musical and cultural aspects of the city. It is also an agricultural festival of thanksgiving.

chunks.name: CityMall
chunks.text:
Mall with restaurants and an arcade.
address: Tacurong City Rd

chunks.name: Isulan Central Plaza
chunks.text:
Little two-storey department store and supermarket with a Mang Inasal and Landbank ATM outside.
hours: 8:30AM-7PM; address: Senator Ninoy Aquino Avenue

chunks.name: Carlito's
chunks.text:
Fine Filipino dining.
hours: 7AM-9PM; address: Senator Ninoy Aquino Avenue

chunks.name: Namaskar Ji Isulan
chunks.text:
Indian cuisine.
hours: 9AM-9PM; address: Isulan-Tacurong Road

chunks.name: Inko's Grill
chunks.text:
T-bone steaks, chicken inasal and silog. Serves alcohol.
hours: 6:30AM-9PM

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text: Most local restaurants will generally be certified Halal to accommodate its Muslim Maguindanaoan population.

chunks.name: Antonia's Hotel
chunks.text:
Two-storey hotel with A/C rooms, but lacks a restaurant. Food available only by contract.
address: Aujero Street, Kalawag I

chunks.name: Jovinaj Traveller's Inn
chunks.text:
Two storey hotel with A/C rooms, but lacks a restaurant.
address: Sen. Ninoy Aquino Avenue

chunks.name: Itbayat
chunks.text: Itbayat is an island municipality of Batanes province in the northern Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Itbayat is the northern-most island and municipality in the Batanes archipelago and also in the Philippines. It is one of the three (out of 10) islands in the province that are inhabited, the others being Batan and Sabtang. It also has jurisdiction over six uninhabited islands, including Mavulis, also known as Y'ami, the most northerly point of the Philippines and a mere 142 km away from Taiwan.

Itbayat island is believed to be the oldest inhabited settlement in Batanes, with archaeological evidence suggesting that humans first arrived there in 4000 BC. However, is the most difficult to access among the Batanes islands, as its coastline is entirely composed of rocky cliffs that are constantly battered by the rough seas while the mainland is constantly battered by winds strong enough to swipe off hats and knock down visitors even in sunny days. As such, it sees the least number of tourists and the most unspoiled views in the province. These consist of windswept landscapes covered with grass and a few bent trees in between, with the occasional goat, cow and other livestock grazing freely.

chunks.name: Jorge Abad Airport
chunks.text: address: Raele

chunks.name: Chinapoliran Port
chunks.text: address: San Rafael (Idiang)

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
The best time to visit is during the dry season between March and June, when the winds and waves are calm. Otherwise, expect frequent cancellations at the last minute.

Itbayat is only accessible from the daily ferry on the faluwa, the traditional Ivatan fishing boat, that disembarks from the provincial capital, Basco, in Batan Island. Travel time takes 3–4 hours in fair weather and 5-6 hours at other times. Expect to share space with goods being imported from Batan and even livestock. There are six seaports around the island, with Chinapoliran port, basically a long and steep set of concrete stairs, being the primary one. Be careful when boarding and disembarking, as the waves frequently throw unsuspecting passengers overboard. Often, you may need to jump to avoid this.

The island also has its own airport, a 15-minute flight by light charter aircraft from Basco.

A mandatory environmental fee is collected from visitors at the municipal hall in downtown Itbayat.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: The road network is less developed than in other islands, so expect lots of hiking. Get a guide with you at all times as the terrain and winds in town can be daunting. Motorcycles, tricycles and some trucks are the predominant form of transportation in town. There are no cars.

chunks.name: Cavaywan Lake
chunks.text:
A lake surrounded by reddish soil.
address: Raele

chunks.name: Santa Maria de Mayan Parish Church
chunks.text:
Itbayat's main Roman Catholic church, built during the Spanish era in a Baroque style in 1872 but was reduced to ruins following an earthquake in 2019 and subsequent typhoons later that year and in 2025. The ruins can still be seen pending a proposed reconstruction.
address: Santa Rosa (Kaynatuan)

chunks.name: Torongan Cliff
chunks.text:
A cliff facing the Pacific coast where the first settlers to Itbayat are believed to have landed in 4000 BC. There is an indigenous Ivatan stone tomb called Axurud dating back to the precolonial era. It also has Torongan Cave, whose mouth was blocked by a typhoon and rendered inaccessible to visitors.
address: Santa Lucia (Kauhauhasan)

chunks.name: Mount Karoboboan
chunks.text:
The highest point in Itbayat Island, with a height of 280 m. A viewdeck provides panoramic views over the island and the surrounding islets, while residents swear they can see city lights from Kaohsiung in Taiwan at night.
address: Santa Rosa (Kaynatuan)

chunks.name: Mavulis Island
chunks.text:
The northern-most island in the Philippines, home to native vegetation, coconut crabs, and a garrison of the Philippine military that forms the only human population, albeit on a rotational basis.
address: Santa Rosa (Kaynatuan)

chunks.name: Rapang Cliff
chunks.text:
A cliff facing the Pacific coast on a jagged series of finger-like promontories known as Karapangan, with a background of grass and rock. Nearby is the Stone Bell, a flat stone that creates a distinct sound resembling a ringing bell when hit and was used by the residents as an alarm clock, warning signal in case of invasion, and to call in their livestock.
address: Santa Lucia (Kauhauhasan)

chunks.name: Tachimus Port
chunks.text:
A promontory on the Pacific coast home to a much-photographed Arius tree that continues to grow despite its truck being continuously bent by Itbayat's ferocious winds.
address: Santa Lucia (Kauhauhasan)

chunks.name: Paganaman Port
chunks.text:
A sheltered cove facing the South China Sea. As the waves are calmer in this side of the island, it is used as a mooring area for the town's fishing fleet and is one of the few seaside areas where residents can swim, although the waves may still be to rough for outsiders. There are tidal pools and a subterranean cave known as the Blue Hole for the color of its waters.
address: San Rafael (Idiang)

chunks.name: Mount Riposed
chunks.text:
A peak that dominates the southern half of Itbayat Island. The summit offers views reaching up to the uninhabited island of Dinem on the Pacific coast.
address: Raele

chunks.name: Mauyen Cliff
chunks.text:
A series of 100 m drops at the southern coast of Itbayat that loom over Mauyen Port.
address: Raele

chunks.name: Yawran
chunks.text:
A village composed of houses built in the indigenous Ivatan style called jinjin. Unlike the more famous stone houses in Batan Island and Sabtang, the ones in Itbayat are made of wood and thatched roofs.
address: San Rafael (Idiang)

chunks.name: Buy
chunks.text:
There is no organized market. Instead, all trades are conducted in the mom-and-pop sari-sari stores typical of the Philippines.

All transactions are in cash due to the absence of banks and ATMs. Prices tend to be higher than in Batan Island due to the costs of transporting goods by sea, and can increase further when bad weather halts the ferries.

A popular souvenir in Itbayat includes handicrafts made from the endemic nito vine.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text: There are no hotels in Itbayat, only homestays.

chunks.name: Itogon
chunks.text: Itogon is a municipality in the province of Benguet, Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Itogon is at the southeastern corner of Benguet, at its triboundary with Nueva Vizcaya and Pangasinan provinces. Situated at the upper reaches of the Agno River, it has historically been a mining town home to some of the country's biggest reserves of gold, copper and other precious metals. It is also undergoing a slow urbanization from neighboring Baguio, resulting in some attractions being mislabeled as being in Baguio itself. Despite this, Itogon, like the rest of the Cordilleras, is a tourist destination in its own right on account of its mountain landscapes alone.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Itogon is primarily connected to Baguio via the Baguio-Bua-Itogon Road, previously the only way in or out of town. It is also along Benguet-Nueva Vizcaya Road, but that highway is useful only if going to the northern barangays. Both jeepneys and passenger vans ply the said routes. Parts of Itogon bordering Baguio are also accessible by taxi.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There are tricycles in town, but a 4WD or any vehicle suitable for mountain roads is best used. Most attractions in town are accessible following extended hikes.

chunks.name: Mount Ugu
chunks.text:
At the boundary with Nueva Vizcaya, the 2150 m high peak offers trails that pass through native communities of the Kalanguya tribes and is becoming a favorite mountaineering destination among outdoor enthusiasts.
address: Pito

chunks.name: Saint Charles Borromeo Parish Church
chunks.text:
Itogon's main Roman Catholic church, somewhat resembling a small chalet.
address: Poblacion

chunks.name: Binga Dam
chunks.text:
A massive hydroelectric complex built in 1960 to control the waters of the Agno River. There is a viewdeck on site.
address: Tinongdan

chunks.name: Mount Ulap
chunks.text:
A 1846 m peak with grassy slopes on the boundary with Tuba. On a clear day, hikers can expect a sea of clouds below the summit.
address: Ampucao

chunks.name: Mount Pigingan
chunks.text:
A 1328 m high peak.
address: Dalupirip

chunks.name: Mount Bidawan
chunks.text:
A 1120 m high peak. Along its trail is a shrine to the Virgin Mary called Ave Maria.
address: Poblacion

chunks.name: Mount Kotkot
chunks.text:
A 1600 m high peak.
address: Ampucao

chunks.name: Balatoc Miner Statue
chunks.text:
A small monument to the town's mining industry at one of the first exploited areas of Itogon, featuring a statue of a miner in his work attire carrying his tools.
address: Balatoc Road, Virac

chunks.name: Crosby Park
chunks.text:
A popular recreational and picnic spot with pine groves.
address: Virac

chunks.name: 1300 Level Swimming Pool
chunks.text:
A hot spring-fed watering hole
address: Poblacion

chunks.name: Mt. Camisong Forest Park and Events
chunks.text:
An extensively-developed high-end mountain resort.
hours: 7AM-8PM; address: Benguet-Nueva Vizcaya Road, Sitio Peday, Loacan

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: There are several hot spring resorts in the downtown area (Poblacion) and in Barangay Dalupirip.

chunks.name: Ivana
chunks.text: Ivana is a municipality of Batanes province in the northern Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Ivana is in the southwestern part of Batan Island, the main island in the Batanes archipelago. It is the main port of entry leading to neighboring Sabtang island. With a population of only 1,368 people as of 2024, it is the second least populated municipality in the Philippines; only Kalayaan in Palawan is less populous.

chunks.name: San Vicente Port
chunks.text:
An alternate, though less used port serving Sabtang.
address: National Road, San Vicente (Igang)

chunks.name: Radiwan Port
chunks.text:
The main port in town, servicing the faluwa ferries to and from Sabtang.
address: National Road, Radiwan

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
The best time to visit is during the dry season between March and June, when the winds and waves are calm. Otherwise, expect frequent cancellations at the last minute.

Ivana is connected to the rest of Batan Island through a scenic highway system, with jeepneys and tricycles running between the town and the provincial capital Basco.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There are not much cars or heavy vehicles due to high costs, logistical difficulties when it comes to importation, and short distances. Motorcycles and tricycles are more common.

chunks.name: House of Dakay
chunks.text:
The oldest house in Batanes, built in 1887 in the traditional Ivatan way of using stones and thatched roofs.
address: National Road, Tuhel

chunks.name: Saint Joseph the Worker Parish Church
chunks.text:
Ivana's main Roman Catholic church, built during the Spanish era in a Baroque style in 1795.
address: National Road, Radiwan

chunks.name: San Jose Bridge
chunks.text:
A rare Spanish-era arched stone bridge that remains in use.
address: National Road, Tuhel

chunks.name: Ivana Lighthouse
chunks.text:
Built beside Radiwan Port, it guards over the strait separating Batan Island from Sabtang.
address: National Road, Radiwan

chunks.name: Maydangeb Beach
chunks.text:
A secluded stretch of white sand near the boundary with Mahatao.
address: San Vicente (Igang)

chunks.name: Toblerone Hills
chunks.text:
A series of moss- and grass-colored limestone hills named after its resemblance to the logo of the Swiss chocolate brand.
address: National Road, San Vicente (Igang)

chunks.name: Honesty Store and Coffee Shop
chunks.text:
Probably Ivana's most famous landmark, it is a store with a self-service cafe next door deliberately left without attendants, leaving its components to the mercy of the customer's moral scruples. Payment its deposited in a box, while you may have to knock next door if you need change. The fact that it has a generally stellar record of not being robbed is a testament to Batanes' low crime rate and Ivatan honesty.
address: National Road, Radiwan

chunks.name: Buy
chunks.text: All transactions are in cash due to the absence of banks and ATMs.

chunks.name: Honesty Homestay
chunks.text:
An accommodation run by the owners of the Honesty Store.
address: National Road, Radiwan

chunks.name: Jagna
chunks.text: Jagna is a small port town of 34,000 people (2015) on the south coast of Bohol. It is to the east of Tagbilaran, which is the provincial capital and has the main seaport and only airport of the province.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Jagna is just a small town with a ferry port. The main reasons to come here would be getting on or off a ferry, or as a transfer point on a land journey between the resorts in Anda and the provincial capital and transport hub Tagbilaran.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus & minivan
chunks.text:
Many buses and minivans from Tagbilaran: two hours (60 km).
There are also buses and minivans from Ubay port, which has ferries from Leyte.

Jagna has a port, and has ferries from Camiguin, Butuan and Cagayan de Oro.

chunks.text:
It has a Mastercard and Visa card ATM.
hours: 24 hour ATM; address: National Highway

fan single/double room with own bathroom.
price: from 450

chunks.name: Jalajala
chunks.text: Jalajala, sometimes spelled as Jala-Jala and pronounced as “hala-hala”, is a town in southeastern Rizal, Philippines. Situated at the tip of its eponymous peninsula, it is one of the last remaining bastions of rural life in the province.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The town's name is said to have been derived from a corruption of the halaan, a species of shellfish. It passed back and forth between Pila, across Laguna de Bay in Laguna province, and Pililla before finally becoming a separate town in 1907.

Jalajala is the most distant town in Rizal from Metro Manila, protecting it from the rapid urbanization and commercial chains that permeate the rest of the province. Its mainstays are agriculture and fisheries along Laguna de Bay.

, making it the least populated town in Rizal.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
From Manila East Road, go straight at the junction at Barangay Halayhayin in Pililla.

Jalajala is accessible by jeepneys from Tanay and Pililla. From Siniloan in Laguna, SINCRODA operates infrequent jeepneys to Jalajala.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Places along the main roads are accessible by jeepneys, while places within the town are accessible by tricycles.

chunks.name: Saint Michael the Archangel Parish Church
chunks.text:
Jalajala's main Roman Catholic church.
address: Ciriaco Villaran Street, First District

chunks.name: Mount Sembrano
chunks.text:
An extinct 745 m volcano at the head of the Jalajala peninsula that is frequented by hikers due to its proximity to Metro Manila and its commanding views of Laguna de Bay into Talim Island and as far as Mount Makiling, on the southwestern shores of the lake.
address: Barangay Malaya

chunks.name: Dragon Wellness Farms
chunks.text:
An agritourism site featuring a dragonfruit farm.
address: Sitio Tanaun, Palaypalay

chunks.name: Jalajala Public Market
chunks.text: address: Third District

chunks.name: Jolo
chunks.text: Jolo is a volcanic island in the southwest Philippines and is the primary island of the province of Sulu in Bangsamoro. The main city of the island, also called Jolo, is the capital of the province.

chunks.name: Jolo Airport
chunks.text: Bangsamor Air from Zamboanga and Cotabato.

chunks.name: Bud Dajo
chunks.text: Volcanic cinder cone and the highest point in the province of Sulu. Site of a battle in 1906; see Mindanao#Understand.

chunks.name: Jovellar
chunks.text: Jovellar is a landlocked municipality in the southwest quadrant of Albay in the Philippines and borders Donsol in the province of Sorsogon.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Once called Quipia after the river that flows down to Donsol, the town has been named after the Spanish Governor-General Joaquin Jovellar y Soler.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: There are buses from Manila to Jovellar, stopping also at other towns and cities along the way. To get to the town is through Guinobatan. There are a lot of jeepneys that ply that route.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Around the town center there are tricycles available heading to the outlying barangays.

chunks.name: Jovellar Underground River
chunks.text:
Dry caving and underground river adventure experience. Short hike are expected. There are caves and rock formations. Life jackets, local guides and boatmen are available.
hours: 7:30AM–5PM; address: Jovellar

chunks.name: Busay Falls
chunks.text: hours: Open 24 hours; address: Barangay Cabraran, Jovellar

chunks.name: Sigpit Falls
chunks.text: address: Quitinday

chunks.name: Jovellar Public Market
chunks.text: address: Jovellar Road, Mercado

chunks.name: Crispy King Jovellar Branch
chunks.text: address: Purok 5, Barangay Magsaysay

Legazpi - the vibrant capital city of Albay.
Ligao - a jeepney ride away from Jovellar.

chunks.name: Kabankalan
chunks.text: Kabankalan is a city in the province of Negros Occidental, Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: According to the 2015 census, it has a population of 182,000.

Ceres liner buses have their own bus terminal.
Ceres liner buses from Bacolod City 102 km. Buses every 30 min.
Ceres liner buses from Dumaguete City 114 km.
Ceres liner buses from Sipalay 66 km.

chunks.text:
Pating Cave

Magballo Falls
Augustina Falls

chunks.name: Kabayan
chunks.text: Kabayan is a municipality in the province of Benguet, Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Located at the triboundary region between Benguet, Nueva Vizcaya and Ifugao provinces, Kabayan is known for having the only-known mummies in the Philippines, which were created by the indigenous Ibaloi inhabitants using a lengthy and complicated process that involved smoking the corpses over certain types of leaves for months before depositing them in burial caves, hence their moniker, the Fire Mummies. Sadly, several of the mummies were stolen by grave robbers since the 20th century, with some of them still being sold on the black market. This has led to restrictions on access to the burial caves.

It is also the main base camp for hikers heading to Mount Pulag, the highest mountain in Luzon.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: There are two main roads leading to Kabayan from Baguio. One is through a junction leading south from Halsema Highway in Buguias town, while another is a junction from the Benguet-Nueva Vizcaya Road in Bokod leading north. There are bus, van and jeepney connections to the town from Baguio.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There are tricycles in town, but a 4WD or any vehicle suitable for mountain roads is best used. Most attractions in town are accessible following extended hikes.

chunks.name: Mount Pulag
chunks.text: At 2928 m, it is the second highest mountain in the Philippines, and the highest in Luzon. It also forms the triboundary between Nueva Vizcaya, Benguet and Ifugao.

chunks.name: National Museum of the Philippines - Kabayan
chunks.text:

chunks.name: Kalayaan (Laguna)
chunks.text: Kalayaan is a town in the province of Laguna in the Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Formerly known as Longos, it is one of the smallest towns in Laguna, having only three barangays: Longos (the old town center), San Juan (which has been the present town center since 1946), and San Antonio (an upland area stretching to the border with Quezon Province).

During the American period, the construction of the Caliraya Dam inundated parts of the town, in the long-term providing opportunities to set up campsites, fishing and glamping spots. However, this has also resulted in a three-way territorial dispute with the neighboring towns of Lumban and Cavinti over the eastern shores of the reservoir. The town was renamed as Kalayaan (Filipino for "Freedom") in 1956.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Kalayaan lies along the Manila East Road heading to Pagsanjan. Motorists from Manila either enter the town from the south via Pagsanjan and Lumban, or from the north via Rizal province and Siniloan.

Kalayaan lies along the Santa Cruz-Siniloan jeepney route.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
Tricycles are the main mode of transportation between barangays, although taking a jeepney between San Juan and Longos is cheaper by cheaper, ranging between P13-15.

While Longos and San Juan are accessible via Manila East Road, a trip to San Antonio and the Kalayaan side of Caliraya Lake involves passing through the winding two-lane Longos-San Antonio Road from its junction beside Petron gasoline station in Longos from Manila East Road.

chunks.name: Saint John the Baptist Parish Church
chunks.text:
The church was built in the 18th century but was neglected through much of the 20th century when it was downgraded into a chapel due to the government's decision to move the town center of Kalayaan from Longos to San Juan. After recovering its parish status in 1996, the church was gradually repaired. The church's façade, partially covered by moss complimented by the shrub-lined plaza in front, gives off a garden-like air. Its doors and carvings have been preserved from the Spanish era, while its interior has also been preserved save for the roof, which was rebuilt following typhoon damage in 2006. Among the interior's highlights is the botafumeiro or thurible, the ornate altar, and the bas reliefs in the baptistery. The church is also frequently used as a shooting location for domestic films and television series.
address: Esperanza Street, Longos

chunks.name: Kalibo
chunks.text: Kalibo is the capital of the province of Aklan, Philippines. It is a large town, with an airport that serves as the main gateway for Boracay, and a rich culture.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
"Kalibo" derives from Akeanon sang kalibo (one thousand), referring to the thousands of Ati (Negritos) who attended the first Catholic Mass in Panay. It was also named as Akean, from another Akeanon word. Kalibo was also spelled as Calivo during the Spanish era.

The town was inhabited by Akeanons, a people believed to have originated from Borneo and sailed into Panay. When the Spaniards under Miguel Lopéz de Legaspi arrived, Kalibo had a population of about 2,000. Lopéz de Legaspi hired about 500 of the locals to help him in the conquest of what would become the Philippines.

Kalibo was then part of Capiz. The town was where the Nine Martyrs of Aklan, a group of nine revolutionaries, were executed. Kalibo became part of Aklan after it was made its own province and was made its capital. It has since expanded to become a large town, with a population of 80,000

chunks.name: Understand / Talk
chunks.text: Akeanons speak their own language Akeanon (or Aklanon), but Ilonggo is also spoken as it's the lingua franca in Panay. Another Visayan language, Kinaray-a, is also spoken here.

chunks.name: Kalinga
chunks.text: Kalinga (pronounced as “Kaling-ga”) is a province in the Cordillera region of Luzon in the Philippines. Long feared for its tribal conflicts and headhunters, it is nowadays renowned for its natural and cultural attractions such as indigenous villages, whitewater rafting, unspoiled mountains and even an indigenous tattoo artist.

chunks.name: Understand / Geography
chunks.text:
Kalinga occupies over of land area, mostly mountainous terrain. The capital is Tabuk. The province occupies some of the highest peaks of the Cordillera Mountains.

The province is bounded on the south by Mountain Province, on the west by Abra, to the north by Apayao and to the east by Cagayan and Isabela.

chunks.name: Understand / People
chunks.text:
Kalinga is predominantly inhabited by the Kalinga, an Igorot subgroup whose name means "enemy" in the language of the neighboring Ibanag people of Cagayan Valley. They are then divided into various tribes and clans, some of whom get into conflict with each other over issues such as boundary disputes, resource sharing or slights against individual members, which requires intricate mediation under the traditional bodong system of customs and laws.

Long seen through the colonial era and much of the post-independence years as a “no-go zone” due to its reputation for being a hotbed of tribal warfare, headhunters and communist rebels, since the late 20th century, Kalinga has seen an influx of predominantly Ilocano migrants who have mostly settled in Tabuk and other lowland areas in the eastern part of the province.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text:
Kalinga's climate varies extensively. While the flat, grassy eastern plateau can be hot in summer, the western highlands have a more temperate climate due to its altitude.

Many visit the province during the dry season between March and May, where temperatures are at its highest but rainfall at its lowest. The rainy season is rather the same as with the rest of Luzon, but precipitation is somewhat higher, with the cool season from November to February also bringing in torrential rains. Heavy rain, especially those brought by typhoons, can cause seasonal road closures due to landslides and rockfalls.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
Archeological evidence suggests that Kalinga has long been settled as early as the prehistoric era, as seen by excavations of fossils from animals hunted down by humans in what is now Rizal town. Throughout the 17th to 19th centuries, the Spaniards based in Cagayan Valley tried to subjugate Kalinga with limited success. In retaliation, Kalinga tribes raided lowland villages and beheaded residents in headhunting raids.

During the Philippine-American War, the town of Lubuagan briefly became the capital of the First Philippine Republic in 1900. The Americans occupied Kalinga shortly afterwards and turned it into a subdistrict of the Mountain Province encompassing much of the Cordillera region in 1908.

In 1966, Kalinga was merged with Apayao subdistrict to became the province of Kalinga-Apayao. In the 1970s and 1980s, the area became a hotbed of rebellions led by the communist New People's Army and a Cordilleran separatist splinter group, the Cordillera People's Liberation Army (CPLA). At the same time, the Kalingas successfully resisted attempts by the dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos to build a large dam along the Chico River that would have inundated large large parts of the province.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text: After Marcos was overthrown in 1986, the government of president Corazon Aquino reached a peace agreement with the CPLA, leading to Kalinga-Apayao's transfer from the Cagayan Valley Region to the Cordillera Administrative Region in 1988. Despite being the CPLA's home base, Kalinga rejected autonomy for the Cordilleras in referendums in 1990 and 1998. Following a referendum in 1995, Kalinga-Apayao was dissolved into two separate provinces comprising its constituent halves.

chunks.name: Understand / Economy
chunks.text: Historically an agricultural and mining society, Kalinga's economy is gradually opening up to tourism in the 21st century, although the province's geography, poor infrastructure and bouts of tribal conflict and political instability make it challenging for large-scale tourist enterprises to take hold unlike in Baguio.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Kalinga is mainly accessed through roads from Tuguegarao and Tuao in Cagayan. The nearest airport is also in Tuguegarao. Apart from Metro Manila, the main transport hubs leading to Kalinga include Baguio, Bontoc in Mountain Province and Tuguegarao. There are secondary roads linking Kalinga with Isabela, Santiago City via Mountain Province and Ifugao, Apayao, Laoag and Vigan via Abra and Baguio via Bontoc.

Unlike other provinces, public transportation to Kalinga operates at an infrequent pace, with some transport companies offering only 1-2 daily trips to the province by transport companies and others operating a monopoly on select areas. There are direct bus services to Tabuk from Metro Manila, Baguio and Bontoc, while passenger vans to Tabuk can be taken from Tuguegarao.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
One can get around the province by public transportation such as jeepney, bus, and passenger van. Tricycles and tuktuks are used within towns.

Due to infrequent services, it is better to take a 4WD or any vehicle suitable for mountain roads. Many attractions are accessible following extended hikes.

Hitchhiking is common in the highland towns.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text:
Most visitors come to Kalinga either to do whitewater rafting along the Chico River or see Balbalasang National Park, an overlooked and mostly unclimbed stretch of the Cordillera mountains. Since the 2010s, a growing trend is to go to the isolated village of Buscalan and have a tattoo from Whang-Od, a centenarian woman from of the Butbut tribe who is known as the last indigenous tattoo artist (mambabatok) in the Cordilleras, although she continues to train apprentices from the village.

Kalinga is also known for its heritage villages of Naneng in Tabuk and Awichon in Lubuagan, offering visitors the chance to live like the natives.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: Partake in cultural activities such as pounding rice, community dances and listening to the chants of the indigenous songs and epics.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text:
Like the rest of the Cordilleras, Kalinga cuisine is comprised of highland rice, starch vegetables, game, and smoked meats.

Tabuk is the only place in Kalinga where there are mainstream restaurant chains.

chunks.name: Drink
chunks.text: Rice and sugarcane wines are the native drink. Another famous, albeit expensive option is civet coffee, which is derived from coffee beans ingested by the Asian palm civet (musang) and expelled afterwards as part of their excrement, giving off a distinct aroma and flavor following fermentation in the animal's stomach.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text: The bulk of tourist accommodation, including small and mid-size hotels, is in Tabuk. Most accommodation elsewhere consists of small inns, hostels or homestays.

chunks.name: Kasibu
chunks.text: Kasibu is a town in Nueva Vizcaya, Philippines. It is the province's "citrus capital" due to its extensive production of the fruit, and also has multiple natural attractions and indigenous tribes coexisting uneasily with one of the largest gold mining operations in the country.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
For much of its history, Kasibu was a small village inhabited by Ilongot (now known as Bugkalot) tribes along the headwaters of the Magat River along the Namamparang mountains separating Nueva Vizcaya from Quirino province. Since the 20th century, it has been one of the country's leading producers of oranges and other citrus fruits on account of its mild temperature, fertile soil and elevation.

Kasibu is an ethnically mixed town inhabited by Ilocano migrants, Bugkalot tribespeople and Igorots relocated there following the damming of several rivers along the Luzon Cordilleras in the 1970s. Its main economic activities are agriculture, ecotourism, and controversially, the extraction of gold and other precious minerals in Barangay Didipio by the Australian company OceanaGold since 1994, a topic that arouses intense debates in Nueva Vizcaya.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Kasibu is bypassed by the Maharlika Highway, the main thoroughfare in Nueva Vizcaya. Instead, it is connected to the road through a two-lane provincial roads linking the area from Bambang. The only forms of public transportation heading to town are jeepneys and tricycles. There are also rudimentary road connections from Solano via Quezon municipality, and Cabarroguis, the provincial capital of Quirino.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the most common transport between barangays, but due to uneven terrain, an SUV or any 4WD is recommended.

chunks.name: Capisaan Caves
chunks.text:
The fifth longest cave in the country at . It has layers of cave network including Lion and Alayan Caves with rare calcite formations and a subterranean river which doubles as a passageway to the best part of the cave. Brgy. Capisaan is about four hours by jeep from Solano on feeder and clay type soil road carved out of mountain sides. Tours can be arranged with the Sang-at-Salug Mountaineering Group or the Provincial Government of Nueva Vizcaya.

Another souvenir from Kasibu is mun-abol textiles made by indigenous weavers.

chunks.name: Kawit
chunks.text: Kawit is a municipality in Cavite. It is famous for being the place where Philippine independence was proclaimed in 1898 and for being the hometown of the Philippines' first president, Emilio Aguinaldo.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Kawit had a major role in the country's history during the 1800s and 1900s. Formerly known as Cavite el Viejo, it was the birthplace of Emilio Aguinaldo, the 1st President of the Philippines, who from 1895 to 1897, served as the municipality's chief executive. The Aguinaldo home, where independence from Spain was declared on June 12, 1898, is now called the Aguinaldo Shrine.

chunks.name: Understand / Orientation
chunks.text:
For purposes of navigation, Kawit is roughly divided into four districts. The old town proper is concentrated around Barangay Kaingin and consists of the coastal strip that is straddled by the Tirona and Magdiwang Highways leading to Noveleta. This is where Aguinaldo Shrine and Kawit Church are located. Zeus Junction divides Kaingin from Binakayan, a major residential and commercial district to the east leading to Bacoor that also straddles Tirona Highway.

In the 2020s, a new commercial hub has developed to the south along the Antero Soriano Highway in Barangay Gahak, where the municipal hall has relocated from Kaingin. This area is also where the big supermarkets and shopping malls are located. North of Binakayan is Island Cove, a sprawling private resort and green space that was controversially sold to Chinese investors in 2018 and turned into a drab concrete high-rise complex and gambling hub that closed in 2024 amid national security and criminality concerns.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Kawit is the terminus of the Manila-Cavite Expressway aka Coastal Road or CAVITEX. The ramp leads immediately to the chronically snarled Zeus Junction, which connects Binakayan Diversion Road, Tirona Highway and Antero Soriano Highway (Centennial Road) in Binakayan. Turn left if heading to Binakayan, right if heading to Aguinaldo Shrine, Kawit Church and Kaingin, straight if heading to Gahak, and a U-turn if heading to Island Cove. Construction is ongoing in the junction as part of plans to connect CAVITEX with the Cavite-Laguna Expressway (CALAX).

Buses heading to Noveleta and Cavite City from PITX in Parañaque, Metro Manila turn right at Tirona Highway towards Kaingin and pass beside and in front of Aguinaldo Shrine after looping around the compound and at the back of Kawit Church. Buses heading to Naic and Ternate pass through Antero Soriano Highway and Gahak.

Kawit lies along the baby bus route running between Bacoor and Cavite City/Naic. The baby buses share the same route with the regular buses depending on their terminus, although a dedicated line connects Bacoor and Binakayan. There is also a similar jeepney service running from Zapote to Binakayan. A less frequent service also connects Binakayan with Imus.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Baby buses connect Kaingin with Binakayan and Island Cove. Gahak is connected to Binakayan by baby bus and to Kaingin by tricycle. Transfers between routes usually occur at Zeus Junction.

chunks.name: Aguinaldo Shrine
chunks.text:
The sprawling house, built in 1849, is the ancestral home of Emilio Aguinaldo, the first President of the Philippines. It is now a museum. It is where independence from Spain was declared on June 12, 1898. The house’s balcony is where the Philippine president annually raises the Philippine flag on Independence Day.The basement has an exhibition dedicated to Aguinaldo’s life and role in the Philippine Revolution, while the upper floors, which contain Aguinaldo’s living quarters, focus on how the Aguinaldo family lived. The grounds of the house is lush with greenery bordered by a river on the east and backed by a fish pond to the south. Aguinaldo's grave lies at the backyard. A nearby outhouse sells souvenirs. Expect hordes of field-tripping schoolchildren from Metro Manila and nearby places on some days. In front of the house is Aguinaldo Park, which has an equestrian statue of Aguinaldo and stalls selling snacks and refreshments.
hours: 8AM–4PM; closed Mondays and holidays; price: Free, donation optional; address: 15, 52 Tirona Hwy, Barangay Kaingen

chunks.name: St. Mary Magdalene Church
chunks.text: One of the oldest churches in the Philippines, construction was started in 1737. It holds Emilio Aguinaldo's baptism certificate and has a finely crafted and gilded altarpiece. The image of its patron saint, Saint Mary Magdalene, has a peculiar mole on its forehead and is placed in a side altar.

chunks.name: Baldomero Aguinaldo Shrine
chunks.text:
An overlooked heritage house museum dedicated to President Aguinaldo's cousin, who held several positions in his cabinet and was also a distinguished military commander during the revolution. Baldomero and several of his relatives are buried at the backyard.
hours: 8AM–4PM; closed Mondays and holidays; price: Free, donation optional; address: Bisita St, Brgy. Balsahan-Bisita, Binakayan

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: Maytinis Festival — An original Kawit tradition that takes place every Christmas Eve, a dramatic retelling of the Virgin Mary and Joseph's search in Bethlehem for a place to stay called "Panunuluyan". This reenactment happens on the streets of Kawit with different floats depicting different biblical scenes from Adam and Eve up to Mary and Joseph. The "Panunuluyan" takes place in several houses and is done in singing until it reaches the 400-year-old St. Mary Magdalene Church, where the Virgin Mary and Joseph are welcomed by angels in a giant belen (Nativity Scene), which covers the whole main Retablo or altarpiece of the church. The songs performed by the angels acted by little girls are mostly in Spanish and Tagalog.

chunks.name: Kayapa
chunks.text: Kayapa is a town in Nueva Vizcaya, Philippines. Situated within the Cordillera Mountains, it is the main point of entry leading to the Cagayan Valley region from Baguio and is dubbed the “Summer Capital” of Nueva Vizcaya for its highland location and cool climate.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Nestled within the Cordillera Mountains, Kayapa is a geographically large town that runs through the length of Nueva Vizcaya (except for its southern panhandle). However, it has only a small population composed of Igorots due to its rugged terrain. It was one of the few places in Nueva Vizcaya that was not conquered by the Spanish. It frequently switched provinces between Benguet and Nueva Vizcaya before finally coming under the latter's jurisdiction during the American occupation in 1905.

Long overshadowed by neighboring Benguet, Kayapa is slowly developing its tourist potential as an alternative hiking and climbing spot to its neighbors in the Luzon Cordilleras. It is also the province’s “Vegetable Bowl” owing to its thriving agricultural sector focused on growing cabbages, potatoes, carrots and other staples.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Kayapa lies along the Benguet-Nueva Vizcaya Road. It is a winding two-lane thoroughfare that is vulnerable to blockages caused by landslides, vehicular accidents and vehicles sustaining mechanical breakdowns. There are few forms of public transportation to town apart from some jeepneys running from Bambang, Bayombong and other towns in lowland Nueva Vizcaya, and the passenger vans that connect Baguio with Nueva Vizcaya and Santiago City in Isabela.

From Maharlika Highway, take the junction in Aritao if coming from Metro Manila. From the north, there is an access road in Bambang leading west towards a junction with Benguet-Nueva Vizcaya Road in Barangay Pingkian.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There are tricycles in the downtown, but due to uneven terrain, an SUV or any 4WD is recommended. There are also jeepneys connecting downtown Kayapa with the outlying barangays.

chunks.name: Kayapa Quad Peak
chunks.text:
A nice loop hike that goes over the ridgeline of the four peaks in the area - Mt. Tugew, Mt. Kuban, Mt. Cabo, and Mt. Sadjatan, with an average elevation of 1460 m. The hike is around 13 km long and takes approximately 5-6 hours, excluding breaks. The starting point is at the Alang-Salacsac Barangay Hall. A guide, available at the barangay hall, is required, in addition to the entry and environmental fees. The barangay also provides some food after the hike, for a price.
address: Alang Salacsac

chunks.name: Kiangan
chunks.text: Kiangan is a town in Ifugao, a province in the Cordillera mountain range in the north of the island of Luzon, in the Philippines. One of the province's cultural capitals, it is famous for its rice terraces and for being the site of Japanese general Tomoyuki Yamashita's surrender at the end of World War II.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Situated on its eponymous valley, Kiangan has long been a major settlement since precolonial times and is regarded as the cradle of Ifugao civilization. During the Spanish era, it was the capital of the Kiangan military district, the predecessor of today's Ifugao province, but was never fully occupied due to the strong indigenous resistance that sometimes drove the Spanish out.

The Americans pacified Kiangan and were able to manage their occupation better, but during the closing days of World War II, it became the final redoubt of the Japanese forces led by the feared General Tomoyuki Yamashita, the "Tiger of Malaya", who surrendered to Allied forces on September 2, 1945 and was subsequently hauled down to the lowlands for his trial and execution for war crimes.

In 1949, Kiangan lost its status as provincial capital to neighboring Lagawe.

In 1995, a section of the town's Rice Terraces in barangay Nagacadan was included in the UNESCO World Heritage Listing of the Rice Terraces of the Cordilleras.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Kiangan is at the crossroads of two of Ifugao's major highways, namely the Nueva Vizcaya-Ifugao-Mountain Province Road, which is traversed by buses from Metro Manila, and the Tinoc-Kiangan-Lagawe Road, which connects Ifugao with Halsema Highway in neighboring Benguet province. The junction for these roads is near the Ibulao Bridge marking Kiangan's eastern boundary with Lagawe, the capital of Ifugao. Downtown Kiangan lies further west along the Tinoc Road.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There are tricycles in town, but a 4WD or any vehicle suitable for mountain roads is best used. Most attractions in town are accessible following extended hikes.

chunks.name: La Trinidad (Benguet)
chunks.text: La Trinidad is a small town which serves as the capital of the province of Benguet which is part of the Cordillera Administrative Region of the Philippines. Tourists to the town mostly come from the neighboring city of Baguio.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: La Trinidad is the capital town of the province of Benguet and is north of the bigger and more popular tourist destination of Baguio. Efforts to promote tourism in Baguio often includes sites that are actually in the town of La Trinidad, especially the Betag Strawberry Farm making the town a detour destination for many tourist visiting Baguio.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Tourists can enter La Trinidad via jeepney from the nearby city of Baguio in the south.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Jeepneys serve passengers in La Trinidad except in most remote areas of the town. Motorized tricycles is another mode of public transportation used in the town.

chunks.name: Colors of StoBoSa
chunks.text:
Inspired by the favela paintings in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, it is a community artwork formed by paintwork of about two hundred houses in the sitios of Stonehill, Botiwtiw, and Sadjap. It was conceptualized by local artist troupe, Tam-awan Artist Village and was painted by residents of the area as well as volunteers.
address: Stonehill, Botiwtiw, and Sadjap Sitios in Barangay Balili.

chunks.name: Bell Church
chunks.text:
A Chinese temple situated in Barangay Balili in La Trinidad. It features Chinese architecture and is a known place of worship for Chinese residents and tourists. It is located near the town's boundary with Baguio.
price: Free; address: Barangay Balili

chunks.name: La Trinidad Strawberry Festival

chunks.name: La Trinidad Strawberry Farm

chunks.name: La Union
chunks.text: La Union, also known as L.U. in short, is a province in the Ilocos region of the Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
La Union is a relatively new province, having been formed in 1850 from the southernmost towns of Ilocos Sur, the westernmost towns of Benguet, and the northernmost towns of Pangasinan. True to its name, meaning “the Union” in Spanish, the region is a melting pot of Pangasinan, Ilocano and Cordilleran (Igorot) cultures. Since the early 2000s, L.U. (as the province is called informally) has a growing tourism industry centered on the coastal towns facing the South China Sea (West Philippine Sea).

Despite the majority of the province being formed out of parts of Pangasinan, Ilocanos now form the majority of the population. The province is also the first in the Philippines to declare a regional language as co-official with English and Filipino (Tagalog), having declared Ilocano as an official language in the province since 2012.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: With the end of rail service in the 1980s, the only main way of reaching La Union is by bus or car. There is one airport at San Fernando, but has no commercial passenger service.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: Buses are available from Manila, Baguio, Dagupan, Vigan and Laoag, running up to San Fernando. Premium express buses are also available from the new bus station at Bocaue, Bulacan.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text:
With the completion of the Tarlac-Pangasinan-La Union Expressway (TPLEX) in 2020, travel times to La Union has been reduced to about 4-5 hours. The expressway ends in Rosario town, on the boundary with Benguet and Pangasinan, but there are plans to extend the highway up to San Fernando.

From the Cordilleras and interior towns, the primary routes are Naguilian Road (Route 54) and the Jose S. Aspiras Highway (Route 208, formerly but still often called Marcos Highway), both radiating from Baguio. Both routes are winding mountain roads and are quite dangerous.

For the coastal towns, the primary road links are Manila North Road (Route 2) and Pangasinan-La Union Road (Route 55).

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There is frequent bus service along the Manila North Road corridor, but other parts of L.U. are only served by occasional jeepneys. Getting around by car is recommended.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text: Most travelers think that L.U. is simply the beaches of San Juan. But beyond this small stretch of sand swarmed by daytrippers from Metro Manila and Baguio, the province has more destinations to offer such as quieter beaches in other towns, pilgrimage sites such as in Agoo and Luna, grape farms in Bauang, and extensions of the Cordillera mountains in the inland towns.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: Learn to surf on the black volcanic sand beaches of La Union. While the waves aren't Hawaii by any stretch of the imagination, the gently sloping beaches provide a steady supply of trainer waves. Seasoned surfers will yawn and stay in the bar. You can also enjoy beaches in San Fernando like in the 5-star Thunderbird resort, Sea Park and you can also go shopping at Manna Mall and CSI.

chunks.name: Drink
chunks.text: You can enjoy drinking in bars while singing in a local videoke.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text: Most tourist accommodation can be found along the coastal towns, particularly in San Fernando, San Juan and Bauang.

chunks.name: Labo
chunks.text: Labo is a municipality in Camarines Norte, Philippines, known for its rich agricultural heritage, scenic mountains, waterfalls, and the Busig-on River. Its culture and natural resources are celebrated through local festivals, particularly the Busig-on Festival, reflecting the creativity, traditions, and warm hospitality of the Laboeños.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The town traces its roots to an early settlement traditionally known as Busog-on, which flourished around its rivers and fertile lands. Local history tells of the community being led by Tarik-Kudook, a local chieftain.

The municipality's name, Labo, is traditionally associated with a story from the Spanish period involving a missionary who asked about the name of the place. A local boatman reportedly answered, “Labo po ng tubig,” referring to the unclear or muddy river water. The name eventually became associated with the settlement.

Labo was formally established as a municipality on September 8, 1800. Over the years, it developed as an agricultural and resource-rich community, benefiting from its extensive forests, rivers, fertile lands, and mineral deposits.

Today, Labo is one of the largest municipalities in Camarines Norte, known for its rich natural resources, majestic mountains, rivers, waterfalls, agricultural landscapes, and vibrant cultural traditions. Its history reflects the enduring connection between its people, land, water, and community—heritage that continues to shape Labo's identity and future.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: The town is accessible by bus from Manila, Daet, and other major cities via the Maharlika Highway, with buses bound for Daet stopping in Labo.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text: Labo, Camarines Norte is accessible via the Maharlika Highway (AH26), approximately 16 kilometers from Daet and about 326 kilometers from Manila.

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text: By plane, fly to Naga Airport () in Pili, Camarines Sur, the nearest airport with scheduled flights, then continue by land to Labo, Camarines Norte.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Jeepneys and tricycles are abundant in downtown. They can take you to the outlying barangays.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text:
Labo People's Park (public recreational space in the heart of Labo, Camarines Norte, where residents and visitors can relax, enjoy community activities, and experience the town’s vibrant local atmosphere.)
Labo Convention Center (multi-purpose venue in Labo, Camarines Norte, designed to host seminars, conferences, meetings, cultural programs, and various community events.)
Amphitheater (open-air public venue in Labo, Camarines Norte, designed for cultural performances, festivals, community gatherings, and special events. It provides a spacious setting where residents and visitors can enjoy local celebrations, entertainment, and activities that showcase the vibrant culture and community spirit of Labo. St. John the Apostle and Evangelist (a historic Catholic church in Labo, Camarines Norte, serving as an important place of worship and community gathering. It stands as a significant part of Labo’s religious heritage, where locals and visitors come together for Masses, religious celebrations, and traditional festivities.)
Hagdang Bato (historic site in Labo, Camarines Norte, once serving as a port where merchants came to trade their goods. It is also believed to be the resting place of the “Kampanang Bato,” a stone bell said to have been sunk in the Labo River during the Spanish period.)
Battle of Tigbinan Shrine (commemorates the historic World War II battle fought from December 17–23, 1941.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text:
Filipino soldiers, USAFFE forces, and local guerrillas bravely resisted the advancing Japanese forces, delaying their advance into Southern Luzon. The shrine honors their courage, sacrifice, and role in Labo’s wartime history.)
Labo Central Terminal (the main transportation hub in Labo, Camarines Norte, serving passengers traveling by buses, vans, jeepneys, and other public vehicles to nearby towns and cities. It provides convenient access to Labo and helps connect the municipality with other parts of Camarines Norte and the Bicol Region.)

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text:
Visit Malatap Falls – Enjoy the refreshing waterfalls and surrounding greenery.
Explore Binuang Falls – Discover its cascading waters and peaceful natural surroundings. Binuang Falls
Hike Mount Cadig – Experience a mountain adventure and scenic views around Bayabas.
Visit Mount Bagacay – Take in the mountain scenery and natural landscape of Labo.
Explore Labo People's Park – Relax, take photos, and enjoy a leisurely visit in the town center.
Discover Maligaya Falls – Enjoy the natural beauty of this waterfall in Barangay Submakin. Maligaya Falls
Explore Mt. Cadig Cave – Discover one of Labo's natural cave attractions with proper local guidance and safety precautions.
Visit Eco Park Bagong Silang I – Spend time surrounded by greenery and enjoy a nature-oriented outdoor experience.
Experience the Busig-On Festival – Celebrate Labo's culture, traditions, and community through its annual festival activities.
Taste Local Food – Explore Labo's local dining scene and sample Bicolano-inspired dishes and other local specialties.

chunks.name: Eusebia Restaurant
chunks.text:
Filipino dishes and casual dining along Maharlika Highway.
hours: Closes 7:30PM; price: ₱500; address: 2nd Floor, Don Juan Bldg 2, Maharlika Hwy
