chunks.name: Macabebe
chunks.text: Macabebe is a municipality in the province of Pampanga, Philippines. It is a primarily commercial and fishing town at the edge of the Pampanga River delta. The guide also covers the municipality of Masantol, which is almost surrounded by Macabebe and is mainly accessible through it.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Meaning "surrounded by waters" in Kapampangan, a reference to its location on the Pampanga River delta, Macabebe is one of the oldest towns in Pampanga, having hosted a community of indigenous warriors that resisted Spanish explorers during their conquest of Luzon in 1571 and was conquered by the Spanish shortly later. Paradoxically, Macabebe supplied loyal auxiliaries to the Spanish colonizers up to the Philippine Revolution. When the Philippine-American War broke out, the town was burned by Filipino republican forces as part of their scorched-earth retreat from the Americans and partially in revenge for the residents' alleged history of disloyalty. In retaliation, Macabebe supplied auxiliaries and scouts to US forces and contributed in the capture of President Emilio Aguinaldo and the collapse of the First Philippine Republic in 1901. They eventually had their own Scouts unit in the US Army during the American occupation.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Since the 21st century, a combination of factors such as climate change, rising sea levels, typhoons, high tide, improper land conversion and excessive groundwater extraction have irreversibly submerged numerous barangays and triggered ground subsidence in other areas of town, resulting in an increase of abandoned homes and edifices surrounded by brackish estuarine water. Looking at maps of Macabebe and Masantol, one could be forgiven to think that both towns eerily resemble Venice, with thinly-stretched settlements gathered around spider web-like roads that double as dikes and fishpond fences stretching southwards into Manila Bay, where many barangays are in danger of disappearing altogether.

chunks.name: First North Luzon Terminal
chunks.text: address: Apalit-Macabebe-Masantol Road, Santa Rita, Macabebe

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
The main entry point into Macabebe and Masantol is a two-lane highway that begins from a junction with MacArthur Highway in downtown Apalit and continues south towards downtown Macabebe and Masantol. There are also secondary roads that connect the towns from Calumpit and Hagonoy in neighboring Bulacan province as well as from Minalin in Pampanga. From Manila, the nearest exits of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) to Macabebe via Apalit are San Simon and Pulilan exits.

Both Macabebe and Masantol are connected to the provincial capital San Fernando through jeepneys and minibuses. In Macabebe, the main terminal is in front of Macabebe Church, while the terminal in Masantol is at the back of Masantol Church. There is also a daily bus service to Masantol from Cubao in Metro Manila operated by First North Luzon Transit.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of land-based transportation between barangays, while outlying areas may require boats such as the western and southern areas of Macabebe and areas south of downtown Masantol. During times of flooding, specifically the rainy season and heavy thunderstorms coupled with high tide, boats are sometimes necessary even in both downtown Macabebe and Masantol.

chunks.name: San Nicolas de Tolentino Parish Church
chunks.text:
Macabebe's main Roman Catholic church, rebuilt in its original Baroque style in 1904 after it was burned by nationalist forces during the Philippine-American War in 1899. The arson also saw the massacre of 300 residents accused of treason, which explains Macabebe’s subsequent support for the Americans. Despite its relative youth compared to other colonial churches, the place retains a dated air and much artifacts and ornaments expected of an old church, including the pulpit.
address: Macabebe Plaza, Santa Cruz

chunks.name: Macabebe Ecopark
chunks.text:

address: Consuelo

chunks.name: Maddela
chunks.text: Maddela (pronounced "mad-dela") is a municipality in Quirino.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Maddela was originally an Ilongot settlement named Pinappagan, literally a place where payment was made, either a reference to its position as a trading site, or as a local legend says, a place were transgressors paid for their offenses with blood under tribal laws.

The town was renamed Maddela in 1950, the same year it became a municipality through the help of a congressman of Nueva Vizcaya (which then ruled over present-day Quirino) who pushed for its status and now shares his surname with the town in recognition for his efforts. It used to cover two-thirds of Quirino's land area until 1983, when much of its southern portion was separated to create the municipality of Nagtipunan.

chunks.text: address: Magsaysay Street, Poblacion Sur

chunks.name: Northern Luzon Bus Line
chunks.text: address: Cordon-Diffun-Aurora Road, Poblacion Sur

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Maddela is at a junction between Cordon-Diffun-Aurora Road, the main thoroughfare in Quirino, and the Maddela-Echague Road which leads to Cauayan in Isabela province and its airport. There are passenger vans connecting the town with Santiago, while the bus from Santiago City to Dinapigue via Aurora also passes through town. Five Star and Northern Luzon Bus Line (NLBL) have bus terminals in town offering once a day services to and from Metro Manila.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of public transportation within town.

chunks.name: Governor's Rapids Nature Park
chunks.text:
Maddela's main tourist draw, it is an undisturbed section of the Cagayan River that was named after a Japanese officer who drowned in the area during World War II. It is a popular swimming, rafting and caving venue.

chunks.name: Magalang
chunks.text: Magalang is a town in northern Pampanga, Philippines. Situated at the foot of Mount Arayat and the border with Tarlac province, it combines cultural heritage, agrarian settings and natural wonders within its territory, despite encroaching urbanization from nearby Angeles.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
First mentioned as part of Arayat in 1598, it became a separate town in 1605. It has long been an agricultural town that had its fair share of peasant revolts, major battles and insurgencies throughout Philippine history, along with having the unsavory distinction of hosting the first recorded serial killer in the Philippines, Father Juan Severino Mallari, who murdered 57 people when he was the town's parish priest in the early 19th century before he was caught and executed. In 1863, the town of Concepcion was separated from Magalang and became part of the newly-created province of Tarlac.

Magalang is also the site of one of the oldest agricultural schools in the Philippines, the Pampanga State Agricultural University (PSAU), which traces its roots to 1885. During the 20th century, it became a commuter town of Angeles City following the expansion of the American military presence at Clark Field. In 1991, Magalang sustained relatively moderate damage from ashfall caused by the eruption of Mount Pinatubo. Since then, PSAU has hosted the main monitoring station for activity relating to the volcano.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
From Manila, take a right turn at the Angeles exit of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX). Capillary roads also connect Magalang with Mabalacat, Arayat, Santa Ana, and San Fernando via Mexico, and Concepcion in Tarlac.

Magalang is also served by regular jeepneys from Marquee Mall in Angeles, along with less frequent ones from Robinsons Starmills in San Fernando and morning-only routes from Arayat. Fares from Angeles cost P17.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of transportation in town.

chunks.name: San Bartolome Apostol Parish Church
chunks.text:
Magalang's main Roman Catholic church, built in its present style in 1866.
address: E. Baluyut Street, San Nicolas 1st

chunks.name: Heliograph Tower
chunks.text:
An obelisk-like structure built by the Spanish to serve as a "sun telegraph" that transmitted Morse code messages using the sun's rays. It is one of a few remains of an extensive Spanish military communications and watchtower system in Central Luzon and was later used to store and manufacture sugar.
address: Phase I, Santa Cruz

One of a few civic buildings in the Philippines that survive from the American occupation, dating back to the 1920s.

chunks.name: Magalawa Island
chunks.text: Magalawa is one of the 19 barangays in the municipality of Palauig, Province of Zambales, Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
According to the latest census, it has a population of 370 people in 71 households.

In the early century, Magalawa was a part of Sitio Luan, Barangay Lipay. The said sitio was bisected by a small body of water fordable by people wherein the current flows southeast during high tide and northward during low tide. The current that runs in this area is about 2-3 knots. In that situation erosion made this body of water wider and wider, which later on became a sea. This came when this part of the land was isolated far from Sitio Luan, so the inhabitants called in their native word "mag-luwa" that means "about two places". This word passed through generation to generation and was later changed to "Magalawa".

Magalawa is an island lying 6 km northwest of Poblacion. Surrounding the island is the China Sea. Beyond the north is the San Salvador Island of Masinloc and on the east is Sitio Luan, Lipay. It is known for beautiful beaches. Magalawa is 56 hectares in area.

Although the island is surrounded by the sea potable water is abundant on the island. The main source of livelihood is fishing and some are engaged in shell craft industry. There is a primary school with two teachers. No rice is planted in this area, so people resort to buying everything they need except fish. Coco trees and century trees are abundant.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Magalawa Island is now one of the newest tourist destination in Zambales. An eco-tourism resort, Magalawa Island Armada Resort, a privately owned resort, has been developed since 2009 and now continually on its rise with its back to basic and nature trip settings. To generate livelihood to the island community, management of the Armada Resort have come up with packages which include meals, snorkeling, rafting, boat riding, mangrove trekking. These helps the community in providing livelihood and help generate income for its barangay and municipality.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text: Magalawa Island Armada Resort - with its creamy white sand beaches and pristine waters Magalawa Island is perfect for swimming, water/sand sports, boat riding, jet skiing, scuba diving, snorkelling or just relaxing on the beach amid the crystal clear waters and white sand. Another attractions of Magalawa Island are coral reefs, mangroves and abundant water resources.

chunks.name: Magallanes (Sorsogon)
chunks.text:
For other places by the name, see Magallanes (disambiguation).
Magallanes is a municipality of the province of Sorsogon.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: According to renowned historians and anthropologists such as Domingo Abella, Luis Camara Dery, Merito Espinas, F. Mallari, Norman Owen, Mariano Goyena del Prado, et al., Magallanes was the location of the ancient settlement of Ibalong.

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text: Book a flight from Manila to Bicol International Airport. From Legazpi, ride a van or bus to Sorsogon City (approx. 1.5 to 2 hours).

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text: Take a provincial bus (such as Philtranco, DLTB, or Cagsawa Travel) bound for Sorsogon City from terminals in Metro Manila (like Pasay, Cubao, or Alabang). The trip takes about 12 to 14 hours.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Jeepneys and tricycles are available in downtown.

Marked as the historic site of the first Christian mass in Luzon.

chunks.name: Magdalena (Laguna)
chunks.text:
For other places by the name, see Magdalena.
Magdalena is a town in the province of Laguna in the Philippines. Situated at the transition zone between the province's lakeside lowlands and the foothills of the Sierra Made and Mount Banahaw, it is dubbed as the "Little Hollywood of Laguna" due to it being a favorite shooting location for domestic television shows and films.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Magdalena was founded during the Spanish era in 1820. Formerly a barrio of Majayjay known as Ambling, it was renamed after its patron saint, Mary Magdalene. The town became a major battleground during the Philippine wars of independence against Spain and the United States, and is commonly associated with Emilio Jacinto, a revolutionary hero who commanded Filipino forces in the area.

Magdalena's reputation as a filming location began in the 1970s, when it was used as a setting for historical and spaghetti western like films about local Robin Hood figures starring action hero Fernando Poe Jr. Since then, Magdalena has been used as a stand-in for domestic films set in the colonial-era, although the town retains a dated air and a quiet atmosphere unlike its neighboring towns.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Magdalena is situated at the southern terminus of F.T. San Luis Avenue, a two-lane provincial road running from Sambat Junction, along the Calamba-Pagsanjan Road in Pagsanjan. Magdalena is also the northern terminus of the Liliw-Magdalena Road for those heading from San Pablo. Before entering the downtown, the road forks into two directions in Barangay Burlungan, with a right turn leading to Majayjay.

The main public transportation routes into Magdalena are the jeepneys running from the provincial capital Santa Cruz via Sambat Junction to Magdalena, Majayjay and Nagcarlan via Liliw. It also has a dedicated jeepney line from Santa Cruz whose terminal in Magdalena is at the intersection of Bonifacio and Mabini Streets, near the Alfamart convenience store and at the back of Magdalena Church. A one-way fare costs PHP25.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main mode of transportation between barangays.

chunks.name: Saint Mary Magdalene Parish Church
chunks.text:
Magdalena's Roman Catholic church was built in the Baroque style and features an austere and unplastered facade and interior, along with a statue of Saint Mary Magdalene seemingly bleeding through her eyes while she holds a skull. Its main claim to fame is being a convalescent home for Filipino revolutionary hero Emilio Jacinto during the war of independence against the Spanish, with a small monument in the adjacent convent showing where drops of his blood fell, although the stains have faded away. The church faces the town plaza and the municipal hall, both of which have been preserved from the colonial era.The front steps leading to the church may be too steep and narrow for some visitors. An alternative option is to approach the building from the jeepney terminal at the back of the structure and walk past Magdalena Mini Park, where the ground is flat, towards the church’s side entrance.
address: Poblacion

chunks.name: Magdalena Town Plaza
chunks.text: An extensive public square with a small garden, a monument to national hero Jose Rizal, and a busts gallery of former mayors in front of the municipal hall. Flanked by the Spanish-era parish church and the American-era municipal hall, the grounds were laid out according to a design established during the colonial era, which explains why the area is a favorite filming shoot. There is a Walk of Fame commemorating actors who visited Magdalena, but the plaques containing their names have faded away due to neglect.

chunks.name: Magdalena Municipal Cemetery
chunks.text:
The town's cemetery, built in 1938, is also a common filming location due to its old design and the original arch at its entrance.
address: F.T. San Luis Avenue, Salasad

chunks.name: Magdalena Mini Park & Children's Playground
chunks.text:
A small park with a Hollywood-like sign of Magdalena, statues of superheroes and animals, including Monstro the Sperm Whale from Pinocchio.
address: Bonifacio Street, Poblacion

chunks.name: Balanac Dam
chunks.text:
An irrigation dam along the Pagsanjan River that is a favorite swimming spot for locals during the summer months.
address: Munting Ambling

chunks.name: Magdalena Public Market
chunks.text: address: Burgos corner Bernardo Streets, Ilayang Butnong

chunks.name: Magsingal
chunks.text: Magsingal (pronounced as “Magsing-gal”) is a coastal town in Ilocos Sur.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Magsingal is one of the oldest towns in Ilocos Sur, having been founded by the Spanish in 1576.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Magsingal is along Route 2 (Manila North Road). Buses heading to Laoag also ply this highway, with some bus companies operating limited direct services from Metro Manila.

The nearest cruise ship terminal is in Salomague Port in Cabugao, 17 km to the north.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of transportation in town, particularly as downtown Magsingal is further inland from the coast.

chunks.name: Saint William the Hermit Parish Church
chunks.text:
Magsingal's main Roman Catholic church, built in a Baroque style during the Spanish period in 1827. It was declared a National Cultural Treasure by the Philippine government in 2001.
address: Manila North Road, San Vicente

chunks.name: Magsingal Municipal Hall
chunks.text:
The seat of local government in Magsingal, built to resemble a Spanish-era government building.
address: Manila North Road, San Julian

chunks.name: Magsingal Belfry
chunks.text:
Magsingal Church's belfry predates the actual church building by about 100 years. It also functioned as a watchtower guarding against pirates and foreign invaders. The belfry and the adjoining convent are part of the National Museum-Ilocos Region and was declared a National Cultural Treasure by the Philippine government in 2001.
address: Manila North Road, San Vicente

chunks.name: Puro Pinget Island
chunks.text: Not really an island but rather a round peninsula connected to mainland Magsingal by the narrow Puro Sandbar. It contains white sand beaches and a large concentration of beach resorts.

chunks.name: Magsingal Public Market
chunks.text: address: Manila North Road, San Lucas

chunks.name: Pagsanaan Beach Resort
chunks.text: address: Pagsanaan Sur

Resort near the Puro Sandbar.

chunks.name: Manzante Farm House
chunks.text: address: Manzante

chunks.name: Majayjay
chunks.text: Majayjay (pronounced as “mah-high-HIGH”) is a highland town in the province of Laguna in the Philippines. Situated at the northern slopes of Mount Banahaw, it is known for its waterfalls, Spanish-era bridges and Romanesque Catholic basilica.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Majayjay is one of the oldest known settlements in Laguna, having existed even before the Spanish occupation. Its name derives from the tired expression (hayhay) locals gave when traveling to the town, which involved hiking through dense woodlands and ascending the foothills of Mount Banahaw.

Majayjay’s cool weather made it a summer capital for both Spanish and American colonizers, predating Baguio. At the same time, its secluded location turned Majayjay into a bastion of anti-colonial nationalists during the Philippine wars of independence and communist rebels in the late 20th and early 21st centuries.

The town proper is crisscrossed by four rivers that form the Pagsanjan River system, necessitating the construction of multiple bridges in the area during the Spanish occupation.

chunks.name: Majayjay Transport Cooperative
chunks.text:
Majayjay's central terminal, though crude-looking, is well-organized and offers services to Lucban, Luisiana, Santa Cruz via Magdalena, and Nagcarlan via Liliw. Be prepared to wait for the jeep to fill up.
address: Ordoñez Street, Poblacion

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Majayjay is situated at a crossroads between Laguna and Quezon Province. To the east, there are roads leading to Luisiana and Lucban. To the north is the road to Santa Cruz via Magdalena and Sambat Junction in Pagsanjan. To the west is Liliw, where transfers to San Pablo can be made.

Majayjay is fairly off the beaten track, with jeepneys not as frequent as in the rest of Laguna. Case in point, jeepneys coming from Santa Cruz are regularly full upon departure, mostly packed with returning residents. Waiting in Magdalena for the jeep to Majayjay can take up to an hour. If you are not planning to stay overnight in Majayjay, make sure to leave town before the late afternoon.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
Tricycles are the main mode of transportation between barangays.

Driving in Majayjay is not for the faint-hearted. The highways are of the two-lane variety and traverse mountainous and sometimes winding terrain, while many secondary roads are in fair to poor condition. Some roads in the town center are one-way only.

chunks.name: Minor Basilica and Parish of Saint Gregory the Great
chunks.text:
The only Catholic basilica in Laguna and a national cultural treasure, Majayjay's church burned several times during the Spanish era, with the last being in 1711. Instead of razing the structure, its priest instead ordered the ruins to be encased inside a 3 m-thick layer of brick and plastered in pink, resulting the façade exuding a fortress-like aura. The interior contains an ornate altar and an upper-level catwalk that rings the space. Unlike most Spanish-era churches in the Philippines, the basilica was built in the Romanesque style. The parish office sells some souvenirs.
address: F. Blumentritt Street, Poblacion

chunks.name: Tulay Pigi
chunks.text:
In the 19th century, a Spanish priest ordered his parishioners to build a bridge connecting Majayjay and Magdalena over the Pagsanjan River. He treated his workers badly and frequently whipped them in the buttocks, hence its name (Tulay Pigi literally means Buttocks Bridge, while Puente del Capricho literally means Bridge of Caprice). This ultimately backfired, and the bridge was left unfinished as Majayjay was depopulated by residents fleeing from the priest's abuses. The bridge's overgrown state and missing span, which was later filled with a steel contraption, is best admired from the bottom of the structure.
address: Ordoñez corner Limquico Streets, Poblacion

chunks.name: Taytay Falls
chunks.text:
The most visited waterfall in Majayjay, with a height of 15 m.
address: Taytay (Gagalot)

chunks.name: Dalitiwan Stream
chunks.text:
A cold stream running from Mount Banahaw. At the gorge surrounding Dalitiwan Bridge are two resorts allowing access to the stream and partially channeling the waters to create man-made cascades and rock pools.
address: Majayjay-Lucban Road, Ilayang Banga

chunks.name: Nuestra Señora de la Porteria Chapel
chunks.text:
An 18th-century chapel containing a venerated image of the Virgin Mary.
address: Arellano corner F. Blumentritt Streets, Poblacion

chunks.name: Old Presidencia
chunks.text:
Majayjay's colonial era municipal hall burned down sometime in the 20th century and was abandoned in favor of a new site near Majayjay Church. Nevertheless, the old building's shell remains as an imposing ruin, with the stairs and parts of its portico still intact.
address: Calles corner Zamora Streets, Poblacion

chunks.name: Nuestra Señora de Porteria Grotto
chunks.text:
Placed beside the Olla (Santa Cruz) river, this was where the Nuestra Señora de Porteria image was originally thought to have been placed before the chapel in the town center was built.
address: F.E. Gozo Street, San Miguel

A privately-owned zoo with more than 900 animals in the woods outside town.
hours: Tue-Sun 9AM - 4PM, closed Mondays; price: Adults: ₱345, concessions: ₱295, group discounts also available; address: Liliw-Majayjay Road, Coralao

A waterfall at the boundary of Majayjay and Liliw that is claimed by both municipalities.
address: Bukal

chunks.name: Sprite Falls

Another set of waterfalls upstream from the Dalitiwan Bridge.
address: Piit

chunks.name: Mount Banahaw
chunks.text: An inactive volcano straddling the provinces of Laguna and Quezon. At 2170 m, it is the highest mountain in the Calabarzon region, and a sacred monument for the Tagalog people.

chunks.name: Majayjay Public Market
chunks.text: address: Balagtas Street, Poblacion

chunks.name: Dali Everyday Grocery
chunks.text: address: Blumentritt Street, Origuel

chunks.name: Hilarion’s Farm
chunks.text: address: Majayjay-Lucban Road, Ilayang Banga

chunks.name: La Triccias Resort Hotel, Events and Restaurant

chunks.name: Makati
chunks.text: Makati lies in the heart of Metro Manila. The city is known for its upscale shopping malls with high fashion brands, restaurants and hotels, and is home to many affluent Filipinos. Makati is considered to be a financial, commercial and economic center; it is home to the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE).

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
The area of Makati City was first dismissed as worthless swampland by the Spanish conquistador Juan Miguel de Legazpi in 1571. In 1670 it was established as a visita of Sta. Ana de Sapa under the Franciscans. The friars established one of their earliest churches in the Philippines, the Church of Sts. Peter and Paul, in Makati, drawing pilgrims from all over the country. At the opening of the 20th century, the Americans established Fort McKinley in Makati. In the 1930s, the first airport, Nielson Airport, opened in what is now the Ayala Triangle. The first centrally planned community was established in the 1950s, and since the 1970s Makati has been the undisputed financial and commercial capital.

Makati has also figured prominently in the political history of the country. The community was one of the cradles of the revolt against Spanish colonial rule, and following the assassination of Ninoy Aquino in 1983, it was the epicenter of the protest movement against the dictatorial rule of Ferdinand Marcos.

chunks.name: Ayala Station
chunks.text:
Serves Ayala Center. Station is connected by overhead walkways to One Ayala, the BGC Bus Ayala terminal and SM Makati. There are some food kiosks before the turnstiles.
address: EDSA, Ayala Center

chunks.name: Buendia station
chunks.text:
Connects with Buendia stop on the EDSA Carousel and jeepneys headed for the CBD from a terminal outside the Bel-Air gated community. Escalator and stairs are present on site. No food establishment at the station but there's a nearby Shell with Jollibee and Mercury Drug store as their landmark.
address: EDSA corner Gil Puyat Ave

chunks.name: Guadalupe station
chunks.text:
Connects with the Guadalupe stop of the EDSA Carousel under the MRT bridge immediately north of the station. Jeepneys to Poblacion are available from nearby terminals at Guadalupe Market (aka "Guadalupe ABC") and Bernardino St
address: EDSA, Guadalupe Nuevo

chunks.name: Get in / By train
chunks.text:
The MRT Line 3 (MRT-3) elevated train has four stations along EDSA. These are the Guadalupe, Buendia, Ayala and Magallanes stations. Getting off at the Ayala Station will set you in the middle of the Ayala Center, a complex of shopping malls and restaurants.

MRT-3 is a quick and inexpensive way to get into the city. The cost of a ticket ranges from ₱13-16.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text:
Two of Metro Manila's main arteries pass through Makati. EDSA (Epifanio de los Santos Avenue) passes along the southeast part of Makati and connects the city with Mandaluyong and Pasay. The South Luzon Expressway (SLEX) runs through the western part of Makati and connects the city with Manila to the north and with southern Metro Manila. The Skyway, an elevated highway built on top of SLEX, provides residents coming from southern Metro Manila a fast way to reach Makati. SLEX and EDSA intersect at the Magallanes Interchange, which is the most complex system of elevated roadways in Metro Manila.

Other major roads in Makati include Gil Puyat Avenue (formerly, but still commonly called Buendia Ave), which connects EDSA and SLEX in the north; Ayala Ave, an important street that runs through the CBD; and Makati Ave, which connects Ayala Ave with Gil Puyat and also extends north to cross the Pasig River to Mandaluyong.

chunks.name: One Ayala
chunks.text:
A three-story city bus station, serving as a connecting hub for several city bus lines terminating at the CBD. Direct connection to EDSA Carousel southbound and the MRT is available. Transfer to EDSA Carousel northbound or BGC Bus requires crossing through MRT Ayala station.
address: EDSA cor. Ayala Ave

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text:
Frequent city bus service from around Metro Manila as well as suburban Laguna, serve Makati. Most buses ply either EDSA or Gil Puyat; buses terminating at Makati usually make a loop passing through Gil Puyat and Ayala Ave through the CBD. The BRT service EDSA Carousel runs from Parañaque to Caloocan, and utilizes median bus stops connecting to the MRT.

Most of Metro Manila's expanding Premium Point-to-Point (P2P) bus network terminates at Makati; common termini are Greenbelt, Glorietta, The Circuit, and Trasierra.

RRCG Transport runs Alabang Town Center–Greenbelt 1, Ayala Malls South Park–Greenbelt 5, Robinsons Cainta–Trasierra, SM Cherry Antipolo–Greenbelt 5, SM City Masinag–Greenbelt 5
DNS Transport (Delta Neosolutions) runs from Eastwood City–Makati CBD, Sucat Exit—Greenbelt 5, and UP Town Center–Glorietta 3.
San Agustin runs Noveleta—Trasierra and SM Southmall—Circuit Lane.
HM Transport runs Robinsons Galleria—Glorietta 3.
MetroExpress Connect runs Camella Homes Dasmariñas—San Lorenzo Place, Robinsons Place Dasmariñas—Trasierra, Vista Mall Daang Hari—Trasierra, and Vista Mall Daang Hari—San Lorenzo Place.

chunks.name: Get in / By taxi
chunks.text: Taxis come from across the metro, including the airport. A single costs ₱200-300 from Ninoy Aquino International Airport or ₱200-250 from Ermita.

chunks.name: Guadalupe Ferry Terminal
chunks.text: address: Epifanio de los Santos Avenue corner J. P. Rizal Avenue

chunks.name: Get in / By ferry
chunks.text: The Pasig River Ferry stops at one station in Makati: Guadalupe (near Guadalupe Bridge) is in a convenient spot for tourists, which makes this option far less convenient than hailing a taxi. It may be worth keeping the ferry service in mind as another means of getting into Makati from other riverside districts such as Manila/Intramuros.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
You can easily walk around the Central Business District by way of the sidewalks or the pedestrian underpasses. Some areas in the Central Business District are connected with overpasses where pedestrians can walk above the streets.

Taxis are also abundant, especially around the malls. The flat rate is ₱40 and a ride across town is ₱100-150.

Jeepneys, both traditional and modern, prowl Makati's inner city roads outside Ayala Center such as Chino Roces Ave, Kalayaan Ave and J.P. Rizal Ave. Even before the introduction of modern jeepneys, Makati had traditional-styled air-conditioned jeepneys, mostly plying Gil Puyat Ave. Rides within the city usually do not exceed ₱5.

It is inadvisable to drive in Makati. Makati has some of the strictest traffic rules in Metro Manila. Traffic marshals actively enforce rules. The metro-wide road space rationing ("number coding" or "color coding") scheme is active all day unlike in neighboring cities where they are only enforced during rush hour. Traffic jams are a headache, one-ways streets are common, and left turns are less common than rights. Parking fees are steep, especially in the CBD, and enforcement is draconian, with clamping or towing for violations.

chunks.name: Greenbelt Chapel
chunks.text:
The church is popular for church-goers, most people find it relaxing though because of the park around it. The church is surrounded by trees and a fish and lily pond is on the side of the chapel. The Greenbelt Chapel might be the most relaxing chapel in the Philippines. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is also found here.
address: Ayala Center, Arnaiz Avenue

chunks.name: Nuestra Señora de Gracia Church
chunks.text:
Built by the Augustinian friars and is inspired by European Baroque. It is named Nuestra Señora de Gracia in honor of the miraculous image of the Virgin Mary that can also be found inside.
address: 7440 Bernardino St

chunks.name: Philippine Stock Exchange
chunks.text:
One of the two stock exchanges in the Philippines, it is known to have Asia's shortest trading times which lasts only for two hours. Nearby the PSE is the Ninoy Aquino Monument.
address: Tower One & Exchange Plaza, Ayala Triangle Gardens, Ayala Avenue

chunks.name: Ninoy Aquino Monument
chunks.text:
Erected in honor of the late Filipino senator, Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino, who was the husband of late Philippines president. Corazon Aquino.
hours: Open 24 hours; price: Free; address: 6766 Ayala Ave, Legazpi Village

chunks.name: Nielson Tower Historical Marker
chunks.text:
The Nielson Airport was built by Laurie Reuben Nielson, a businessman born in New Zealand. It was built in 1937 and served as the control tower and passenger depot of the city's airport. Until 1948. The Nielson Airport was built on a 42-hectare piece of land owned by Ayala y Cia. During World War II, commercial flights were relocated so that Nielson could serve the U.S. Army Air Corps.

chunks.name: Ayala Museum
chunks.text:

Also present are some famous paintings by Filipino painters such as Fernando Amorsolo, Juan Luna and Fernando Zobel. Guided tours are available if booked in advance for large groups.

chunks.name: Yuchengco Museum
chunks.text:
The museum was created to house the art collection of Secretary Alfonso T. Yuchengco, and highlight his distinguished career as a businessman, diplomat, collector, philanthropist, patron of the arts, and advocate for education in the Philippines. The museum’s primary goal is to foster a greater public appreciation of the finest in Filipino and Filipino-Chinese visual arts and creativity. The Yuchengco Museum houses paintings by Fernando Amorsolo, Juan Luna and Carlos “Botong” Francisco.
hours: 10AM-6PM; price: ₱200/adults, ₱100/students, PWD, senior citizens; address: RCBC Plaza, Corner Ayala Avenue and Senator Gil J. Puyat Avenue

chunks.name: Drink
chunks.text:
The epicenter of Makati's famous nightlife is Greenbelt where some of the city's best restaurants, cafes, bars and karaoke joints cluster around a park in the middle of the main business district. Meanwhile, there are a series of bars stretched out along Makati Avenue, northeast of Ayala Triangle, including the infamous P Burgos Street red district area.

The Poblacion area is next to (or arguably a part of) the Red Light District, and is possibly the best place for bar hopping in the Metro. The historically low rent (by Makati standards) of the area has led to several trendy bars and restaurants popping up, ranging from cheap beer gardens to some of the best bars in the country. Just start in the area around Don Pedro St. and walk around until you find a bar you like.
In Greenbelt:

chunks.name: Malapascua
chunks.text: Malapascua is an island in Cebu Province north of Cebu Island. The first image Malapascua offers will stay with you for a long time: an exceedingly beautiful pristine stretch of white sand, crystal clear waters bordered by coconut trees and a dozen scattered native-style resorts. But as with all up-and-coming islands experiencing a boom in tourism, Malapascua is rapidly becoming a second Boracay with modern concrete hotels to cater for the varied needs of the many. Despite this modernization, even the largest of resorts embrace the native build styles for a portion of their rooms. The north of the island remains untouched where the fishermen are just fishermen in native style houses.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Malapascua is known to the locals as Logon and the local beach was named Bounty Beach by the resort on the island Cocobana, some 20 years ago. It lies 8 km off the north of Cebu, and has a community of about 11,000 inhabitants (as of 2012). A walk or a tour of the entire island will take about 3 hours. The island's main income is from tourists who flock to the island to see the rare thresher sharks, white tip sharks and various rays, or visit for a romantic weekend break.

There are ATMs, a Smart Money store, and a money changer store on the island. Many of the more popular resorts accept major credit cards.

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text: Mactan-Cebu International Airport is the main gateway to Cebu Island for international and domestic flights. It is 7 km SE of the North Bus Terminal in Cebu city.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text:
There are 3 bus companies that ride to/from Maya from the North Bus Terminal in Cebu:
Ceres, Cebu AutoBus and Rough Riders. The journey takes 3½ to 4 hours, video and air-con ₱230, non air-con ₱160. Air conditioned buses can also have WiFi for usage. Ask the bus conductor for help.

You could hire a taxi, or a private car from Cebu to Maya, as well as arrange a pick-up with one of the resorts.

chunks.name: Get in / By boat
chunks.text:
From Maya a local ferry (bangka) goes across am and pm with a break at lunch time, 'till 4:30PM.
It takes about 1/2 hour and costs ₱100. First boat from Maya is at 6:30AM. A ferry will not leave unless it has enough people, so aim to arrive earlier rather than later.

Crossing can be rather wet and bangkas have very little shelter from the elements.

When arriving/departing from Malapascua shores be prepared to either jump into the shallow waters or walk down a rickety plank. At low tide you can transfer to a smaller boat for ₱20.

When arriving to Maya you may have to transfer to a very small banca for the last 200 m.

A private bangkas to Malapascua can be hired from Maya for ₱1200.

If you have arranged transportation with your resort you don't need to worry about any of the above.

Malapascua can also be reached from Bantayan and from Leyte (San Isidro), but there's no ferry service.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
There is no transport on the island — not that you will need any, as you can walk everywhere.

Alternatively, there are many locals who own mopeds called habal habal, who are willing to give you a lift. They charge a fee of ₱10 for short ride, and ₱20-30 from south to north. You can rent a motorbike for a whole day for ₱1000.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text:
Snorkeling and fishing. With its spectacular underwater flora and fauna there is much to see, making snorkeling a fine experience. A resort will rent boats, alternatively locals will take you on their fishing rakie.
Marine Protected Areas for Snorkeling are:
Coral Garden (close to Aabana Beach & Watersport Resort) east side,
Lapus Lapus (close to Los Bamboos Resort) northwest point,
Dakit Dakit (close to Blue Corals Resort) southwest point

Scuba diving. Waters off the island offers some of the most exciting extreme dives in the Philippines, with adrenaline pumping adventure, thresher sharks encounters. Malapascua is the only place you can see them reliably, and they are as good as guaranteed. . The dive shops seem mindful of the environment and have a caring attitude towards their customers, which is as well considering the kind of fish roaming around. Dive shops offer introductory courses to advanced Scuba diving and there are a couple of wrecks to explore.

Walks. With about 6 km circumference, Malapascua has more than a few spots to see. It has a handful of exotic beaches like Bounty Beach, or Mangrove Bay, and to tower it all there is the lighthouse, very popular when it comes to watching the sunset.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text:
Malapascua is a diving destination. The main attractions are the thresher sharks which are regularly encountered at the Kimud Shoal. At other divesites, you can see an incredible diversity of marine life, including many creatures on your bucket list: mandarin fish, pygmy seahorses, blue-ringed octopus, nudibranchs, frogfish and many species of seahorse and pipefish.

PADI Divemaster and PADI IDC (Instructor Development Course) are available.

See also Diving in the Philippines—Malapascua.

chunks.name: Evolution
chunks.text:
Malapascua's only 5-star Instructor Training Facility rating from TDI. Evolution offers a full range of TDI tech classes. Day trips and local dives are run 365 days a year by a professional team. Evolution is a full service resort with 16 rooms and a well-known restaurant on site and is owned and operated by a seasoned Irish and English duo. In 2015 Evolution became a Green Fins top member having the 6th least environmental impact of dive centres audited in Asia and is the only dive centre resort on Malapascua to make the list.
hours: 7AM- midnight; address: info@evolution.com.ph

chunks.name: French Kiss Divers
chunks.text:
French Kiss Divers is a small diveshop who offers SSI courses from open water to Instructor and a panel of specialties such as Nitrox, Deep, Night, and Wreck, a very good knowledge of the dive sites. The dive group doesn't exceed 4 people. They often organize day trips in surrounding islands like Kalanggaman or Carnaza.
hours: 8AM-7PM; address: Bounty Beach front, Hipocampus Resort

chunks.name: Malapascua Exotic Dive & Beach Resort (IDC Centre)
chunks.text: Offers all in one - accommodation, restaurant, bar, diveshop, travel service. This eco-friendly resort has its own recycling plant and 24-hour generator. This PADI 5-star Instructor Development Resort is the only National Geographic Center in Malapascua. Courses range from beginner through to Instructor (100% pass rate) and technical diving courses. They cover more than 22 dive sites around Malapascua, have daily dives to see the thresher sharks, as well as Nitrox, Wreck and Night dives.

chunks.name: Sea Explorers
chunks.text:
Located at the center of Bounty Beach beside Ocean Vida Resort with a bar on the island. In the Visayas since 1989, offering all PADI recreational courses from beginner up to Instructor courses.
hours: 7AM-5PM

chunks.name: Thresher Shark Divers
chunks.text:
PADI 5-Star Career Development Centre was established in 2004, offering guided dives and PADI courses from beginner to professional level with very experienced PADI Pros. Regular trips include morning thresher shark dives at Kimud Shoal, local reef and macro dives, Gato Island, night dives and wreck dives. Open Water divers may be able to join some shark dives with instructor supervision; deeper or overhead-environment sites require suitable experience and certification.
hours: 8am-7or 8pm, dive schedule confirmed the day before; price: 1800 PHP; address: Bounty Beach, Logon, Daanbantayan, Cebu 6013 Philippines

chunks.name: Malapascua Scuba Eco Adventures,
chunks.text:
PADI Diving courses from beginner to professional. Especially for SPANISH Divers .Diving in small groups with experienced divemasters in a fun environment. More 10 years experience on Malapascua and Divemasters. Eco-friendly resort, Dives to see the thresher sharks Monad Shoal, Kimud Shoal, Kalanggagamn, Gato Island,
hours: 9AM - 5 PM; address: Aabana Beach & Watersport Resort

chunks.name: Buy
chunks.text:
Souvenirs. There are a couple of Malapascua T-shirt vendors around Bounty Beach, as well as craftsmen that sell wooden threshers shark figurines.

Groceries. There are a bunch of local shops scattered around the island. That sell from toiletries and painkillers to light bulbs, water, sodas, and snacks. There are fruit shops that sell bananas, apples, coconuts, tomatoes and other products.

Dive Shop. The big dive centers have a dive shop where you can buy wet suits, masks, knives, etc.

Books. A few hundred books up for free exchange at Malapascua Exotic Dive & Beach Resort (IDC Centre)and also at the Blue Corals Resort.

chunks.name: Oscar's Restaurant
chunks.text: An eclectic mix of international dishes with a daily changing menu. Open air beachfront restaurant located above Thresher Shark Divers.

chunks.name: The Craic House
chunks.text:
The Craic House serves up delicious daily specials based on the best local produce and quality imported ingredients personally sourced by the owners. Everything that can be homemade is homemade from bread, wraps, falafel, cakes, pies, relishes, pates.
hours: 7AM-midnight; address: Bounty Beach, Malapascua Island

chunks.name: Purple Snapper Bar & Restaurant
chunks.text: They have great burgers. Also try their pizzas and fettuccine chicken alfredo.

chunks.name: Angelina
chunks.text:
Original Italian food.
hours: 8AM-10PM; price: ₱300-500; address: Angelina Beach

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text:
You will see local eateries spread all over the island. Do not let their worn aspect put you off of a good and cheap meal; usually rice with choices of veggies, meat, and fish. Some evening stalls barbecue finger-licking pork satay.

La Isla Bonita offers Philippine dishes and pizzas
Ging Ging's is a popular choice, eatery with a large array of options
Kiwi's Restaurant down a track behind Ging Ging's, a small family run eatery with great food and good prices.

chunks.name: The Pub Upstairs
chunks.text: An open air bar located above Thresher Shark Divers, nestled amongst the palm trees with a sea view, The Pub Upstairs is a lively watering hole for an apres-dive beer or cocktail. An excellent selection of local and imported beers and spirits.

chunks.name: Drink
chunks.text: Disco. During high season, there is a popular disco event every Saturday, surrounded by stalls that sell beers and sodas, or food. Not to be missed!

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text:
On arrival a few official-looking touts await the visitors but they are superfluous, considering the number of resorts, so take your time to choose what suits you best.

Touts won't charge you a fee; they'll get ₱50 or more from the resorts, so they might just take you to the closest one or the one paying them the most rather than the best one.

chunks.name: Mike & Dioses Beachcottage
chunks.text: Mike is the manager and owner; Kiko his friend, caretaker and representative. Only a few cottages are left over cause of building all new rooms. They have a thatched roof, bamboo (amakan) wall and veranda. The cottages are simple fan rooms with sea views and are located in the garden area. Price range is ₱500-600 per night, including breakfast. Mike & Diose's Beach cottage have the widest and cleanest beach on Malapascua, pure white sand and some bahay kubos for their guest are located on the beach.

chunks.name: Bebes Lodging House
chunks.text:
Fan and AC double rooms, outside bathrooms. Said to be the cheapest on the island.
price: ₱400/₱650

chunks.name: Villa Sandra
chunks.text:
Environmentally conscious and socially-active, guest-house featuring in-house organic vegetarian restaurant, small gym, yoga classes, hammocks and a community-oriented souvenir shop. Can arrange tours, snorkel gear, tent, tattoos, paintings, etc.
price: ₱350 for dorm bed; privates available

chunks.name: Sleep / Budget
chunks.text:
Daño Beach Resort, cell +63 915-666-1584 or +63 927-381-7894. Lemuel Daño is the manager. There are 20 odd bungalows, all facing the sea; they have a thatched roof, bamboo veranda and the concrete cottages are simple, with a large room, and come equipped with a bathroom.
MGmatterhorn a small and very clean guesthouse, managed by Marites Monteclar, not on the beach. It's on the way to Bakaw-Kiwi eatery. One fan room good for two and about November 2011 two more air-con rooms. Free Wi-Fi. Prices starting from ₱700 per day and room. Strictly no cooking in the rooms. Cell +63 915-554-3310 or e-mail maritesmonteclar@yahoo.com. Look the pics on www.malapascua.de. Look for matterhorn. Or go to: https://sites.google.com/site/abougibi/

chunks.name: Aabana Beach and Watersports Resort
chunks.text:
Beach resort. Cottages are about 60 meters from their own beach, having extra small bamboo huts for their guest on the wide and nice beach. All cottages have big terrace, air-con, warm and cold water shower, flatscreen LCD satellite TV, individual safety digital box, refrigerator and free Wi-Fi. There are also cottages which have a kitchen on the terrace for private guest use. They offer boat tours around the island, fishing tours, snorkeling tours and jet ski.
price: ₱1600-2000

chunks.name: Slam's Garden Resort
chunks.text:
Superior and deluxe rooms, all equipped with air-conditioning, safe and Wi-Fi. Facilities and services are scuba diving, Slam's Garden Bar & Pub and massage service.
price: From ₱2400; address: Barangay Logon, 6013, Daan-Bantayan

chunks.name: Malay (Aklan)
chunks.text: Malay is a municipality in Aklan; its main barangay is Caticlan. Most travellers come here en route to Boracay; the commonest route to get there is via Caticlan's port.

chunks.name: Caticlan or Godofredo P. Ramos Airport
chunks.text: Much smaller and closer airport, only a few kilometers away from Caticlan Jetty Port and Tabon Port. It now handles jet flights to Manila operated by Cebu Pacific, Philippines airlines, as well as turboprop aircraft from Cebu operated by Cebu Pacific, Philippine Airlines and SkyJet.

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text:
The airline will drop you off at the east side of the airport. After exiting the airport on the east side, find the tricycle stand across the street, past the various resort offerings. A tricycle from Caticlan Airport to the Tabon jetty is ₱50 per person.

Ground transportation. From the Caticlan airport, you can either take a tricycle (₱50) or walk (10 minutes) to Caticlan Jetty Port. Besides, Cebu Pacific airlines offers hotel transfer for ₱350 per person.

chunks.name: Malaybalay
chunks.text: Malaybalay City is the provincial capital of Bukidnon Province, on Mindanao Island in the Philippines.

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text: There is no commercial airport in the province of Bukidnon. The nearest airport is in Cagayan de Oro about 100 km away. Cagayan de Oro has several airlines providing flights to Manila, Cebu, Davao, Iloilo, Bacolod, Zamboanga.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text: Sayre Highway crosses Mindanao from Cagayan de Oro City in the north to Davao City in the south. To Cagayan de Oro, it is about 90 minutes drive. Taxi can be hired starting at ₱1500.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text:
Rural Transit, Super 5 and some smaller companies are plying the route frequently, usually every 20 minutes, even at night frequent buses can be found. Rates vary between ₱85 and ₱140 (air con).
To Davao, it is a 5-hour bus trip.

chunks.name: Get in / By boat
chunks.text: Next harbor is in Cagayan de Oro. Boats are available to Manila, Cebu City, Iloilo City, Bohol (Jagna), Dumaguete and Nasipit (Butuan). A small harbor in Balingoan provides Boat service to Camiguin island.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Along the highway small minibuses "Multi cab" ply the route between Casisang in the south and Kalasungay in the north. For the smaller roads within the town, passenger motorcycles can be utilized, they adjust their route to their passengers needs. All transportation costs between ₱6 and 7.

chunks.name: Bukidnon Gov web site
chunks.text: has lots of info about Bukidnon.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text: A monastery in San Jose, the Pines View Park, the Matin-ao and Nasuli springs.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text:
Malaybalay does offer lot of hiking opportunities, which still have to be developed. It serves also as a base for climbing the 2nd highest mountain of the Philippines Mt. Dulang Dulang (2935m) in the Mt. Kitanglad Range Natural Park. To get started with the tour visitors should visit the PENRO office near the capitol to get permits and arrange for guide.
There are horseback riding facilities, for example at D'Stables resort in Sumpong. Day hikes is also a pleasant activity for visitors, you can get off the beaten path and experience scenery most other visitors don't get to see. The hike up the slopes is rewarded with views across neighboring valley and towards the panoramic view of the Kitanglad range. These range from 2 hours to half-day hike. There are a lot of routes to choose from.

chunks.name: Malilipot
chunks.text: Malilipot is a municipality in the east coast of Albay. It is sandwiched between the city of Tabaco and the municipality of Bacacay. Its shoreline faces Lagonoy Gulf. The town is stretching along Legazpi-Tiwi coastal road and is one of the five municipalities that has a jurisdiction over the foothills of Mayon Volcano.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: The name Malilipot comes from the Bikol word malipot which means cold. Located at the east coast of the province, it has two mountains — Mount Bulakawan and Mount Toktokan that protect the entire town against the dangerous eruption of Mayon Volcano. Barangay San Roque is the only vulnerable place in town.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: There are buses from Manila to Malilipot, stopping also at other towns and cities along the way, and there are also UV Express vans from Legazpi and jeepneys from Tabaco.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text: It is 20 km from Legazpi and 547 km from Manila.

chunks.name: Get around

The festival’s highlight is the Street Presentation and Exhibition (Sayaw Paralubid). The festival also coincides with the observance of the Feast of Mt. Carmel that will bring out the spirit of piety amidst the days of gaiety.

chunks.name: Malinao
chunks.text: Malinao is a laidback municipality in the northeast quadrant of Albay and sandwiched between the city of Tabaco and the municipality of Tiwi located along the Legazpi-Tiwi Coastal Road. Its shoreline is facing Lagonoy Gulf.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Malinao was founded in 1600.
Between 1600 and 1616, Malinao was then part of the Diocese of Cagsawa (now Daraga). It became an independent bisita or sitio attached to Sawangan (now Legazpi) until 1619, when separate religious administration was exercised with Rev. Francisco de Santa Ana, OFM, as first pastor.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: There are buses from Manila to Malinao, stopping also at other towns and cities along the way, and there are also UV Express vans from Legazpi and jeepneys from Tabaco both are Tiwi bound and stopping over at Malinao.

chunks.name: Malolos
chunks.text: Malolos is a city in the province of Bulacan, Philippines. It is the capital of Bulacan and occupies a special place in Philippine history as the capital of an independent Philippines in between the Spanish and American occupations.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Malolos is the capital (since 1901) and second most populous city of the province of Bulacan. . It was the site of the constitutional convention of 1898, known as the Malolos Convention, that led to the establishment of the First Philippine Republic, at the sanctuary of the Barasoain Church. The convent of the Malolos Cathedral served as the presidential palace at that time. Malolos gave birth to the first constitutional republic in Asia.

The town was burned on the orders of President Emilio Aguinaldo during the Philippine-American War in 1899 as the Americans approached, but unlike other major population centers in the country, managed to retain a sizeable number of colonial era houses concentrated around Camestisuhan aka Pariancillo District, which was declared a Heritage Town by the government in 2001. Malolos became a legally-designated city in 1999.

chunks.name: Understand / Orientation
chunks.text: Today’s Malolos was formed by the merger of two towns divided by the Malolos River. Old Malolos, with its historic core lay south of the river, while Barasoain, to the north, was a separate municipality with its own parish church until it was dissolved into Malolos during the American period. Further north, a new commercial core has sprung up along the MacArthur Highway and the provincial capitol.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text:
The North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) provides access from Manila and Angeles, and exits near Malolos are Tabang and Santa Rita. Tabang exit is best used from Manila, while Santa Rita exit is best used from the north.

The MacArthur Highway passes north of Barasoain between Calumpit and Guiguinto.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text:
Golden Bee and First North Luzon Transit has buses between Manila and the towns of Paombong and Hagonoy. The main bus stop is on McArthur Highway, near the flyover. These buses do not pass through downtown Malolos but instead pass through Blas F. Ople Diversion Road.

From Quezon City, minibuses and a Point-to-Point bus terminate at Robinsons Malolos. The P2P buses run every 30 minutes from 6AM to 10:30PM. A one-way bus fare costs P120.

Malolos is also a stopover on some Victory Liner buses along the San Fernando-Metro Manila route, especially if the bus signages indicate “Inner Cities” and enter MacArthur Highway via NLEX Tabang Exit in Guiguinto.

chunks.name: Get in / By jeepney/minibus
chunks.text: There are passenger jeepneys, vans and minibuses connecting Malolos with neighboring towns such as Calumpit, Bulakan and Plaridel, and as far as Hagonoy, Baliwag, Santa Maria, and Meycauayan in Bulacan and San Fernando in Pampanga.

chunks.name: Get in / By train
chunks.text:
There are no trains to Malolos since the main line to La Union closed in 1988.

Since the 2020s, there is ongoing construction of an electrified standard-gauge railway from Metro Manila to Clark International Airport in Angeles, Pampanga, and New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac. The first segment of that rail project will run up to Malolos. As of 2026, the line is still under construction, with a station serving Malolos being built in front of the provincial capitol along MacArthur Highway.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
Public transportation in Malolos is served by buses, jeepneys, and UV Express AUVs. The city is also served by tricycles, which offer their services on a for-hire basis.

Malolos is known for its Karatig Jeepneys which serves as an intra-city public transportation. The name came from the word karatig, which means nearby places or barangays. The Karatig jeepney is the smaller version of the jeepneys which usually have the size of about 3 meters long and can board 8-10 commuters at the back plus 2 passengers in the front seat. Longer models can accommodate about 10-12. Its capacity varies according to the jeep’s length and size. There are two Karatig routes around Malolos, including one that runs from the downtown to the Provincial Capitol via Paseo del Congreso.

Some coastal barangays of Malolos may be only accessible by boat.

chunks.name: Bulacan Provincial Capitol View Park
chunks.text:
City park with many flagpoles and monuments to local heroes.

chunks.text: Manaoag is a town in Pangasinan. It is a popular pilgrimage site for Roman Catholics seeking the venerated Marian image of Our Lady of Manaoag.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Formally an agricultural town in the middle of the eastern Pangasinan plains, Manaoag’s economy is also sustained by the throngs of pilgrims seeking to see and pray before Our Lady of Manaoag, a 17th-century sculpture of the Virgin Mary that is regarded by believers to be miraculous.

chunks.text:

Manaoag is directly connected by bus from Cubao in Metro Manila. Minivans traveling from Pozorrubio and Binalonan towards Dagupan also pass through Manaoag.

chunks.name: Mandaluyong
chunks.text: Mandaluyong is a city in Metro Manila, Philippines. While not touristy as its neighbors owing to the lack of historical sites, the city is by the way a shopping destination, bordered by Makati to the south, Manila's southeast suburban districts to the west, Pasig to the east, and San Juan and Quezon City to the north.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
The city used to be the historical center of the ancient Namayan kingdom, which used to cover much of some of the districts of Manila, and eastern and southern Metro Manila. When the Spaniards arrived, the remnants of the kingdom have been re-established as the municipality of Santa Ana, which survived as the easternmost district of Manila. Namayan, in turn, survived as the name of one of the city's barangays.

Mandaluyong is established in 1843 as the town of San Felipe Neri, named after the patron of Rome. Its first church and parochial school was built in 1863. The city played a strategic role for the revolutionary Katipunan during the Philippine Revolution.

Civil government is established during the early 1900s. San Felipe Neri is merged into the nearby town of San Juan del Monte (present-day San Juan City), and has served as the provincial capital of Rizal for four months in 1904, until it was transferred to Pasig. In 1907, the American colonial administrators restored the municipality, now renamed as Mandaluyong. Many of the city's government buildings and infrastructure, most notably the Welfareville complex, which included the Correctional Institute for Women, Boy's Town, and the National Center for Mental Health (NCHP), are built during the American era.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
World War II in the Pacific was devastating in Mandaluyong; it is heavily damaged and many of its people killed. Liberation forces arrived on February 9, 1945, and saved the rest of the municipality from damage. February 9 has since been turned into a local public holiday, Liberation Day

Postwar years is marked by progress and prosperity. Rebuilding was done quickly, and Mandaluyong have undergone an economic boom during the 1950s and 1960, and became the most developed municipality of Rizal. The municipality became part of Metro Manila in 1975, and became a city in 1994.

Mandaluyong is connected to Makati through three bridges (Guadalupe, Estrella–Pantaleon, and Makati-Mandaluyong). From Manila, it is either by Lambingan Bridge or Sevilla Bridge.

Elsewhere, you go with jeepneys, taxis and tricycles. Jeepneys mostly ply the main east-west roads, Boni Ave and Shaw Blvd.

chunks.name: Mandaue
chunks.text: Mandaue is a city in the Philippines, part of Metro Cebu. Mandaue is just north of Cebu City and, like that city, it is on Cebu Island. Just off the coast opposite Mandaue is Mactan Island with the city of Lapu-Lapu on it. From Mandaue two bridges lead to Lapu-Lapu and several good (if sometimes jammed) roads go to Cebu.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Mandaue is the least glamorous and least touristed of the three cities that make up the core of Metro Cebu, though it has quite a few resident foreigners because its housing costs are lower.

Cebu City is the main center, with better shopping and a wider range of hotels and restaurants, and Lapu-Lapu has the airport and quite a few high-end resorts and condos. Mandaue is mostly residential and industrial; quite a few people live there and commute to work in Cebu.

On the other hand, Mandaue has almost 365,000 people (2020), so it does have all the services one might expect in a medium-sized city anywhere. There are even a few resorts along its coast.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text: Like the rest of the Philippines, Mandaue has a tropical climate. It has considerable risk of typhoons, though not as much as some other areas of the country. See Metro_Cebu#Climate for more detail.

Metro Cebu has two major long-distance bus terminals, the north terminal in Mandaue and south terminal in Cebu City.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
See the Metro Cebu article for general information on getting around within the urban area that Mandaue is part of.

Within the town, most people travel by taxi or jeepney. Motorcycle rideshare by Angkas and car rideshare by Grab are also popular.

Going beyond those, anywhere on Cebu Island is readily accessible by road, and there are many buses. Metro Cebu has two main long distance bus terminals; the north terminal is in Mandaue and the south terminal in Cebu City.

For other modes of travel, Metro Cebu is the main hub for the Visayas region and has connections to many cities outside that region. Mactan-Cebu International Airport is in Lapu-Lapu. For travel by sea, the main port is in Cebu City.

chunks.name: Manila
chunks.text: Manila (Tagalog: Maynila) is the capital of the Philippines and a major attraction in terms of culture and heritage in the country. Sprawling, congested and polluted will likely be the first words to enter your mind when you think of Manila but don't let that impression stop you from exploring its places of interests: its churches; its diverse and complicated culture; colonial history; gigantic malls; bustling markets; hidden architectural gems and vibrant nightlife. Take the opportunity to explore Manila and make your own personal connection with the city.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The City of Manila is in the western part of Metro Manila, facing the Manila Bay. It is bordered on the west by Manila Bay, to the north by Navotas, Quezon City and Caloocan City, to the east by San Juan and Mandaluyong City and to the south by Pasay and Makati. It is the oldest part of Metro Manila and the seat of the government of the Philippines.

However, despite its historical and administrative importance, the City of Manila is not effectively the "Downtown" or "City center" of Metro Manila in the traditional sense. Metro Manila is a multipolar city, with other cities of the urban area such as Quezon City, Makati, Taguig and Parañaque rivalling or exceeding Manila in business, education, shopping, entertainment and tourism.

In contrast to other parts of the Metro area, the City of Manila is a place for travellers rather than for tourists. Even the so-called "tourist areas", such as Intramuros, Binondo, Ermita and Malate, may feel a bit gritty and chaotic, and the beauty of the city is not obvious, as World War II has wiped out much of Manila's historical architecture.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: However, there's much more to Manila than meets the eye. The immaterial heritage, the unique blend of Spanish, American, Chinese and native Filipino culture, remains present, and can be felt even without going to the Intramuros historical district. The City of Manila remains the cultural centre of the Philippines, containing many of the country's best museums and cultural performances. And there are many hidden gems to be discovered, such as the colonial churches, the intricate mausoleums of the Manila Chinese Cemetery, the stunning modernist architecture of the Cultural Center of the Philippines, the fantastic food of Binondo, making Manila an "off the beaten path destination" despite being a country's capital.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
For over three centuries Manila was colonized and administered by Spain which left an enduring architectural heritage throughout the Philippines, especially with respect to churches, forts and other colonial buildings which can still be seen in the ruins of Intramuros, built in the late 16th century. Manila began as a settlement on the banks of the Pasig River, and its name originates from "Maynilad," referring to the mangrove plant known as nilad, which was abundant in the area. Prior to the arrival of the Spanish in the 16th century, Manila was home to Muslim-Malays. In 1571, 50 years after Magellan's visit to the islands, Spanish conquistador Miguel Lopez de Legazpi claimed the Philippines as a colony and established Manila as its capital. Manila was also colonized by the British for two years. Manila was part of the Spanish East Indies until 1898, when the U.S. took over the Philippines after the Spanish-American War.

Manila was first sought by the Spaniards, then the Americans. The Spaniards wanted a counterbalance to the expanding Portuguese empire which had almost taken a big slice of the pie in the lucrative Spice Trade. They got it through Manila, so strategically placed between China together with the rest of Asia, and Mexico - the next closest transit point for goods from Asia to Europe.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
Its location seemed a well thought out choice. Legazpi took five years after arriving in the Philippines and settling in Cebu in 1565 to mull over before deciding to finally move up north to Manila in 1571 and make it the capital of the new territory. By numbers, it shortened the traveling distance to the other side of the empire in Acapulco. Manila is also in a much easy and straighter drafting reach for sailing ships to catch the Pacific Trade Winds as they blow northeastward to Japan for Acapulco and blow precisely at San Bernardino Strait for the westward-bound return trip without being diverted any farther. Most importantly, Manila is much closer than Cebu to China.

When Mexico pushed for its independence from Spain and finally shoved her out, the Philippines' glittering importance began to dwindle due to the discontinuance of the Manila-Acapulco Galleon Trade, cutting off the Acapulco to Vera Cruz segment and it accelerated more when the Suez Canal was opened enabling the Chinese exports to go in the opposite direction and making Singapore the most important transit hub to Europe in the region. Just a token administration was maintained in Manila since the Philippines had been confined to the doldrums as one of the unreachable and hard to maintain colonies of Spain. That obscurity lasted until a new imperialist era dawned, with countries embarked on a new competition for raw materials and market.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
Netherlands, Britain, and France were already there now with Germany, lurking somewhere and ready to fill in the voids about to be vacated by waning superpowers. Germany was already sniffing its way around the Pacific Ocean like a shark smelling a kill when the US, spurred by the windfall of acquiring Hawaii and which desperately wanted a toehold in Asia for her trade, notably with Japan and China, grabbed the first opportunity of grabbing the Philippines. The Philippines once more, so strategically placed as the soon-to-be-linchpin of American imperialism, extended her colonial servitude to the US.

With dynamic geo-politics working, the Philippines, and Manila in particular, proved to be manna from heaven as Japan began to flex her muscles. The result was that the Philippines served as first line of defense for Australia and the mainland US to buy time and it really proves more beneficial as another realignment was in force after World War II when communism comes into the scene and is threatening to swallow the whole of East Asia except Japan, putting the Philippines as a buffer zone for whatever adverse contingency and as long as the Manila leadership sides with the US, things will be OK.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
Now that communism is under control and every country on both sides of the Pacific seemed to be embracing free market economy, all of Southeast Asia are grinding strong and busy buzzing. The factors of time, location, and distance are not a consideration anymore and what needs to be important is that Manila is as peaceful, orderly, productive, and creative as all her neighbors to win visitors' attention.

Being a city with its ears and antennae acutely tuned in to American and some European trends, and in the forefront of modernization and constant cultural refinement more than any other city in Southeast Asia or Asia as a whole, Manila witnessed or hosted innovations - political, cultural, civic etc.
