chunks.name: Quezon (Palawan)
chunks.text: Quezon is a 2nd class municipality in the province of Palawan, Philippines. According to the 2000 census, it has a population of 41,669 people in 8,453 households. It is where the Tabon Man lived long time ago in the Philippines.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: The easiest way to reach Quezon is to catch a bus or van from the San Jose terminal in Puerto Princesa. Charing Bus lines has several buses leaving approximately hourly, starting between 4AM and 6AM. There are also vans departing from behind the Charing terminal - just ask around, someone will point you in the right direction. Bus fare should be around ₱165, vans will be about the same. All buses or vans will make a meal/bathroom stop around Narra.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There are plenty of tricycles roving around. At the port, bancas of different length are available to take you to beautiful spots within Quezon waters.

chunks.name: Tabon Caves
chunks.text: The Tabon cave complex consists of 29 explored caves, but there are 200 caves known on Lipuun Point. They are maintained and managed by the National Museum. Diwata Cave and Liyang Cave are open to the public. The Caves were the discovery site of the Tabon Man, one of the oldest discoveries of human inhabitants found in the Philippines.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: Snorkelling, Scuba Diving, Island Hopping, Bird Watching, Fishing, Hiking, Hunting,

chunks.name: Cafe Atreyu
chunks.text: address: Underground 1, Quezon, Palawan

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text: Experience the unique Palawan cuisine. More often than not exotic foods will be available eg Wild Boar (Baboy Damo), Wild birds (Labuyo), Lobsters, Giant Crabs, Palawan Tamilok, seafoods (shells, exotic fish & edible seaweeds).

chunks.name: Drink
chunks.text: There are bars, restos, cafes scattered all over the place.

chunks.name: Tabon Village Resort
chunks.text:
Fan double cottages.
price: ₱450

chunks.name: Quezon (province)
chunks.text: Often called Quezon Province to distinguish it from Quezon City, Quezon is a province in Calabarzon which is rich in culture and nature. It has a bad reputation as a rainforest backwater along the highway to Bicol, but its festivals, hidden beaches, and historical monuments are things worth visiting.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Quezon is equally known as a destination for nature lovers and a backwater of southern Luzon, being a province of rainforests, small towns, and coconut plantations. Except for the beaten-path part of the province around Mount Banahaw, most of Quezon is unknown to most travelers, and the province is quite overshadowed by its more prosperous and frequently visited neighbors, Batangas and Laguna. You'll likely see the rest of the province only in transit: from the windows of a long-distance bus barreling down the highway from Manila towards the south.

The natives of Quezon often called themselves Quezonins or Quezonians or by their town, such as Lucbanin, Unisanin, and Infantahin. They are mostly Tagalog speakers, but there are also Visayans, Ilocanos, and Bicolanos, the former being concentrated in Lucena, the second at the boundaries with Aurora, and the latter at the boundaries with Bicol. The population is at around 2 million as of 2020.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Quezon is largely a rural province with an economy reliant on agriculture, fisheries, forestry, power generation and tourism. Rice paddies abound in western Quezon, and most of the rainforest has been cut down to provide space for the coconut plantations that dominate the landscape of the lowlands and hills in most of the province. There is logging activity on the remaining forests, sometimes involving illegal operations. The province is home to two major power plants, one in Pagbilao and another in Mauban; both use coal, that they are much hated by the locals, but also critical lifelines for Luzon's power supply. Tourism is already established in western Quezon, but remains largely unknown elsewhere in the province.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
What is now Quezon used to be parts of the current provinces of Batangas, Laguna, and Nueva Ecija. The boundary of the current province is formally defined as the Spaniards, under Juan de Salcedo, entered the Philippines. The province, originally named Kalilayan, has its first provincial capital at the present-day town of Unisan, which was moved inland to Pagbilao after its destruction and pillaging by Moro pirates. In 1749, the capital was moved to Tayabas, which also became its name until its renaming in 1946.

Because of the oppressive rule by the Spaniards, Tayabas also witnessed uprisings against the colonial authorities, most notably the rebellion led by mystic Hermano Pule (real name, Apolinario de la Cruz).

Civil government was established by the Americans in 1901, and the capital moved to Lucena. The Americans quelled remaining rebellions led in Quezon, as the province served as a supply point for rebels in Batangas and Laguna. Marinduque became part of Tayabas between 1902 and 1920. In December 1941, the Japanese arrived in Quezon, and stayed until their surrender in 1945.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text: Quezon gained its current name after a law was passed to name it after President Manuel Quezon, who previously served as the province’s governor, in 1946. Aurora was carved out as a subprovince within Quezon, until it was separated officially in 1979; it was transferred to Central Luzon in 2002. A referendum was held on the question of dividing the province into two in 2007, but was defeated by a vast majority.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text: Quezon has a climate generally characterized by an almost equal distribution of rainfall through the year, but as the province is vast, there are variations, with western parts having a dry and wet season, and the eastern parts having a rainforest climate. The provinces gets struck by typhoons frequently, with the eastern parts the most vulnerable due to undeveloped infrastructure.

chunks.name: Understand / Politics
chunks.text:
Quezon is quite conservative in politics, but is more so to the east of the Sierra Madre. This manifest in cultural differences between the more urbanized west (Pagbilao, Lucena, Tayabas, Sariaya, Candelaria, Tiaong, and San Antonio), who are open to development, and the rural east, north and outlying islands, where locals strive to protect their traditional lifestyle reliant on fishing, agriculture and forestry.

Due to geographical barriers, lifestyle differences, and political preferences, inhabitants of Quezon have been increasingly polarized, and regionalism has increased, especially in the mountainous Bondoc Peninsula, where there is an active regionalist movement demanding the creation of their own province. A plebiscite to divide Quezon was held in 2008, but was rejected by a sweeping majority of the province's residents.

As is common with the people of Calabarzon, Quezonians are staunch environmentalists. Major environmental challenges includes protecting the province's remaining rainforests, opposing construction of new fossil fuel power plants, and controlling land development.

chunks.name: AB Liner
chunks.text: Regular bus service from Manila (Alabang or Sampaloc, Manila) to Guinayangan and Tagkawayan via Lucena and Calauag.

chunks.name: DLTBCo.
chunks.text: Services from Manila to Lucena, and onward to Bicol with stops at towns in Eastern Quezon. Tickets can be purchased on board from the conductor on the Manila-Lucena services, but for services stopping at Eastern Quezon, reservation is required if coming from major stops.

chunks.name: JAC Liner and LLi
chunks.text: Frequent bus service from Manila to Lucena (Grand Terminal, SM City Lucena and Dalahican port), stopping at most towns and cities from Calamba.

chunks.name: JAM Liner
chunks.text: Frequent regular AC bus service from Manila to Lucena terminal, and daily service to Mauban via Tayabas. Stops at Tiaong, Candelaria, Sariaya, and Tayabas (Calumpang). Mauban-bound buses stop at Gulang-Gulang (at Lucena) and Tayabas poblacion.

chunks.name: P&O Transport
chunks.text: Air-conditioned buses run from Manila (Alabang) to Tagkawayan and Guinayangan via the Maharlika Highway and Batangas City to Tagkawayan via San Juan and Eco-Tourism Road.

chunks.name: Supreme
chunks.text: Run both regular AC and non-AC buses between Batangas City and its own terminal in Lucena, with stops at Candelaria, Sariaya and Calumpang (Tayabas).

chunks.name: Superlines
chunks.text: Daily runs from Manila (Alabang and Cubao) to Santo Tomas Batangas, San Pablo Laguna, Alaminos Laguna, Catanauan and San Francisco via Pagbilao and Padre Burgos, with a layover at Lucena. Buses either AC or non-AC, with restrooms on board. Reservations required if traveling from their Manila (Alabang and Cubao) or Superlines and own sister company Daet Express bus stations.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: Major destinations in Quezon Province is regularly served by buses from Metro Manila and also Batangas. Most bus traffic through the province are bound for Bicol, Eastern Visayas, and Mindanao.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text:
The Maharlika Highway (Manila South Road, or Rte 1) passes through Quezon and serves as a major transport backbone. Most motor traffic in the province passes through Maharlika Highway, but it has been experiencing major bottlenecks in the most important towns, resulting to the construction of bypasses. Other entry points when travelling by car are the new Quezon Eco-Tourism Road (Rte 422), the Batangas-Quezon Road (Rte 435) Pagsanjan-Lucban Road (Rte 605) and Majayjay-Lucban Road.

To northern Quezon from Manila, most go through Marcos Highway aka the Marilaque (Marikina-Rizal-Laguna-Quezon) Highway, popular with motorcyclists for its bends and scenery (though crashes are all too common). Alternatively, you can take Santa Maria-Infanta Road (Rte 601) which begins in eastern Laguna.

Northern Quezon will be connected to Aurora Province and Nueva Ecija through a road through the eastern Sierra Madre from Dingalan, but as of the moment, it will be a long drive through Manila (the same goes for the rest of Aurora).

Construction of an extension of the South Luzon Expressway (SLEX) to Quezon Province is ongoing.

chunks.name: Get in / By train
chunks.text:
Philippine National Railways (PNR) operate a regional train service between Calamba and Lucena, stopping at Los Baños, San Pablo and Candelaria.

Service from Bicol remains suspended as of 2022. The Metro Commuter service from Manila has been discontinued in 2023; to connect with the regional train, you must take a bus from Manila, get off at Calamba Crossing and walk or ride a trike to the station in Calamba.

chunks.name: Get in / By ferry
chunks.text: RORO ferries connect Marinduque with Dalahican port at Lucena, on Avios Lines, Montenegro Shipping Lines (with M/V Marie Kristina) and Starhorse Lines (with M/V Virgen de Peñafrancia).

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
The province is vast, and distances can be rather deceptive. With no expressways until the completion of an extension of the South Luzon Expressway (SLEX) to Lucena by the late 2020s, travel by road can take long, as many major highways also serve as main streets of the towns they serve. That said, many large towns have bypass roads being built, which should shorten travel times a bit until the expressways open.

Northern Quezon (Infanta, Real, General Nakar) can be reached only from the rest of the province through eastern Laguna. There is a highway along the eastern coast, but is incomplete; as of 2020, the remainder of the route is still being built through difficult terrain at the Sierra Madre facing the Pacific.

chunks.name: FOC Transportation
chunks.text: Services between Lucena and Northern Quezon via Tayabas, Lucban, and Eastern Laguna.

chunks.name: NCR-Rienton Lines
chunks.text: Non-AC minibuses between Lucena, Tayabas, and Mauban.

chunks.name: Get around / By bus
chunks.text:
While the bulk of bus services crossing the province are headed for Manila or Bicol through the Maharlika Highway, there are also local bus companies with routes originating from Lucena to points within the province, usually to towns in Bondoc Peninsula and Northern Quezon.

Services to the Bondoc Peninsula are provided by AB Liner (to Guinayangan via Gumaca, Lopez and Calauag), Superlines (to Mulanay and San Francisco via Pagbilao), and smaller companies running minibuses. Those by AB and Superlines are usually continuation of services from Manila, which have a layover at Lucena.

chunks.name: Get around / By jeepney
chunks.text: Jeepneys connect Lucena with Lucban and Pagbilao, Gumaca with towns in BonPen, and Lopez and Calauag (with onward service to Santa Elena in Camarines Norte). Lucena City has its own jeepney network. Other routes are more likely to be run by unlicensed ones (e.g. Lucena-Sariaya), and must be avoided in favor or buses that also serve those destination pairs and places in between.

chunks.name: Get around / By boat
chunks.text: Boats and ferries connect Polillo Island with the mainland; the same also applies to Alabat and Jomalig.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text:
Western Quezon has the most diverse dining options, which become scarce as one goes further east, north or to the island municipalities.

Quezon Province's local cuisine is Tagalog, but as the crossroads of Ilocano and Bicolano cultures, you can also find dishes from their respective regions as well.

Quezon dishes often include coconut milk (gata), which reflects in the province's large coconut industry and its Bicolano influences. Others originating from Quezon are:

Longanisa - The town of Lucban is also known for a variety of this sausage.
Pancit habhab - stir-fried noodles, served in a banana leaf and served without utensils. A local specialty of the town of Lucban.

Quezon is also known for pastries and snacks like budin, puto-bao, bonete, broas, kalamay, letse puto, pinagong and yema cake.

The province’s homegrown restaurant chain is Buddy’s, which serves Lucban-based dishes and contains Pahiyas-inspired interior decorations. Its first location opened in Lucban in 1985, and the chain has since expanded across Calabarzon and Metro Manila.

chunks.name: Drink
chunks.text: Lambanog is the local alcohol of choice, made from coconut.

chunks.name: Go next
chunks.text:
You can head for Bicol, which just borders the province to the south.
You take a ferry to the island province of Marinduque.

chunks.name: Quezon City
chunks.text: Quezon City (Tagalog: Lungsod Quezon) is the largest city in the Philippines and is one of the constituent cities of Metro Manila. Commonly called QC or Kyusi, it has a population of almost 3 million people in 2020. It has become the hub of information technology and its entertainment industry in the Philippines. Quezon City is a city of contrasts, mixing old and new, rich and poor, and traditional and modern.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Quezon City was created to become the future capital of the Philippines. It houses various government agencies whose buildings were constructed under the original masterplan laid out by the American architect and urban planner William Parsons. Quezon City is the largest city in terms of population, resulting from its gradual expansion and rural-urban migration; the 2015 census gives a population of over 2.9 million. The city is home to every person from all walks of life, from the richest to the poorest, and the contrasts are almost ubiquitous to this city.

Quezon City has no single place considered the city center; it is a multipolar city, with central business districts and commercial centers scattered at different points. Quezon City sprawls out in almost every direction, and this is manifested by the low-density developments that border each business and commercial center, and the scarcity of high-density homes for poorer residents have led to its notorious overcrowding illustrated by slums forming overnight, even after demolitions or fires break them down. The major business districts are grand old Cubao, glitzy North EDSA at the North Triangle neighborhood, with its large malls, and the classy Libis or Eastwood area at the southeast (a little version of Singapore's Orchard Road, but with its Hollywood-esque twist: the Philippines' Walk of Fame). If you are seeking the city's nightlife, the Scout Area provides all you need to hang out through the night.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text: Quezon City was conceived as the future capital of the Philippines under the Philippine Commonwealth government, as Manila had become overpopulated. Most of the city was planned by the urban planner, William E. Parsons. Most areas that are now Quezon City are acquired from various municipalities in Rizal. Many government buildings were built to house the agencies as they move from Manila. Only parts of the plan had come to fruition when the Japanese invaded the Philippines in 1941. After World War II, Quezon City further expanded by ceding parts of Caloocan to form the Novaliches district, resulting in the geographic division of the municipality.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text: The city has a tropical climate; daytime temperatures fall between 30s (86–102 °F), and has two seasons: dry and wet. Because of its location near the forested and rainy Sierra Madre, the dry season is rather cut short by the southwest monsoon. Average annual humidity is high, making the heat very unbearable, so dry season heat can take toll on your body; you will sweat easily on a short stay outside and do frequent changes in clothing.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: For information on airports and seaports, see Metro Manila#Get in.

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text:
Ninoy Aquino International Airport () is to the south, straddling Pasay and Parañaque. From there, travelers generally take a taxi or bus.

Taxi: All three terminals have taxi stands, served by yellow airport taxis, which charge double as the white ordinary taxis, which can only be used on trips to the airport and can only be hailed outside. It is also possible to just use the ride-hail service Grab from the airport.
Bus: For comfort, there are premium point-to-point buses provided by UBE Express, which alight at Cubao. Cheaper, but possibly slower due to Manila's perennial congestion are city buses with more frequent stops, which terminate near Terminal 2.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: As of 2022, provincial bus service only serve the Araneta City Bus Port bus terminal in Cubao, served by commuter routes from Bulacan and provincial routes from Central Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao. From elsewhere in the north and south, buses terminate at the North Luzon Express Terminal (NLET) in Bocaue, the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) in Parañaque, and Starmall Alabang in Muntinlupa. All of these three terminals have connections with the Manila city bus network.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: A huge majority of Metro Manila's bus routes serve Quezon City; general info is at Metro Manila#Get around

chunks.name: Get in / By train
chunks.text:
Quezon City is served by all of Metro Manila's three extant rapid transit lines, the LRT Line 1 (LRT-1), LRT Line 2 (LRT-2) and the MRT Line 3 (MRT-3). LRT-1 enters Quezon City using EDSA, terminating at the Fernando Poe Jr. (formerly, but still Roosevelt) station, with a future interchange with MRT Line 3 at North EDSA. LRT-2 connects Manila and the eastern suburbs, passing through Cubao. MRT-3 enters Quezon City from the south, following EDSA.

Quezon City will also be served by the Metro Manila Subway (MRT Line 9). Opening is expected by 2029.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Several options are available covering various distances and some areas are accessible only by certain means of transportation.

chunks.name: Get around / By bus
chunks.text:
Privately-operated city buses are plenty in Quezon City, and there is also a government-run free-fare bus service.

EDSA Carousel: BRT-like service running from the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) and Monumento (Caloocan) and uses a dedicated lane at the middle of EDSA. Serves Cubao and the Triangle areas.
2 Antipolo-Quiapo: Local bus service between Antipolo (PITX) and Quiapo (Manila via Aurora Boulevard). Major destinations served are Katipunan area, Cubao and New Manila.
6 PITX-Sapang Palay, 7 PITX-Fairview and 34 PITX-Montalban: Local bus services plying Quezon and Commonwealth avenues. 6 runs between Sapang Palay in Bulacan and PITX, 7 runs between PITX Fairview (with stops along Timog and East avenues) and 34 runs between PITX and Rodriguez (Montalban), turning off Commonwealth near the Batasang Pambansa.
18 BGC–North EDSA: Local bus service between SM North EDSA and Bonifacio Global City via Congressional, Luzon, Katipunan and E. Rodriguez avenues. This is one of 4 city bus routes that serve Eastwood to the southeast.
QCityBus: intracity bus service operated by the Quezon City government, composed of 7 radial routes (QC1-QC6 and QC8) emanating from the Quezon Memorial Circle and 1 crosstown route (QC7 Katipunan–Welcome Rotonda). Services use air-conditioned coaches.

chunks.name: Get around / By train
chunks.text:
While covering only parts of QC, LRT Line 2 and MRT Line 3 run through the main points in the city, namely Cubao, North EDSA and Katipunan.

The MRT Line 7, nearing completion, will extend train coverage to Fairview, most of Commonwealth Avenue, the UP campus, Quezon Memorial Circle and North EDSA. Most of the line is already complete, with potential opening by 2026.

chunks.name: Get around / By taxi
chunks.text: Metered taxis are probably the most comfortable option - just be wary of large taxi fares during rush hours and drivers being picky on their passengers (they try to avoid destinations in crowded areas).

chunks.name: Get around / By jeepney
chunks.text:
Jeepneys, either traditional or modern ones, are most useful in areas of QC not already served by city buses such as UP Diliman, which is served by a loop service known as the "UP Ikot".

A lot of jeepney routes in QC also take the main roads primarily served by buses such as Commonwealth Avenue, but for trips that involve those roads, taking a bus is preferable.

chunks.name: Get around / By car
chunks.text:
Driving in QC is not recommended, especially if your destination is along EDSA. Traffic is badly congested, streets are often narrow, left turns are rare than rights, parking can be expensive in the CBDs and there is constant road construction round the clock. Reckless driving, road rage and police corruption are also problems.

Main roads in QC are EDSA, C-5 (E. Rodriguez Jr., Katipunan, Tandang Sora, Luzon, Congressional and Mindanao avenues), Commonwealth Avenue, Quezon Avenue, and Quirino Highway. With the exception of Quirino Highway, most of them are wide avenues with a median divider, but these are expected to be snarled during rush hour. Left turns are often prohibited on those roads, with street intersections crossing the median closed and replaced by U-turns.

QC implements the regionwide road space rationing ("number coding") scheme, with window hours before and after noontime except along EDSA.

Parking can be elusive and/or expensive at key locations. Parking spots at malls are bound to be scarce during peak shopping periods and weekly sales.

chunks.name: Get around / By tricycle
chunks.text: Smaller lanes and roads in residential areas are plied with bicycles fitted with side cars, termed padyak or traysikel.

chunks.name: Get around / On foot
chunks.text:
While very large, walking around Quezon City is possible and a great way to experience local street life and culture, but presents many of the same challenges as walking around the rest of Metro Manila, with extreme temperatures, smelly or unpleasant streets, and big dangerous roads. Despite this, many parts of Quezon city have sidewalks, or side streets that are similar to the alleys in Japanese and Korean cities. when crossing a major street, drivers will most likely stop for pedestrians like in the rest of Metro Manila

Jaywalking, is illegal on major streets but the chance of catching a fine for doing so are basically zero.

While walking is a great way to get around Quezon City, searching how far the places your trying to get to is always a good idea, as Quezon city is significantly larger than other cities in Metro Manila, and thus other methods of transit may be needed for long distances.

chunks.name: See / Landmarks and parks
chunks.text: Quezon Memorial Circle, in the Triangle Area, is a national park and shrine bounded by the Elliptical Road. At its center is a mausoleum containing the remains of Manuel L. Quezon, the second President of the Philippines. Mabuhay Rotonda in Quezon City/West was built to welcome people to the new national capital that was being built in Quezon City. Tandang Sora National Shrine is the place where the house of Melchora Aquino stood in Northwestern Quezon City It was in this site that she took care of the wounded Katipuneros and provided them food and shelter. Known as "Tandang Sora" she was adopted "Heroine of Quezon City" by a City Council Resolution. She died at the age of 107 on March 12, 1919.

chunks.name: See / Churches
chunks.text: In Santa Mesa Heights, you'll find Santo Domingo Church, home to the statue of the Our Lady of the Most Holy Rosary, said to be more than 400 years old, and San Pedro Bautista, which is one of the oldest churches in the country, housing the bones of the patron saint. There is also a catacomb in the basement of the church where the friars of the past were buried. Hearts of Jesus and Mary Parish Church is a quiet church in Brgy. West Triangle.

chunks.name: See / Other places of interest
chunks.text: Tomas Morato and Timog Avenue Tourist Belt Area in the Scout Area is where restaurants, bars, clubs, and other retail and entertainment establishments are found. Araneta Center is a mixed-use residential and commercial complex in Cubao housing several malls and budget accommodations. An ideal transport base as it's LRT-2 and MRT-3 stations connects 2 major lines. It also houses several city and provincial bus terminals for travel within the metro or to other provinces. It is home to the Araneta Coliseum, aka the "Big Dome", which is the biggest arena in the country.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text: Dining options vary upon each area or district of this large city. In the Diliman/Katipunan area, where some of the best universities in the country are located, dining options are largely geared towards the student population (though this does not say anything about the range or quality of available options -- posh dining is equally possible). The Tomas Morato area is a known nightlife area and serve good options for both dining and drinking, especially afterwork. When all else fails, people flock to the nearest mall (within just this city, there are several) survey the dining options there (from posh and chic restaurants to fast food dining in food courts).

chunks.name: Go next / Within Metro Manila
chunks.text:
Visiting Manila may come to your mind after staying in Quezon City. Other options within the metro are:

Makati – Philippines' financial capital, with towering skyscrapers, the glitzy Ayala Center, and high society, contrasting with the hassles of crowded residential districts.
Marikina - The "Shoe Capital of the Philippines", not complete without visiting its Shoe Museum or strolling the Riverbanks.
San Juan – Shop till you drop at the Greenhills Shopping Center, or if you're lucky to visit in June, join the Wattah-wattah Festival, part of the Feast of St. John the Baptist celebrations with water fights resembling Songkran celebrations, and get wet.

chunks.name: Go next / Northern Luzon
chunks.text:
Quezon City is a hub for buses to northern Luzon.

Alaminos – The Hundred Islands with its pristine beaches.
Baguio – The "Summer Capital of the Philippines", with cool climate, pine trees, and mountains.
Banaue – World-famous rice terraces and Ifugao culture
San Fernando – Taste of Kapampangan cuisine and the spirit of Filipino Christmas.
Vigan – Heritage city with a well-preserved downtown

chunks.name: Quezon City/Cubao
chunks.text: Cubao is the commercial heart of Quezon City, at the intersection of EDSA and Aurora Boulevard. While long overshadowed by North EDSA with its large malls, the districts's status as the traditional shopping center of Quezon City refuses to die; the Araneta family, who owns Araneta City, has begun a redevelopment project for the area to return it to its former glory.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
While the Triangle and Scout Area is the government, entertainment and nightlife hub, Cubao is the grand old commercial heart of Quezon City, with Araneta City, formerly Araneta Center, at its core. This district only developed in the late 1950s, when the Araneta family bought a piece of rural land once owned by RCA and built its first buildings. Cubao started to blossom with the construction of the Araneta Coliseum, which further become famous for the "Thrilla in Manila" boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier in 1975. The first shopping mall to open is Ali Mall, named after Muhammad Ali; other buildings followed, like SM Cubao, New Frontier Theatre (Kia Theatre from 2015 until 2018), Fiesta Carnival (formerly a Shopwise supermarket), and Farmers Plaza. The popularity of Cubao slowly declined as larger shopping malls and commercial developments begin to appear outside the area.

Cubao is not limited to Araneta Center, administered as part of barangay Socorro; the district extends into barangays Immaculate Conception, Kaunlaran, San Martin de Porres (Arayat), San Roque, and Silangan, all part of the former barangay until it was divided into smaller barangays. Local addresses continue to utilize Cubao as the barangay.

chunks.name: Get in / By public transit
chunks.text: Cubao lies at the intersection of LRT Line 2 (LRT-2) and MRT Line 3 (MRT-3) and is reachable from both of them. The stations of both lines are named Araneta Center-Cubao, though these do not have any physical connection and transferring between the lines would involve walking on local streets. LRT-2 runs above Aurora Avenue west from Manila into Santolan in Pasig. MRT-3 is built at the middle of EDSA and runs from Taft Avenue in Pasay to North Avenue within Quezon City.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: Cubao is served by three bus routes as of August 2022, which is EDSA Carousel, 3 Antipolo–Quiapo, 51 VGC-Cubao via Mindanao Avenue and 53 Cubao-Pacita. Route 51 and 53 buses terminate at Araneta Center, EDSA Carousel buses stop near P. Tuazon Boulevard, and route 3 buses stop along Aurora Boulevard

For services from South Luzon and interisland trips, there are:

For trips roughly within or 2 hours long, there are often no frills, but there will be vendors entering the bus at certain points and selling food and drinks at inflated prices. Longer trips will tend to have meals included on the fare, tickets must be purchased at a counter at the terminal, and on overnight trips and interisland services, there will be complimentary blankets and a ferry and port surcharge, respectively.

chunks.name: Quezon City/Diliman and Katipunan
chunks.text: Diliman and Katipunan Avenue are the two university towns of Quezon City, housing two major rivalling universities, the University of the Philippines Diliman and the Ateneo de Manila University.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Diliman, named after the Tagalog name for Stenochlaena palustris, a species of medicinal fern, formed parts of the towns of Marikina and San Juan, then parts of Rizal province; when Quezon City is created, their governments supported the handover of those areas as part of the new capital of the Philippines that time. Formerly one barangay, Diliman has been since split up into eleven barangays, but its name survives in many addresses around the area, and is a de facto district.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus or jeepney
chunks.text: Commonwealth Avenue, which runs through this area, is served by numerous bus routes; buses can take you here from most corners of Metro Manila. Major bus and jeepney stops are Philcoa (nearest to Maguinhawa Street), UP Technohub (nearest to University of the Philippines Diliman), Central Avenue, Tandang Sora, Luzon Avenue, Ever Gotesco, Batasan Road, and Litex. If you take a bus, the conductor will call out the next stop.

chunks.name: Get in / By train
chunks.text: Diliman will be served by the future MRT Line 7, with one new station, University of the Philippines, at the middle of Commonwealth Avenue in front of Ayala Technohub. Katipunan, meanwhile, is served by LRT Line 2, with Katipunan station at the corner of Katipunan and Aurora Avenues.

Commonwealth Ave (Rte 170), an 18-lane avenue which provides access to the northeastern areas of the city. It indirectly connects with EDSA through the Elliptical Road, a giant circular road with Quezon Memorial Circle in the middle.

chunks.name: Quezon City/Northern Quezon City
chunks.text: Commonwealth Avenue is Quezon City's second major thoroughfare, with its notorious traffic and contrasting areas, with a mix of opulence and poverty. Lying to the north of the Commonwealth Area is Fairview and Lagro areas, both mid-class communities to the north, centered on three malls facing each other along Quirino Highway. This article also covers Pasong Putik, and the Balintawak, Novaliches, Project 8, and Project 9 areas in northwestern Quezon City.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Commonwealth Avenue area covers the Commonwealth Proper, one of the most densely district in the city. The area includes the areas of Riverside, Manggahan, and Litex. Urban sprawl dominates the area with few business centers, primarily located along the Commonwealth Wet Market.

Meanwhile to the north of Commonwealth Proper, Fairview is consists of the Baranggays of Greater Fairview, and North Fairview. The area is well-known for mid-range restaurants and malls. Most of neighborhood in the area are mid-class communities. Lagro is located to the north of Fairview, is also an extension of mid-class neighborhood with some small business centers.

Northwestern Quezon City is the birthplace of the Philippine Revolution. Today it is a busy commercial district, with Balintawak's bustling public market, the up-and-coming Cloverleaf mixed-use development nearby, and the many restaurants along Congressional Avenue.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
This part of the city is sprawling. With a mix of car-dependent subdivisions in Fairview-Lagro area, noisy slums in the Commonwealth Proper, and the district's main artery, Commonwealth Avenue, known for its cacophony and high accident record mitigated by a 60 km/h speed limit and pedestrian overpasses, is more catered for travel by bus, jeepney or car. Walking in the areas is more of a strenuous activity that exposes you to the dangers of the city's heat and the district's criminal den. Shopping options are rather far apart, with just only one mall, some supermarkets, and non-air conditioned public markets.

Fairview is more of a mid-class neighborhood, but it is just as sprawling as the Commonwealth area. There are few places to visit, like its commercial district dominated by three malls, mid-range restaurants, and the La Mesa Ecopark. The MRT Line 7 project will mostly boost the district's growth by providing a faster connection to the rest of the city, but the line is not expected to open until around 2023.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: The wide Commonwealth Avenue, a 6 to 18-lane highway, also the namesake for the area and a barangay along it, is the main thoroughfare for this district. Travel is quite a breeze with many bus and jeepney routes plying it, and the wide carriageways that makes it look more of a superhighway, yet you must watch out for many quirky local driving habits if you're going to drive through it.

chunks.name: Iglesia Ni Cristo Templo Central
chunks.text:
Central Temple of the Iglesia Ni Cristo (Church of Christ). The Central Complex includes the Central Temple, which is an 8,000-seat church with one of the largest pipe organs in the Philippines; the Iglesia Ni Cristo Museum, which showcases the history of the Church in exhibits and artifacts from all over the world, marking its global expansion; the Tabernacle, a large multi-purpose meeting and presentation hall; and the New Era University and College of Evangelical Ministry, which are the flagship educational campuses of the Iglesia Ni Cristo, established in 1979.
hours: Daily 8AM to 5PM; address: 1 Central Avenue, New Era

chunks.name: La Mesa Eco Park
chunks.text: A beautiful 5-hectare eco park on the outskirts of Quezon city. A haven for people who'd like to get away from the heat and dust of the city. Quite hard to find though, and there is little public transport going there.

chunks.name: Payatas Dumpsite
chunks.text: Clearly not for the normal traveller easily shocked by the stench and the poverty, this dumpsite, which receives a third of Metro Manila's waste, is one of the district's local landmarks. This was once an empty ravine until it was converted into a landfill to replace Tondo's Smokey Mountain. Though touring the facility requires advance permission, you can see the life of Payatas's poorer families from roads surrounding this fenced-off pit. There is a monument erected to the northeast, dedicated to the victims of a garbage landslide that killed over 300 on July 10, 2000.

chunks.name: Tandang Sora National Shrine
chunks.text:
A national monument and memorial park dedicated to Filipino revolutionary and centenarian, Melchora Aquino. It covers an area of 1,000 m² and features a 10.67-m bronze sculpture. An art gallery is also hosted within shrine grounds which features paintings and other sculptures dedicated to Aquino. It also has a pavilion and stage for events, and a mini-museum dedicated to Melchora Aquino. It was completed in 2008.
address: Banlat Road

chunks.name: Quezon City/Southeast
chunks.text: Southeast Quezon City, despite being primarily residential, has much to offer for those passing by.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Southeast Quezon City is composed of seven barangays, which are commonly divided into three broad neighborhoods. The westernmost portion forms Camps Aguinaldo and Crame, home to the national headquarters of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and Philippine National Police (PNP), while the easternmost portion forms Libis and Bagumbayan, a rapidly-growing former industrial area. Separating the two in the middle are Barangays Saint Ignatius, White Plains and Ugong Norte, home to gated communities that are among the most exclusive in the entire country.

Much of this area was part of neighboring Pasig until the creation of Quezon City in the 1930s. It was not seriously developed until well into the 20th century.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Southeast Quezon City is served by several bus and jeepney lines, and on MRT Line 3 serves this part of the city.

Eastwood City is the hub of most non-rail-based public transport in the area. While most services in this area head to other parts of Quezon City, Pasig or Marikina, a few services head south: the Citylink bus service operates to Ninoy Aquino International Airport via Taguig during peak hours (except Sundays), while Yellowdot Transport operates a service between Taguig and Antipolo which stops here.

Public transportation generally does not serve Barangays St. Ignatius, White Plains and Ugong Norte, or inside Eastwood City. The Metro Manila Subway's Camp Aguinaldo station will serve this area once it opens in 2032, but until then, there is an informal habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) terminal along Katipunan Avenue in White Plains, in front of a 7-Eleven, if you need public transportation to or from this area. Otherwise, if going to or from this area it's strongly recommended to get a taxi to move around, or be prepared to walk.

chunks.name: Quezon City/Triangle and Scout Areas
chunks.text: The Triangle Area and Scout Area of Quezon City forms the heart of the city's government center, entertainment industry, and nightlife. On the four avenues forming the Triangle Area, you may either find yourself in a row of government offices, shopping malls, residential areas, and commercial strips.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
This article includes also barangays Roxas, Obrero, and Kamuning, through those places are not traditionally associated the Scout Area; Muñoz (Katipunan, Veterans Village), Bago Bantay (Bagong Pag-asa, Project 6, Ramon Magsaysay, Santo Cristo, Vasra), Santa Cruz (around Fisher Mall) and Nayong Kanluran are also included as part of the larger North EDSA area, with its glitzy malls.

The Scout Area gets its name from the 22 Boy Scouts of the Philippines who died on the way to the 11th World Scouting Jamboree in Marathon, Greece; this area encompasses barangays Laging Handa, Sacred Heart and South Triangle. Most streets, except Mother Ignacia Avenue, Panay Avenue, Sergeant Esguerra Avenue, Timog Avenue and Tomas Morato Avenue, are named after the 22 Scouts, hence the district's common name.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The Triangle Area is part of the former barangay of Diliman. It was originally intended to be the location of all the offices of the Philippine government as Quezon City is envisioned, and the northeast corner (present-day Quezon Memorial Circle) was the supposed site of a new Philippine capitol building, but as World War II erupted in the Pacific, many of the proposed building have never been constructed. The west and south sides of the Triangle grew into middle-class neighborhoods; the east side only became filled with government offices, and the north side is partially filled with government offices and commercial developments, with interspersed slums. The north side of the Triangle Area is undergoing redevelopment as part of the Triangle Business Park commercial development.

The Scout Area's major streets are Timog Avenue (Route 173), a four-lane street running east-west from EDSA to Quezon Avenue, and Tomas Morato Avenue, a north-south avenue running from the area near the ABS-CBN Broadcasting Complex south to E. Rodriguez Sr. Avenue in New Manila. Both streets are nightlife centers; expect to find many classy restaurants and bars at almost every corner.

South Triangle, a barangay, is a mid-class neighborhood home to the two major television networks, ABS-CBN and GMA Network, and film production firms; it is home for many Philippine TV celebrities, and is the Philippines' Hollywood.

chunks.text: The Triangle and Scout Area is near to Diliman and Cubao; from the streets of Diliman, crossing East Avenue brings you immediately to the East Triangle area. From Cubao, you can just hop onto MRT Line 3, a jeepney, or a city bus, and get down at points along EDSA.

chunks.name: Quezon Memorial Circle
chunks.text: The Quezon Memorial Circle is a national park and shrine in Quezon City, Metro Manila, Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The site of the Quezon Memorial Circle had been intended for the National Capitol to house the Congress of the Philippines. While foundation works for the structures were laid in 1940, construction was interrupted by the onset of the World War II. After the war, Philippine President Sergio Osmeña issued Executive Order No. 79 stipulating the creation of a Quezon Memorial Committee to raise funds by public subscription to erect a memorial to his predecessor, President Manuel L. Quezon. In 1951 a competition for the Quezon Memorial project was conducted where architect Federico S. Ilustre's design was selected as the winner. The monument designed by Illustre which serves as the centerpiece of the park and houses the remains of President Quezon and his wife.

The Quezon Memorial Circle except the monument area is managed by the city government since 2008. The monument is under the jurisdiction of the National Historical Commission of the Philippines since 1972. Before 2008 but not before the People Power Revolution, the park area except the monument area is managed by the Quezon City Parks Development Foundation.

chunks.name: Get in / By foot
chunks.text: For those who wish to access the park by foot, there are no pedestrian lanes for pedestrians to cross the Elliptical Road which encircles the park. It is very dangerous to cross the road. There are two underpasses present which provides a safe passage for pedestrians, one located in front of the Quezon City Hall and another in front of the Philippine Coconut Authority (Philcoa) Building at the Commonwealth Avenue intersection. Elevators are present at the Quezon City Hall underpass for the benefit of senior citizens and people with disabilities.

chunks.name: Get in / By rail
chunks.text: Quezon Memorial Circle is accessible from the Quezon Avenue and GMA-Kamuning Stations of the Manila Metro Rail Transit System Line 3 and Anonas Station of the Manila Light Rail Transit System Line 2. From there are jeepneys that have routes passing by the park. A station for the future Metro Rail Transit Line 7 is being built to the northwest, but will not open until 2024 or 2025.

chunks.name: Get in / By jeepney
chunks.text: From Line 2 Anonas Station, board a jeepney at Molave Street en route to the Philcoa or Quezon Memorial Circle. From Line 3 Kamuning Station, walk towards Timog Avenue-East Avenue intersection then board a jeepney en route to Philcoa or Quezon Memorial Circle. From Line 3 Quezon Avenue Station, board a jeepney en route to Philcoa or Fairview. From Manila proper, you can board a jeepney along Espana Boulevard en route to Fairview, Quezon Memorial Circle and Philcoa. Ask the jeepney driver to drop you at the Philcoa jeepney terminal and cross the footbridge to access the Philcoa underpass, or you could ask the driver to drop you by on the jeepney terminal in front of the National Housing Authority and proceed to the underpass directly in front of the Quezon City Hall.

chunks.name: Get in / By taxi
chunks.text: From most points in Metro Manila, Taxi drivers will agree to take you to the park. The taxi driver will likely drop you by the main entrance facing the Commonwealth Avenue.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text: Visitors can access the park two entrances, the one near the food complex just before the East Avenue section and the other through the main entrance facing the Commonwealth Avenue. The park also has a physical entrance at the North Avenue intersection but is closed to the public.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: The primary mode of transport inside the park is by foot. There are roads inside the park that is open for private vehicles but the road surrounding the Quezon Memorial Shrine and the area around the dancing fountain is off-limits to vehicles.

chunks.name: Quezon Memorial Shrine
chunks.text: The main attraction of the Quezon Memorial Circle. The Art-Deco monument which is adorned by mourning angels on each of its three pillars is a national shrine dedicated to the late President Manuel L. Quezon. Embedded artworks are also decorates the base of the shrine. At night the monument is illuminated with lights that gradually shifts its colors.

chunks.name: Dancing Fountains
chunks.text: The centerpiece of the Liwasang Aurora. It is illuminated at light with moving water features accompanied by music.

chunks.name: Liwasang Aurora
chunks.text: A circular paved plaza decorated in a style of a compass rose. Along with the adjacent stage, the Liwasang Aurora serves as the venue for various events such as concerts held at the Quezon Memorial Circle.

chunks.name: World Peace Bell
chunks.text: The World Peace Bell, housed in a gazebo, is a donation by the World Peace Bell Association, a Japanese organization promoting awareness on the world peace movement. It was inaugurated in 1994. The World Peace Bell grounds also has other features such as the Peace Wall, a mural and flag poles with names countries at its base (although flags are no longer hoisted). The grounds is also the location of the Agong of Peace dedicated to the Bangsamoro Peace Process.

chunks.name: Peace Monument
chunks.text: A marker erected to mark Quezon City as a Rotary Peace Community as part of the "Community Peace Cities/Towns" concept conceived by the Rotary Club of Wagga Wagga, Australia.

chunks.name: Philippine-Israel Friendship Park
chunks.text: A small secluded area beside the Quezon Heritage House which is dedicated to the bilateral ties of the Philippines and Israel. It features a small three-sided monument which commemorates; President Manuel Quezon's "Open Door Policy" to Jews escaping from Nazi Germany, the United Nations Resolution 181 of November 29, 1947 which led to the creation of the State of Israel where the Philippines voted in favor of Israel, and the 60th anniversary of the establishment of formal diplomatic relations between the two countries.

chunks.name: See / Monuments and markers
chunks.text: According to the book Arkitekturang Filipino: A History of Architecture and Urbanism in the Philippines by Gerard Lico, the monument also houses an observation deck at top of the monument but this feature is not accessible to the public.

chunks.name: Museo ni Manuel Quezon
chunks.text: A museum at the triangular base of the Quezon Memorial Shrine, dedicated to the political career of President Quezon. The remains of President Quezon are inside a marble sarcophagus inside the museum. His wife Aurora Quezon is also interred at the site.

chunks.name: Quezon City Experience
chunks.text: Focuses on the history of Quezon City. The interactive museum is divided into multiple pod buildings which were designed to be green building compliant.

chunks.name: Quezon Heritage House
chunks.text:
A historic house museum which used to be the house of the family of President Manuel L. Quezon and was at 45 Gilmore Street in New Manila, Quezon City. The museum focuses on the personal life of Quezon in contrast to the Museo ni Manuel L. Quezon which focuses on Quezon's political career.
hours: Tue-Sun 9AM-4PM

chunks.name: Presidential Car Museum
chunks.text:
Museum featuring land vehicles which were owned and/or used by past Philippine Presidents.
price: Free admission

chunks.name: Hardin ng mga Bulaklak
chunks.text: The Hardin ng mga Bulaklak is a flower garden which is a project of the city government, the Succulent and Cactus Society of the Philippines, and the Philippine Horticultural Society. It features various indigenous flowers and is often a location of gardening and flower shows by various gardening societies of the country.

chunks.name: Tropical Garden
chunks.text: Garden featuring tropical plants which was inaugurated in October 2012. It features a small pond as well and is another venue for gardening and flower shows.

chunks.name: Joys of Urban Farming
chunks.text: The urban farm where vegetables are planted in the park is part of Vice Mayor Joy Belmonte urban farming project, "Joys of Urban Farming". A custodian is available within the farm's premises where visitors could learn about growing crops at their own backyard.

chunks.name: Charito L. Planas Garden
chunks.text: A small fenced garden dedicated to Quezon City Parks Development Foundation head, Charito L. Planas who was responsible for the rehabilitation of the park in the early 2000s.

chunks.name: Fern Garden
chunks.text: A garden dedicated to ferns, however as of 2016, only a few ferns are present at the garden. Nevertheless, the garden provides a secluded place for park visitors that prefers a quieter place.

chunks.name: Cactus Garden
chunks.text: In a secluded area behind the Hardin ng mga Bulaklak, the Cactus Garden features cactuses and succulents of various types and sizes some almost as tall as a human. It also has a greenhouse but is usually off-limits to visitors.

chunks.name: Quezon City Memorial Circle Zipline
chunks.text:
For the adventurous and definitely not for the faint-hearted. Zipline from a height equivalent to about four-stories. The path of the zipline crosses the Pedal N' Paddle Pond. One Zipline station is near the Children's Playground and the other near the Joy of Urban Farming.

chunks.name: Circle of Joy
chunks.text: A children's playground within the park. The playground features various slides and other attractions such seesaws. The grounds are either covered in concrete or artificial grass which reduces the likelihood of little kids from getting dirty while still having fun.

chunks.name: Circle of Fun
chunks.text:
An amusement park within the park. It features various attractions and rides such as the "Fun Drop" a drop tower ride and the "Sea Dragon", a pirate ship type of amusement ride.

chunks.name: QMC Bicycle Rental

chunks.name: Quirino
chunks.text: Quirino is a province in the Cagayan Valley region of Luzon. One of the country's least-known provinces, it has underrated natural and cultural attractions such as indigenous communities and unspoiled mountains, rapids, caves and waterfalls.

chunks.name: Understand / Geography
chunks.text:
Quirino occupies of land area, mostly mountainous and forested terrain. The capital is Cabarroguis. The province occupies some of the last remaining jungles of the Sierra Madre Mountains, and hosts some endemic species.

The province appears as a roughly triangular-shaped entity on maps. It is bounded on the west by Nueva Vizcaya, on the east by Aurora, and to the north by Isabela. It is bisected by the upper reaches of the Cagayan River, which runs through the length of the province on its way to Isabela and Cagayan.

chunks.name: Understand / People
chunks.text: Quirino is one of the least populated provinces in the Philippines, with only 210,000 residents, mostly squeezed into northern towns bordering Isabela. It is predominantly inhabited by Ilocano migrants, followed by indigenous Bugkalot (formerly known as Ilongot) and Aeta tribespeople. There are also some Aeta tribes related to those in the Sierra Madre and Zambales mountains.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text:
Quirino's climate is similar to the rest of the Cagayan Valley, with scorching heat during the dry season from March to May, rains from June to October, and cold weather and torrential rains from November and February. The southern regions have a more temperate climate due to its altitude, but the dense jungle makes things humid.

Many visit the province during the dry season between March and May, where temperatures are at its highest but rainfall at its lowest. The rainy season is rather the same as with the rest of Luzon, but precipitation is somewhat higher, with the cool season from November to February also bringing in torrential rains. Heavy rain, especially those brought by typhoons, can cause seasonal road closures especially in southern Quirino due to landslides and rockfalls.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
Quirino was uncharted territory during the Spanish occupation, inhabited by indigenous Ilongot tribes. Throughout the 18th to 19th centuries, the Spaniards based in Cagayan Valley tried to subjugate what the area with limited success. In retaliation, Ilongot tribes raided lowland villages and beheaded residents in headhunting raids. In the early 1900s, the Americans occupied Quirino and largely calmed things down, although headhunting attacks continued until well into the 1970s.

Quirino frequently switched jurisdictions between Isabela and Nueva Vizcaya until 1971, when it finally became a separate province named after Elpidio Quirino, the sixth president of the Philippines. In the 1970s and 1980s, the area became a hotbed of rebellions led by the communist New People's Army. At the same time, cronies of the Marcos dictatorship entered Quirino and were awarded logging concessions before proceeding to ravage large swathes of the province's forest until the 1990s, when they were finally driven out by a belated effort by the government to stop large-scale deforestation. Despite this, migration to the province continued as Ilocano settlers sought new farmlands and homesteads, at the cost of displacing the Ilongots, now renamed Bugkalots in a bid to move on from their headhunting reputation, to the outlying mountains.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text: Long seen through the colonial era and much of the post-independence years as a “no-go zone” due to its reputation for being a hotbed of tribal warfare, headhunters and communist rebels, since the 21st century, Quirino has seen an influx of tourists.

chunks.name: Understand / Economy
chunks.text: Historically an agricultural society, Quirino's economy was interrupted with the entry of commercial logging in the 1970s that left deep scars on the environment after the loggers moved on. Since the 21st century, Quirino has began to open up to tourism, although the province remains obscure to many non-residents and is often the butt of jokes questioning its existence.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Quirino is mainly accessed through roads from Isabela and Aurora. The nearest airport is in Cauayan, from where transfers towards passenger vans heading to Quirino can be made in Santiago City, while most bus services from Metro Manila usually stop just outside of Quirino, in towns of Isabela bordering the province such as Cordon, Santiago and Echague. An exception to this is Maddela, where there are bus terminals providing once-a-day direct services to Manila.

There is a rudimentary road connection to Kasibu in Nueva Vizcaya from Cabarroguis, while a road connects Aurora province to the south and is frequented by buses running from Santiago City to Dinapigue, on the southeastern coast of Isabela. Since the 2020s, construction has been ongoing to connect Nagtipunan with Dupax del Norte in Nueva Vizcaya.

Public transportation to Quirino operates at an infrequent pace, which usually involves waiting for an indefinite period for your vehicle to fill up before it leaves the terminal.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
The main thoroughfare in Quirino is the Cordon-Diffun-Aurora Road, which runs the length of the province from the boundary with Isabela down to Aurora and passes through all six municipalities.

Due to infrequent public transport services, it is better to take a 4WD or any vehicle suitable for mountain roads. Many attractions are accessible following extended hikes. Tricycles are used within towns.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text: Tourism is still in its early stages in Quirino, with many waterfalls, mountains and caves still waiting to be discovered and identified even by the locals themselves. It is common practice in the towns to consolidate a cluster of natural attractions into ecoparks. The most visited of these are in Maddela and Nagtipunan. There is also a growing interest for cultural tourism featuring the Bugkalot.

chunks.name: Buy
chunks.text: Among popular products and souvenirs are handicrafts made from forest products such as bags, mats and fossilized flowers.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text: Quirino cuisine is dominated by Ilocano cooking. A popular export, particularly from Maddela, is bananas and banana chips.

chunks.name: Sleep
chunks.text: There is less accommodation in the province due to low visitor numbers, forcing many to sleep in Santiago City instead. The bulk of tourist accommodation in the province, including small and mid-size hotels, is in Diffun, Maddela and Cabarroguis. Most accommodation elsewhere consists of small inns, hostels or homestays.

chunks.name: Rapu-Rapu
chunks.text: Rapu-Rapu, the only island municipality in Albay, is a tranquil "hidden gem" featuring breathtaking natural attractions, including stunning rock formations, pristine beaches, and panoramic views of Mayon Volcano with a coastline facing Albay Gulf. The town comprises three islands: Rapu-rapu Island, Batan Island, and Guinanayan Island.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Rapu-Rapu and Batan Islands were historically part of Prieto Diaz in Sorsogon. Before it became a municipality on 1901, it was a bario of Prieto Diaz, Sorsogon. The Visita (Chapel) here and the spiritual and pastoral needs of the people were taken care of by the Parish Priest of Prieto Diaz. Records show that Rev. Fr. Santiago Nepomuceno was in charge here in the early part of 1891, then Rev. Fr. Juan Brusola took over. It was during his term that the Parish of Sta. Florentina was founded.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Rapu-Rapu is 374 km southeast of Manila and 36 km east of Legazpi, the provincial capital.

chunks.name: Get around

chunks.name: See and do
chunks.text:

Pristine beaches - Explore unspoiled beaches, often highlighted for their clear waters and relaxing atmosphere.
Panoramic views - Enjoy spectacular, uninterrupted views of the Mayon Volcano across the sea.
Local island life - Experience the serene lifestyle of this island municipality, providing a quiet getaway from mainland city life.

chunks.name: Rizal
chunks.text: The province of Rizal is the "R" in Calabarzon. It is a province to the east of Metro Manila with boundaries of the westernmost towns and cities of Cainta and Taytay blurring into the city of Pasig in the capital region. While becoming increasingly urbanized in the past few decades, it holds some rich secrets in both cultures and sights that are untouched by heavy and popular tourism yet are beauties of their own to be enjoyed.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Formerly a large province which hugged the north shore of Laguna de Bay and included most of Metro Manila’s component cities, Rizal now forms half of what it used to be. The province used to be called Morong until the American occupation, when it was renamed after the national hero, Jose Rizal.

The bulk of the province lies on the rugged Sierra Madre, which encouraged mass settlement on the lakeside and on the foothills before increased populations led to encroachment on the highlands, which in turn results in continuing environmental issues such as landslides, illegal logging and quarrying, and displacement of the indigenous Dumagat peoples to build water reservoirs for the rest of the province and Metro Manila. Parts of western Rizal have become part of the urban sprawl of the national capital region, with no distinguishable boundaries for the unaware traveler, except for the Morong Peninsula, a spur of the Sierra Madre that separates Binangonan from Cardona.

It is surrounded by Metro Manila to the west, Bulacan to the north, Quezon to the east, and Laguna and the Laguna de Bay to the south. Situated at the heart of the Tagalog homeland (Katagalugan), Rizal is culturally and linguistically Tagalog; much of the province's inhabitants are Tagalog speakers, except for a very small minority of Ilocano and Bicolano migrants.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
The nearest airport is Ninoy Aquino International Airport, but getting to Rizal from the airport is rather bewildering; you will have to get by Manila's notorious traffic and inefficient public transport. Bus service is severely lacking to serve most corners in Rizal, so you might need a car to cover everything not covered well by a jeepney. From Metro Manila, the main public transport hubs leading to Rizal are Quiapo in Manila, Cubao in Quezon City, and Ortigas and Rosario in Pasig.

As a de facto suburb of Metro Manila, western Rizal is served by buses and jeepneys traveling between the two regions. The Light Rail Transit 2 (LRT-2) is the only train service, running from Recto Station in Manila and terminating at Masinag Station in Antipolo, with a penultimate stop at Marikina-Pasig station on the boundary with Cainta. Expect heavy crowds during rush hour (From Antipolo in the mornings and the reverse at the end of the day).

Raymond Transport Inc operates services from Manila to Infanta in northern Quezon Province via Manila East Road.

From Laguna, SINCRODA operates jeepneys from Siniloan to Cainta, entering Rizal at Pililla and passing through Antipolo and Teresa via Manila East Road. There are also separate jeepney services connecting Siniloan with Jalajala, Pililla and Tanay.

There are no interprovincial ferries in Laguna de Bay.

Taxis and Grab can also be used to access areas of Rizal directly bordering Metro Manila.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
Rizal's roads are notoriously small, crowded, and winding due to its geography, and public transportation is severely lacking once you head east. Driving around the province (by car or motorcycle) is much practical, although western Rizal’s traffic congestion has worsened due to its proximity to Metro Manila.

Bus service is severely lacking on most of the province. Jeepneys mostly provide most service in much of the province, but are in short supply in upland areas. A unique and ubiquitous type of jeepney in Rizal and connecting routes is the “patok”, jeepneys of a longer, highly-decorated and heavily-built frame than the jeepneys elsewhere to negotiate the changing road terrain, and running on noisier engines with blaring stereos. The main jeepney hubs are in Antipolo, Tanay, Binangonan, Angono and the towns directly bordering Metro Manila. Some jeepney services may have been replaced by minibuses, such as the one running from SM Masinag in Antipolo to Pililla, which passes through Teresa, Morong Junction, Baras and Tanay.

The major highway through Rizal is Manila East Road, which runs east to west from the boundary with Laguna toward the suburban areas of Cainta and Taytay via the lakeside towns. While most of it has been widened to four lanes and sections through town centers have been bypassed, traffic is fairly slow.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
The Marcos Highway (aka the Marilaque Highway), which crosses the Sierra Madre mountain range and leads to Infanta (Quezon Province), serves the central part of the province; it is a favorite route by motorcyclists with its climate and its winding route, but crashes occur often especially on its hairpin curves.

Talim Island is serviced by ferries from Binangonan and Cardona.

chunks.name: See
chunks.text:
Antipolo Cathedral is popular with travelers who are about to embark on far away trips and other well-wishers and devotees. While Antipolo Cathedral is a modernist reconstruction, fans of Spanish-era colonial churches usually flock to Pililla, Tanay, Baras, Morong and Binangonan.

Rizal is also a popular hiking destination for daytrippers and campers from Metro Manila, particularly the highlands of Rodriguez, Antipolo, Baras, Tanay, Pililla, Jalajala and Talim Island.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text:
Rodriguez, San Mateo, Antipolo, Baras, Tanay, Pililla, Jalajala and Talim Island are favorite destinations for hikers seeking to climb a mountain within an hour or two from Metro Manila.

The lakeside towns of Rizal are included in the Laguna Loop, a bicycling circuit that encompasses the towns and cities around Laguna de Bay. Some cyclists deviate by passing through landlocked Antipolo in western Rizal from Manila before joining Manila East Road at Morong Junction via Teresa.

chunks.name: Eat
chunks.text:
Dining choices in Antipolo and western Rizal are indistinguishable from Metro Manila. This decreases the further you go eastward, although a few fashionable chains and novel restaurants are gradually setting shop along the Marilaque highway for motorists and prospective property buyers.

chunks.name: Rizal (Cagayan)
chunks.text: Rizal is a town of Cagayan province in the Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Rizal was established in the early 17th century on the foothills of the Cordillera mountains leading to present-day Apayao province. Formerly known as Malaueg, its name was changed in 1914 to Rizal in honor of the Philippine national hero. That same year, the town annexed the neighboring municipality of Mauanan to the east, resulting in its present shape.

The town's isolated location, tucked away on the southwestern corner of Cagayan along the valleys of the Matalag and Zinundungan Rivers and secluded from the rest of the province by a spur of the Cordillera mountains, made it a bastion of guerrilla resistance to Japanese forces during World War II. It also gave the town a notorious reputation as a lawless place due to the presence of the New People's Army rebels since the 1970s and heated political rivalries that have led to the recurring assassinations of local politicians, including that of three mayors since the 1980s.

Rizal is a sparsely-populated and primarily agricultural town trying to shed its reputation for lawlessness through promoting its natural attractions for ecotourism purposes. While nominally part of the Itawis-speaking region of southwestern Cagayan, it is home to an endemic and endangered language called Malaueg.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Rizal is mostly accessible through a road running north from Tuao, where it is connected to the rest of the province and the provincial capital Tuguegarao via the Cagayan-Apayao Road. There are passenger vans and jeepneys running to town from Tuguegarao, although this may entail waiting for an indefinite period for the vehicle to fill up. During the rainy season, access through this road may be hindered by the overflowing of the Chico River and the submerging of the Itawes Bridge that connects Tuao with the municipality of Piat, forcing a lengthy detour through the Cagayan-Kalinga Road from Tabuk.

There are efforts to develop a dirt road along the Zinundungan River leading to the town of Lasam in the north into a paved and alternate access route. A new road was opened in the 2020s running parallel to the Cagayan-Apayao Road and directly connecting Rizal with the town of Conner in Apayao, ending Tuao's stranglehold on transportation links.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of transportation within town. Due to the poor state of roads, a 4WD is necessary to reach the outlying barangays.

chunks.name: Saint Raymond of Peñafort Parish Church
chunks.text:

It was declared a national cultural treasure by the Philippine government in 2001 on account of its age and dual function as a fortress against raids by Kalingas and Isnegs from Apayao.
address: Poblacion

chunks.name: Rodriguez
chunks.text: Rodriguez is a town at the foothills of the Sierra Madre at the province of Rizal.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The town was known as Montalban from its inauguration in 1908 to 1982, when it was renamed as Rodriguez, after a local politician. Despite the name change, it is still commonly called by its former name.

Lying at the northern edges of Rizal, Rodriguez hugs the foothills of the Sierra Madre and is a refuge from Manila's sprawl; however, the town forms a huge part of the mess which spilled eastward along the Marikina River. The municipal area covers 26% of Rizal's land area, big enough for space for various developments.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
There are UVs and minibuses that are bound for Sta. Lucia in Cainta and Araneta Center in Cubao, Quezon City.

Jeepneys from terminals in the town center are bound for Marikina town proper and SM in San Mateo. Jeepneys from terminals near Eastwood are bound for Aurora Boulevard in Cubao. Jeepneys from terminals in the Sub-urban village in San Isidro are bound for Commonwealth Market in Fairview. Jeepneys from terminals in Sitio Licao-Licao in Macabud are bound for Tungko in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.

Taxis (both car and motorcycle) and Grab can also be used to access areas of Rodriguez directly bordering Quezon City.

To get to far flung areas like Puray, Mascap and San Isidro, a mountainous barangay, there are special jeepneys at San Rafael Public Market.

There are available jeepneys in Kasiglahan Village in San Isidro that are bound for Burgos, near the town's boundary with San Mateo, and Wawa Dam.

chunks.name: Romblon
chunks.text: Romblon is an archipelago province of the Philippines. It is located in the middle of the small Sibuyan Sea which separates Luzon from the Visayas.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Romblon's name derive from a corruption of the Romblomanon word nagalumyom, referring to the act of how a hen sits over its eggs, but local historians argue it is from Spanish ronblon (screw) or doubloons.

While administratively part of the Tagalog-majority Mimaropa region, the people of Romblon are more closely related to those in the Visayas than to the Tagalog. People of Romblon belong to the Romblomanon, Inonhan and Asi ethnic groups and have their own languages, that are part of the Visayan subgroup.

The archipelago's economy is mostly dependent on agriculture and fishing. Also, another source of local income is Italian-quality marble extracted from the islands' mountainous interior. Ecotourism is an emerging industry, but tourists are few and far in between. Most items sold on the island has to be shipped from Luzon or Mindoro, and can be expensive.

chunks.name: Rosario (Cavite)
chunks.text:
For Rosario of Argentina, see Rosario.
Rosario is a town in the northern coast of Cavite.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Rosario was established by the Spanish in 1845 following the merger of two barrios of San Francisco de Malabon (now General Trias), namely Salinas and Tierra Alta, and their separation from the mother town. Its current name derives from the town's patron saint, Our Lady of the Holy Rosary. Downtown Rosario is often alternately known as Salinas.

Rosario was also the site of the Tejeros Convention, where the Philippine revolutionary government that replaced the Katipunan during the revolution against Spain in 1897 was established, and where the feud between the movement's two leaders, Andres Bonifacio and Emilio Aguinaldo, turned into a civil war that culminated with Bonifacio's execution less than two months later.

As a coastal town along Manila Bay, Rosario is mostly known for its fishing industry, particularly its dried and smoked fish which is commonly branded as "Salinas". Since the 1980s, an alternate economic lifeline has sprung up inland with the establishment of the Cavite Economic Zone (CEZ), a sprawling industrial estate that takes up roughly half of the town's territory. It also hosts a massive oil depot by the energy firm Petron.

chunks.text: The colorful baby buses (custom-made minibuses) commonly running between Bacoor and Cavite City and Naic ply the main coastal highway which passes through the downtown.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text: The main roads are Marseilla Street (Route 401, pronounced MAR-SAY-leeah) leading from Noveleta, and General Trias Drive, which runs north from Tejeros Junction along Antero Soriano Highway in General Trias before converging with Marseilla Street in Rosario Town Plaza.

chunks.text: Take the baby buses if traveling along the main highways and trikes when going to inland destinations.

address: General Trias Drive, Tejeros Convention

chunks.name: Caracol Festival
chunks.text:
The town's patronal festival is held twice a year to commemorate the feasts of Saint Isidore the Laborer and Our Lady of the Most Holy Rosary. Both occasions feature a procession of the Marian Caracol image, accompanied by street dancing to the tunes of the pandanggo folk dance at a slow pace resembling that of a snail (caracol).
