chunks.name: Tanay
chunks.text: Tanay is a town in Rizal, Philippines. The northern portion of the town lies within the Sierra Madre mountains.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The town's name was derived from its old name "Monte de Tan-ay", meaning "Mountain of Tanay", which reflects the area's mountainous location within the Sierra Madre. This explains the existence of Camp Capinpin, a military camp in the highland barangay of Sampaloc where the Philippine Army trains its soldiers in jungle warfare.

Tanay virtually has two town centers: the old poblacion at the floodplain of the Tanay River leading to Laguna de Bay, and Sampaloc, the commercial hub of the upland barangays that has grown thanks to the opening of the Marcos Highway, the presence of the Camp Capinpin garrison, and an influx of hikers and affluent people and property developers seeking to find a spot in the Sierra Madre to build their dream resthouse far from the stress of Metro Manila.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Tanay is 46 km away from Manila and 22 km away from Antipolo. It is accessible via Manila East Road (for the barangays along Laguna de Bay) and Marcos Highway (for Sampaloc and other upland barangays). A two-lane inner road parallel to Manila East Road connects the town center of Tanay with those of Baras and Pililla. The Tanay-Sampaloc Road serves as a capillary between the three roads and runs from Sampaloc to the town market at Plaza Aldea.

Jeepneys from the terminal in the town market are bound for Cainta, Starmall EDSA in Mandaluyong, Pililla, Jalajala and Siniloan. Jeepneys from the terminal in Sampaloc are bound for Cogeo in Antipolo. The minibus service from SM Masinag in Antipolo bound for Pililla passes through Tanay.

There is an airfield in Camp Capinpin in Sampaloc, but is only used for military purposes.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Places within the town proper are accessible by tricycle. Northernmost barangays, such as Daraitan, San Andres and Santa Ines, are accessible by jeep from the town market via Sampaloc Road.

chunks.text: Tangalan is a municipality in the province of Aklan, Philippines.

In the town: a beautiful old church. The town is very quiet and peaceful, with very little traffic and many trees around the town plaza and church.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text:
Swimming in the Jawili waterfalls and at the white sand Jawili beach (pronounced 'Ha Willy'). At night there is 'phosphorescence' in the sea water: when you move in the water, the water glows. Very cool. This effect could be seasonal.

The coral reef was severely damaged by cyanide and dynamite fishing in the past, but as of few years ago it has been turned into a Marine Sanctuary, and many concrete blocks were planted in the water for coral to get established on. It has been a huge success, and after only few years, most species have come back.
You can go hiking in the nearby reforestation project. You can hike on a trail from the Falls. There is also a park entrance along the highway.

Originating as a small town near Panguil Bay, it became a city in 1967, but it retains a small-town charm. With the opening of the Panguil Bay Bridge, it became the new gateway to Misamis Occidental from Northern Mindanao.

chunks.name: Tanza
chunks.text: Tanza is a town in Cavite. A coastal settlement along the shores of Manila Bay, it is at the limit of the urban sprawl of northern Cavite and contains some beaches and sights of historic importance.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Formerly known as Santa Cruz de Malabon, Tanza was originally part of San Francisco de Malabon (now General Trias) and was settled as part of extensive pastoral landholdings created during the Spanish era. The area saw some of the major battles of the Philippine Revolution against Spain from 1896 to 1897 and briefly hosted the revolutionary government of General Emilio Aguinaldo. Its current name was adopted in 1914.

The town underwent extensive urbanization beginning in the 1980s, resulting in the eastern part of town becoming integrated into the urban sprawl originating from Metro Manila, albeit physically separated from neighboring General Trias and Rosario by the Cañas River. Its southern hinterlands have been taken over by middle-class gated subdivisions. Despite this, Tanza retains a sizeable small-scale fishing fleet along Manila Bay and beach resorts in its western shores leading to Naic.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Antero Soriano Highway passes through the southern outskirts of downtown Tanza. It is also the terminus of a road running directly north from Tagaytay, passing through Mendez, Indang and the provincial capital, Trece Martires. Both roads converge at the junction next to SM Tanza.

Buses bound for Ternate from Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) and Lawton in Metro Manila ply Antero Soriano Highway, from where transfers to Tanza proper via jeepneys and tricycles can be made, usually at the junction next to SM Tanza. An alternate mode of transport is through the baby buses, minibuses and jeepneys that ply the Bacoor-Naic route along Antero Soriano Highway and the jeepneys along Tanza-Trece Martires Road.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the most convenient form of public transportation within downtown Tanza and if heading to the coast, while jeepneys connect downtown Tanza with the southern barangays leading to Trece Martires, as well as the western barangays leading to Naic.

The convent hosts a small ecclesiastical museum.

chunks.name: Tarlac
chunks.text: Tarlac is a province in Central Luzon. Tarlac is best known for its fine foods and vast sugar and rice plantations, and its fine cooking scene is due to its position as the crossroads of four major cultures. It offers some of the best cuisines from the places of ancestry of its settlers, the provinces of Pampanga, Bulacan, Nueva Ecija, Zambales, Pangasinan, and the Ilocos Region.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Tarlac is the most multicultural of the Central Luzon provinces, with a mixture of four major ethnic groups, the Kapampangan (or Pampangos) in the south, the Ilocanos and the Pangasinan (or Pangasinenses) in the north, and the Tagalog at the border with Nueva Ecija.

Tarlac is a predominantly flat province, with plains abounding with rice paddies dominating its landscape, except to the west where it is rugged, hilly and mountainous. The local economy is largely dominated by agriculture.

Tarlac is often seen only as an agricultural backwater north of Pampanga, and a mere obligatory stopover along the route to northern Luzon. With the possible exception of Capas, which is anchored by Mount Pinatubo and the under-construction New Clark City, tourist infrastructure remains rudimentary.

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text: While having no airports within its borders, Tarlac is served by air through Clark International Airport () in neighboring Pampanga.

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: Most of Tarlac is well-served by provincial buses, mostly traveling out from Manila into Pangasinan, Baguio or the Ilocos provinces, and trips to those usually make a major service stop at Tarlac City. Major bus companies are Victory Liner and Five Star, and Philippine Rabbit, all of which have their dedicated bus stations in Tarlac City.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text:
The primary route to Tarlac is the Subic-Clark-Tarlac Expressway (SCTEX), which terminates at Tarlac City but its immediately followed by the Tarlac-Pangasinan-La Union Expressway (TPLEX). An older and slower alternative is MacArthur Highway (Route 2); these roads form the main north-south axis through Tarlac. While having separate toll systems and are two distinct routes, SCTEX and TPLEX form one long continuous high-speed route through the province and is numbered E1 on some maps. These motorways have exits in Concepcion, Tarlac City, Victoria, Pura, Ramos and Anao. TPLEX also has an interchange in Tarlac City with the Central Luzon Link Expressway (CLLEX), which connects the province with Cabanatuan in Nueva Ecija.

From Pangasinan, the primary route is the Romulo Highway (Route 55). From Nueva Ecija, the primary route is the Santa Rosa-Tarlac Road (Route 58). Both highways terminate at the MacArthur Highway in Tarlac City.

chunks.name: Get in / By train
chunks.text: Rail service to Tarlac ended in 1988, but is planned to be restored with an extension of the North-South Commuter Railway (NSCR) to New Clark City in Capas. No construction has begun yet as of 2026.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Buses and jeepneys are the best way around, with frequent departures from terminals in Tarlac City. Modern jeepneys go from Tarlac City to serve most towns.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: Trek Mt. Pinatubo: visit the canyons, the Aeta Village, take a dip in the crater lake.

chunks.name: Tarlac City
chunks.text: Tarlac City is the provincial capital of Tarlac. While it is the economic and educational center of Tarlac, it is a rather small provincial city, with little in the way of sights, and is more of a stopover for long-distance buses.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Previously a part of a larger municipality of Porac in Pampanga during Spanish times, Tarlac City's residents are mostly Kapampangan speakers, but ethnically, a mix of Kapampangan, Ilocano, and Tagalog. It became the capital of Tarlac province upon its establishment in 1872 and became a legally-designated city in 1998.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: The city's nearest airport is Clark International Airport in Angeles, but it takes time to transfer to a bus to Tarlac City.

chunks.name: Tarlac Public Transportation Terminal
chunks.text: hours: Open 24 hours; address: Tarlac-Pangasinan Road

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text:
Most buses to Ilocos Region stop at Tarlac City, except some services (usually Baguio-bound buses) which bypass the city via the new Tarlac-Pangasinan-La Union Expressway.
Victory Liner, Zamora Street, buses between Manila and Dagupan or Alaminos and vice versa regularly stop at Tarlac City. Northbound services stop at a sheltered bus station behind the Motorway diner restaurant, while southbound buses stop at the Siesta Travel Break bus station, shared with other bus operators.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text:
Tarlac City is served by the Subic-Clark-Tarlac Expressway (SCTEX), Tarlac-Pangasinan-La Union Expressway (TPLEX) and the partially opened Central Luzon Link Expressway (CLLEX). The three intersect at an interchange at barangay Balingcanaway. Major toll-free national highways serving Tarlac City are the MacArthur Highway (Rte 2), Romulo Highway (Rte 55) and Santa Rosa-Tarlac Road (Rte 58).

As of August 2026, access to Tarlac City via Romulo Highway is restricted due to the collapse of the Aquino and Agana Bridges liking the city center to the rest of western Tarlac.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of public transportation in the city.

chunks.name: Hacienda Luisita
chunks.text:
A sugarcane plantation that is the center of landmark decisions on land reform in the Philippines. Straddling the boundaries of the nearby municipalities of La Paz and Concepcion, It used to be a Spanish-owned tobacco plantation until it was turned over to the Filipino-Chinese Cojuangco family (the family of Corazon "Cory" Aquino). An operational azucarera (sugar factory) inside the hacienda, the Central Azucarera de Tarlac is declared a National Historical Landmark. chunks.name: Tayabas
chunks.text: Tayabas is the former provincial capital of Quezon. The city is home to much Spanish-era architecture, including historic ancestral houses and stone bridges.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The city lies in the middle of Quezon, at the foot of Mt Banahaw. The old town has many old Spanish-era houses, once enough to rival those in Vigan or Taal, but many were burned down during World War II.

Despite being designated a city after long legislative debates, Tayabas feels more like a town, and is far quieter than nearby Lucena.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text: Tayabas was founded as a Spanish Augustinian mission to evangelize the native Tagalog population, and was the capital of the province of Tayabas (now Quezon) until 1901 when nearby Lucena became the capital. After a prolonged legal battle, Tayabas became an officially-recognized city in 2013.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text: Tayabas has a rainforest climate, with no dry season. Temperatures vary little by year, and rainfall is distributed all throughout the year.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Tayabas is a stop for the daily Manila-Mauban route operated by JAM Liner. NCR-Rienton Lines has ordinary buses plying Lucena-Mauban, with a stop at downtown. Jeepneys plying Lucban-Lucena also serve the town.

Tayabas is served by the Maharlika Highway (Route 1) which passes through barangay Calumpang and is connected to the town center through the Tayabas-Sariaya Road. Tayabas town proper is also connected by a two-lane provincial Route 603 (Pagsanjan-Lucban-Lucena Road) from Lucena which directly serves the old town, where it becomes the narrow Quezon Avenue and Luis Palad Street. Tayabas-Mauban Road (Route 605) runs from the coastal town of Mauban and ends at Tayabas. The Tayabas-Pagbilao Bypass Road leads to the town from Pagbilao and Bicol Region.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of transport within town.

chunks.name: Tayabas Basilica

chunks.text:

address: Tayabas-Pagbilao Road, Malagonlong

chunks.text: An inactive volcano straddling the provinces of Laguna and Quezon. At 2170 m, it is the highest mountain in the Calabarzon region, and a sacred monument for the Tagalog people.

chunks.name: Do
chunks.text: Tayabas has its reputation for festivals at various times of the year.

chunks.name: Do / Festivals
chunks.text: Taytsinoy Festival (February 2–5) Part of the Chinese New Year celebrations, it is celebrated as appreciation to the Filipino Chinese community in the city. Turumba Festival (Holy Week) - a celebration in honor of the Nuestra Senora de Turumba based in Pakil, Tayabense dance as a thanksgiving to the Virgin Mary in the main thoroughfares of Tayabas. Thousands of devotees from Quezon visit the Nuestra Senora de Dolorosa Church. Mayohan Sa Tayabas - (May) Celebrated since 1989, it blends Flores de Mayo celebrations with the colorful local traditions like Parada sa Baliskog. Hagisan ng Suman - Bundles of suman, a kind of rice cake, are paraded in bamboo bundles called bagakay, and as the image of St. Isidore the Worker passes, the suman bundles are thrown into houses and crowds. Pa'yas kay san Isidro (May 13-15) - Houses throughout town are decorated with native material. This celebration rivals Lucban's Pahiyas Festival festivities. Aguyod Festival - Showcases the local arts and the commitment to sustainable development. Hermano Pule Day - Commemorates the martyrdom of Apolinario dela Cruz (Hermano Pule or Ka Pule), a local of nearby Lucban who led a religiously-motivated rebellion against the Spaniards from 1832 until 1841 when he was executed and quartered in Tayabas. Araw ng Tayabas (August 13) - Commemorating the heroism of the locals of the city. Feast of San Miguel Arcangel - (September 29)- Celebration dedicated to St. Michael the Archangel.

chunks.name: Do / Festivals
chunks.text: Festejo de los Angeles (September 22-29) - People wearing angel costumes parade through the major streets.

chunks.name: Taytay (Palawan)
chunks.text: Taytay is a municipality on the island of Palawan in the Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Taytay is located 220 kilometers northeast of Puerto Princesa. It is bounded in the north by El Nido, in the south by San Vicente and Dumaran, in the east by Taytay Bay and the Sulu Sea, and in the west by the South China Sea.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Most tourists go to Taytay by road. From El Nido in the north, it is about 1½ hours by bus or van. From Puerto Princesa in the south, it is about 4 hours by bus or van. Private hire vans are available in Taytay to take you to the next part of your journey, or vice versa.

The Company RoRo Bus offer rides from Puerto Princesa (4½ hours, Non-AC ₱280, AC ₱360; Status 2014).
Some mini-buses from El Nido hold in Taytay. Ask around.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the most common means to get around Taytay, and are widely available. Tricycles can be fairly limited to certain areas and may not be able to go very long distances, so ask before boarding. State the road name and the district (Barangay), as some road names are repeated. Standard tricycle fare around the city is ₱20 if you just want to go a few streets away, or about ₱60-150 if you are going to the outskirts (i.e., 7 km away, or the place is on an unpaved road, etc.) Tricycle drivers are generally nice and quote only about 50% more than the standard rate if you look foreign, so just nicely counter-offer them a fair value and they will usually accept.

Some of these attractions are more known by native visitors, not much by tourists.

chunks.name: Taytay (Rizal)
chunks.text: Taytay is a town in Rizal, Philippines. It is nicknamed the "Garment Capital of the Philippines" due to the thriving garments industry in the town and the presence of a tiangge within the town proper.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Taytay was founded by the Spanish in 1579. , and is part of the urban sprawl extending eastwards from Metro Manila.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Taytay is 20 km away from Manila. It is accessible via Ortigas Extension. Manila East Road is one of the town's major roads, with Tikling as its northern terminus.

The terminal for buses to Quiapo are in Muzon.

The terminal for jeeps bound for Crossing in Mandaluyong and Santa Lucia at the edge of Cainta and Pasig are situated near the town's new market and tiangge.

Taxis (both car and motorcycle) and Grab can also be used to access areas of Taytay from Metro Manila.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Places along the main roads are accessible by jeepneys and buses, while places far from the town center are accessible by tricycles.

chunks.text:

chunks.text: Teresa is a municipality of Rizal in the Philippines. This town serves as a quieter alternative to nearby urban areas.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Named after a local politician, Teresa, is situated on a plateau surrounded by the Sierra Madre Mountains and is bordered on four corners by Antipolo on the north, Angono on the west, Tanay, on the east, and Morong, on the south. The town is passed by motorists heading to the towns of Rizal along Laguna de Bay, and the provinces of Laguna and Quezon. The town center is located almost at the center of the plateau.

chunks.text:
For other places by the name, see Ternate (disambiguation).
Ternate is a municipality in Cavite, at the boundary with Batangas. Its name derives from the island of Ternate, one of the Spice Islands (present day Maluku in Indonesia). Some of the Christianized natives from that island settled here after volunteering with the Spanish, who immediately left their garrison on Ternate.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: . Unlike the rest of Cavite, Ternate and Maragondon remain predominantly rural and laid-back areas, with Ternate’s extensive coastline and position at the mouth of the Bahra (Maragondon) River providing it with a fishing industry. The population is swelled by the students of the Polytechnic University of the Philippines campus in Maragondon.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
This town got its name from the island in present-day Indonesia. The Portuguese who were seeking for the Spice Islands, subjugated the Sultanate of Ternate and the Jesuits converted the Islamized natives to Catholicism. The Spaniards captured Ternate island, which they turned into a garrison against the Dutch seeking for the other Spice Islands, but they were forced to leave when the Chinese pirate Koxinga planned an invasion to pillage Manila. Some of the natives helped the Spaniards, and they were given a settlement near the Maragondon River estuary, first named Bahra. Koxinga died and the invasion never materialized, and the Ternate natives integrated into the local Tagalog population, but they are able to keep the Spanish creole they have, which survives as Bahra Chabacano.

Adjacent Maragondon has its name from Tagalog madagundong, meaning "full of rumbles". During the Philippine Revolution, it was the site of Andres Bonifacio's show trial under Emilio Aguinaldo, the leader of the rival Katipunan faction, Magdalo, in 1897, and his following execution at the foot of Mount Buntis. This event marks one of the darkest chapters in Philippine history and has been the root of a lingering historical debate whether Bonifacio or Aguinaldo is the first president of the Philippines.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Unlike most towns in Cavite, there are no jeepneys connecting both Ternate and Maragondon with the rest of the country, leaving buses as the only available option.

chunks.name: Saulog
chunks.text: address: Governor's Drive, Poblacion I

chunks.name: Saint Anthony of Padua
chunks.text: address: Governor's Drive, Poblacion I

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text:
Many bus companies have trips to and from Ternate from Manila. Most trips are on companies like Erjohn and Almark, Saulog, and Saint Anthony of Padua, with departures from Parañaque bus station (PITX), but there are small players as well; see Parañaque#Provincial buses for a comprehensive list.

For those heading to Maragondon, the main bus stop is at the junction with Governor's Drive and Captain A. Rillo Street, which is marked by the Galaxi Gas Station.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text: The direct route from Manila is through Antero Soriano Highway passing through coastal Cavite until its merger with Governor’s Drive in Naic, from where it continues toward Maragondon. From Batangas, take Ternate-Nasugbu Road. Secluded secondary roads connect Maragondon with Indang and Tagaytay via Alfonso.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
Both town centers are small enough to be explored by foot, and between them, there are tricycles and buses plying Governor's Drive. Unlike other towns, there is no dedicated jeepney service. A tricycle traveling one way between Ternate and Maragondon may cost between ₱45-50. Buses are cheaper at ₱15.

The mountains southwest of Maragondon town center are quite off the beaten track, so it's useful to have a car. This can be true also to access the resorts around Puerto Azul. It's possible to ride a tricycle for both, but be prepared for an extortionate fare unless you haggle it down to something tolerable.

chunks.name: Fort Drum
chunks.text: A heavily fortified sea fort, shaped like a battleship, built by the United States in 1909 as one of the harbor defenses at the wider South Channel entrance to the bay during the American colonial period. It was unique among forts built by the United States between the Civil War and early World War II, both as a sea fort and in having turrets. It was captured and occupied by the Japanese during World War II, and was recaptured by the U.S. after igniting petroleum and gasoline within the fort, leaving it permanently out of commission. The now-abandoned fort was named after Brigadier General Richard C. Drum, who served during the Mexican–American War and the American Civil War, and died on October 15, 1909, the year of the fort's construction. The fort is administratively part of Cavite City, but is geographically closer to Ternate.

chunks.name: Mount Pico de Loro
chunks.text: A dormant volcano. The mountain is one of the ancient volcanic features of the Bataan Arc. Pico de Loro was first named by Spanish seafarers as its pointed summit resembles the shape from afar. The summit is commonly used as a signal by seafarers to turn east to get to Manila Bay. The Mt Palay-Palay–Mataas-na-Gulod is a protected landscape.

chunks.name: Santo Niño de Ternate Parish
chunks.text:
Ternate's main Roman Catholic church. It was built in the 19th century and houses a venerated image of the Christ Child.
address: Santo Niño Street, Poblacion I

chunks.name: Andres Bonifacio Shrine
chunks.text:
The site where the two Bonifacio brothers, including Andres, were executed by the Emilio Aguinaldo administration after a show trial that convicted them of treason, amidst their contributions to the downfall of the Spanish colonization. The neglected shrine is reachable through a drive on unpaved roads, used mostly by trucks quarrying the nearby mountains. There is parking at the end of the winding road to the site, where you will trek through pasture to the shrine at the foot of Mount Nagpatong.
address: Mt. Nagpatong

chunks.name: Bonifacio Trial House
chunks.text:
A Spanish-era heritage house that was converted into a makeshift courtroom for the kangaroo trial of Andres Bonifacio and his brother by his comrades following a political rivalry with Cavite's own Emilio Aguinaldo in 1897. It now houses a museum explaining one of the most controversial events in Philippine history.
hours: 9AM–4PM; closed Sun and holidays; price: Free, donation optional; address: Col. C. Riel Street, Barangay Poblacion 1-A

chunks.name: Maragondon Church
chunks.text:
The town's Roman Catholic church is a Spanish-era structure that is a government-recognized national treasure. It retains its original interiors, except for the pulpit which collapsed in 2025 and is being restored. It was also one of the places in Maragondon where the Bonifacio brothers were detained during the period of their trial and execution.
address: Col. Infante St

chunks.name: Mount Kalanggaman
chunks.text: It takes about 2 hours to reach the summit of this mountain, the cone of an extinct caldera volcano.

chunks.name: Mount Palay-palay
chunks.text: There are multiple trails up to this peak, the dried-up cone of a caldera. The shortest trails takes about 45 minutes to an hour to complete. At the summit is a campsite.

chunks.name: Do / Hiking and mountaineering
chunks.text: Mount Palay-Palay/Mataas na Gulod Natural Protected Landscape has one of the remaining patches of lowland rainforest in Luzon, and its seven peaks, two of them being extinct volcanoes, receive many hikers and mountaineers from Manila.

chunks.name: Tiaong
chunks.text: Tiaong (pronounced as “CHAH-ong”) is a town in western Quezon. It is the gateway to the province and is a primarily agricultural town with a few natural and man-made attractions in between.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Tiaong lies at a fertile and forested valley running south from San Pablo in neighboring Laguna. It is bordered by two inactive volcanoes: Mount Malepunyo to the west and the Mount Banahaw-San Cristobal complex to the east.

chunks.name: PNR Tiaong Station
chunks.text: address: Lalig

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Tiaong is along the Maharlika Highway (Manila South Road, numbered Route 1/AH26) which also serves as the town's main street and a major bus route. The highway is a major bottleneck on the route in Quezon, necessitating the construction of a bypass road northeast of the downtown. An alternate route is through the Tiaong-Lipa Road from Batangas, but involves driving through a narrow and sometimes secluded two-lane road that is not fully illuminated at night. From a junction with Maharlika Highway in Barangay Talisay, Marcial C. Punzalan Jr. Highway leads to the coastal resort town of San Juan in Batangas.

Tiaong will be served by one exit on the South Luzon Expressway extension to Lucena.

Tiaong is also along the Philippine National Railways line running between San Pablo in Laguna and Lucena, the capital of Quezon.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: The town proper is fairly small, and easily explored by foot. Tricycles connect Tiaong town proper with other barangays.

chunks.name: Villa Escudero
chunks.text:
Tiaong's main draw is a sprawling family-owned agricultural estate that began in 1872 as a sugarcane plantation before switching to coconuts following a blight. The hacienda was opened as a resort showcasing rural life in 1981 and features a myriad of amenities such as a museum showcasing the landowners' art collection, a reconstructed Spanish-style chapel and ancestral houses, as well as a man-made dam and natural waterfalls.
address: Maharlika Highway, Bulakin

Tiaong's main Roman Catholic church, built during the Spanish era and extensively altered since then.
address: Rizal Street, Barangay III

chunks.name: Doña Concha Umali Ancestral House
chunks.text:
A 1920s Art Deco mansion built for one of Tiaong's leading families but later abandoned except by a few caretakers and subsequently rumored to be haunted. While prior permission is needed from the owners to enter, the low fences allow for bystanders to admire the fountain in the front yard showing a man wrestling with a crocodile, and even peek into the glassware laid out at the dining table.
address: Claro M. Recto Street, Barangay II

chunks.name: Lake Tikub
chunks.text: A volcanic crater lake west of downtown Tiaong. It was formed as part of the Laguna Volcanic Field and is an extension of the more famous Seven Lakes of neighboring San Pablo, but is less visited and has few tourist infrastructure apart from two viewdecks.

chunks.name: Moises Escueta Alaala Park
chunks.text:
A small recreational space with civic monuments, including that of Ye Fei, a Filipino-Chinese mestizo who moved to China and rose to become a senior general and politician under the Communist regime.

chunks.name: Tigaon
chunks.text: Tigaon is a semi urban-rural municipality of 61,000 in the Partido district of Camarines Sur. It is a rural area, with a compact town, and is known for Mount Isarog. Tigaon's coast has a beach, which still has a few resorts.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Tigaon is named after the Bikol word tigaw, a species of shrub whose leaves produced extracts that is used as poison to catch fish.

It started as a sitio of Sagñay in 1701, and had its own parish in 1794, when the St. Clare of Assisi Parish church was completed. Little is known when Tigaon became a municipality due to conflicting records.

The municipality is divided into 23 barangays, one being the town proper or poblacion. The town is small, and streets set on a rough grid. Most of the surrounding land are rice paddies. In general, Tigaon is fairly rural.

address: Terminal: P.T. Leelin St, Poblacion

chunks.name: Get in / By bus
chunks.text: Bus stops are at Leelin corner Gomez, the bus terminal, and the municipal hall. The Leelin corner Gomez stop is generally used by buses headed for Tiwi, and the stop at the town hall by buses from Caramoan, Lagonoy and Goa. The stop around the bus terminal has an Angel's Burger shack at the waiting area, and is served by buses headed for Goa, Lagonoy, and Caramoan.

chunks.name: Get in / By car
chunks.text: Tigaon is along Route 610, which follows part of the Jose T. Fuentebella Highway from Pili to the town center, and Tigaon-Sagñay-Tiwi Road which heads to Albay.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
The town itself is small, and easily walkable, but you can get around with a habal-habal or a padyak (cycle rickshaw or pedicab)

Mt. Isarog is reachable through barangay Hanawon in the nearby municipality of Ocampo. Habal-habal drivers are waiting around the bus and jeepney stop, though it's possible to take a tricycle as long you've negotiated the fare beforehand. It takes 20 minutes to reach the trailhead up to Mt. Isarog and the road is steep and winding. During the wet and typhoon season, it can get blocked by landslides.

address: Aguinaldo St, Poblacion

chunks.name: Tiwi
chunks.text: Tiwi is a municipality in the northeast quadrant of Albay, Philippines at the endpoint of Legazpi-Tiwi coastal road and borders the municipality of Sagñay in Camarines Sur's Partido District. Being a neighboring municipality of Malinao, its shoreline is facing Lagonoy Gulf. It is known for its pottery industry and the geothermal power plant at the foot of Mount Malinao.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Tiwi is the home of the Shrine of Our Lady of Salvation at Barangay Joroan. The municipality is dubbed as the Pilgrim capital of Albay.

chunks.name: Trece Martires
chunks.text: Trece Martires, or Trece in short, is a city in Cavite in the Philippines and the de facto capital of the province. The city lacks almost anything of tourist importance, but it is a major point for travellers to the inland of southern Cavite.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The city was established in 1954 as the new government center for Cavite, supplanting Cavite City, and is named after the Thirteen Martyrs of Cavite, who were executed by the Spaniards during the Philippine Revolution. Trece Martires was created from Quintana, a barrio (or barangay) of Tanza. The capital was officially transferred to Imus during the presidency of Ferdinand Marcos, but the government offices remain at Trece Martires, and is further reinforced by the construction of a new provincial capitol building at the edge of town in 2025.

There are plenty of restaurants and shopping around town, but hotels are rather scarce.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Trece Martires lies at the crossroads of Governor's Drive (Governor Juanito Remulla, Sr. Drive, or Routes 65 and 403), Tanza-Trece Martires Road (Route 64), and Trece Martires-Indang Road (Route 404). Travelers will usually travel via Dasmariñas or Kawit and Tanza, with convenient access to Cavite-Laguna Expressway via General Trias.

From Metro Manila, there are buses serving Trece Martires from the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX). Passenger vans also operate from Calamba, Laguna and Santo Tomas, Batangas. Jeepneys also connect Trece with neighboring towns such as Indang, Tanza, Naic and General Trias.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of transportation in town, with fares starting at P25. A trip from the city center to the New Provincial Capitol may cost P50.

chunks.name: New Cavite Provincial Capitol
chunks.text:
Opened in 2025, the complex replaced a previous office at the back of SM Trece Martires that became too cramped. The new building is a massive and imposing edifice whose design is inspired by the Aguinaldo Shrine in Kawit, complete with a towering spire at its center. At the front are large bronze statues of Cavite's own Emilio Aguinaldo and his main rival for leadership of the Revolution, Andres Bonifacio, who died at the hands of Aguinaldo supporters in Cavite. Construction is underway on other buildings in the area that would compose a new set of offices for the Cavite provincial government, along with a helipad.

chunks.name: Tuao
chunks.text: Tuao is a town of Cagayan province in the Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Tuao was established by the Spanish as a fortified settlement in the early 17th century along the Chico River guarding the approaches to the Cordillera mountains leading to present-day Kalinga and Apayao provinces. During World War II, it became the capital of Free Cagayan, the section of the province that was left unoccupied by the Japanese until they launched an offensive in 1943. Much of the town was devastated by an earthquake in 1949, but there are many colonial-era houses that remain, albeit in varying conditions from decrepit to well-maintained and partially used as commercial space.

Tuao is primarily an agricultural town. It is part of the Itawis-speaking region of southwestern Cagayan.

chunks.name: Tuao Bus Station
chunks.text: address: Cagayan-Apayao Road, Alabug

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Tuao sits at a four-way junction leading to the provincial capital Tuguegarao to the east, the municipality of Rizal to the north, the municipality of Conner in Apayao to the west, and the municipality of Pinukpuk in Kalinga to the south.

Along the Cagayan-Apayao Highway from Tuguegarao, there are passenger vans and jeepneys going there from the latter city, although this entails waiting for an indefinite period for the vehicle to fill up. During the rainy season, access through this road may be hindered by the overflowing of the Chico River and the submerging of the Itawes Bridge that connects Tuao with the preceding municipality of Piat, forcing a lengthy detour through the Cagayan-Kalinga Road from Tabuk.

Victory Liner and GV Florida operate daily bus services to Tuao from Metro Manila. Most travelers instead switch vehicles in Tuguegarao, where there are more frequent services by van. Travel time from Tuguegarao is between 45 minutes to an hour.

chunks.name: Get around

For the city in Arizona, see Tuba.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Tuba is at the southwestern corner of Benguet, at its triboundary with La Union and Pangasinan provinces. It has long been dismissed as the penultimate stopover on the way to neighboring Baguio and is slowly undergoing urbanization from the latter city, resulting in some attractions being mislabeled as being in Baguio itself. Despite this, Tuba, like the rest of the Cordilleras, is a tourist destination in its own right on account of its mountain landscapes alone.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Tuba is along the main highways running to Baguio. Kennon Road, a highway built during the American period runs through town on its way from Rosario in La Union to Baguio. It is the shortest and most scenic route from Metro Manila, but is frequently subjected to accidents due to its narrow lanes and treacherous curves, and closures to natural disasters such as rockslides, especially during the rainy season. Further north, Marcos Highway (Aspiras–Palispis Highway, Route 208) connects Baguio with Agoo in La Union, and passes through downtown Tuba. Most buses and private vehicles from Metro Manila ply this route, which is better-maintained and has wider lanes compared to Kennon Road.

There are also jeepneys and passenger vans going to Tuba from Baguio. Parts of the town bordering Baguio are also accessible by taxi.

chunks.name: Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park
chunks.text: Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park is a Philippines national park, administratively in Palawan province, but geographically out in the middle of the Sulu Sea. It is regarded as one of the world's finest diving destinations, either snorkelling or SCUBA.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park is in the middle of the Sulu Sea, some southeast of Puerto Princesa. It has a large area, about 970 sq km or 375 sq miles, mostly underwater.

The park is managed by the Tubbataha Management Office which issue a set of guidelines each visitor needs to respect. Divers also need to read and adhere to the Diving Best Practice to minimise impact on the reefs

chunks.name: Understand / Landscape
chunks.text: The area has a lot of coral reefs under shallow water. There are some small uninhabited islands.

chunks.name: Understand / Flora and fauna
chunks.text: The park boasts over 1000 marine species and beautiful corals and the islets serve as a home to nesting birds and turtles.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text: The region is tropical, hot all year. There are some typhoons.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Since the reefs are in the middle of the sea, the only way in is by boat. The closest inhabited islands are Cagayancillo, but boat trips usually start from Puerto Princesa, from where it takes about ten hours to reach the reef.

These are live-aboard boats that stay over the reefs for several days. Only a limited amount of vessels are granted a license to visit the park. Liveaboards vessels like the Philippine Siren usually carry up to 20 persons.

The main season is from March to June when the seas are calm, and as places sell out quickly you are advised to book well ahead.

chunks.name: Tuguegarao
chunks.text: Tuguegarao (pronounced as "tu-ge-garao" and commonly shortened as Tugue) is the only city in Cagayan province, and is the transportation hub for the region. It is the regional center of Cagayan Valley, with a reputation for hot weather.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Lying at a plain surrounding the meandering Cagayan River, Tuguegarao is the provincial capital of Cagayan. and forms a minor urban conurbation with the neighboring towns of Peñablanca (which is only accessible through Tuguegarao), Iguig, Solana and Enrile.

Tuguegarao is at the homeland of the Ibanag and the Itawis, both living along the banks of the Cagayan River. Those ethnic groups, along with their native languages, continue to exist today, despite the Ilocano migration from the 1900s displacing them.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
Tuguegarao's name is shrouded in legend and historical debate, and there is little information about Tuguegarao before the Spaniards arrived, but some land documents specify that it was called Tubigarao, an Ibanag settlement. The most accepted origin of the name "Tuguegarao" is the Ibanag phrase tuggi gari yaw, which means "this was cleared by fire", a reference to slash-and-burn agriculture the Ibanag practiced.

The American colonial era brought changes to Tuguegarao, becoming the provincial capital in 1909 with the construction of a new provincial capitol. It was then a town, with a traditional public market, a high school, and a trade school. The Japanese captured Tuguegarao during an invasion from Aparri in 1941, but the Philippine army and American forces retook the city following fierce fighting in 1945. Further changes happened in 1975, when Tuguegarao became the regional capital of the new Cagayan Valley region, and in 1999, gained city status.

chunks.name: Understand / Climate
chunks.text:
With its inland location, nestled between the Cordilleras to the west and the Philippine Sea to the east, Tuguegarao has a fair reputation for extremes, with a record high of , and a record low of . Tuguegarao is the hottest city in the Philippines, with Cabanatuan far south at second. The climate somewhat combines savanna, rainforest, and subtropical climates, with highs hovering around and lows around , so dry season is brutal, rainy season have hot mornings followed by rainy afternoons or unpredictable rainfall, and the cool season can be as cold as Baguio due to the northeast monsoon.

Cool season runs from December to February, when the northeast monsoon (amihan) is at full blast. The cool, dry wind from Siberia directly hits the city, so the nighttime low can drop below , or even below .

Hot season spans the months of March and April, and is brutal, with the heat index around the 40s or even extreme, the range.

Rainy season covers much of the year from May to November. Rainy weather on the early part is due to moist Pacific air, which gives way to the dry northeast monsoon by November. October is the rainiest month, and typhoons pass through Tuguegarao between August and October.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text: Tuguegarao is along the Maharlika Highway (Pan-Philippine Highway, Asian Highway 26), and is a key destination for buses heading from Metro Manila. It is also the hub of public transportation leading to other towns of Cagayan and the neighboring provinces of Kalinga and Apayao. It is also the terminus of the Tuguegarao-Roxas-Santiago Road, which runs parallel to Maharlika Highway in western Isabela down to Santiago City. Long distance commutes are handled by buses, while commuters to neighboring provinces and towns usually ride passenger vans.

chunks.name: Tuguegarao Airport
chunks.text:
It is Tuguegarao's main airport, north of the city proper. Small aircraft, helicopters and military aircraft also use the airport. Cebu Pacific and Philippine Airlines flies daily from Manila. Sky Pasada also operates flights from Palanan, Calayan and Basco, while Northsky flies from Itbayat and Palanan. As of 2026, the terminal building is being rebuilt, so expect problems in getting around.

Peñablanca lies on a curving section of the Maharlika Highway that was built to bypass downtown Tuguegarao. Buses to and from Tuguegarao pass by the town, while passenger vans running from Isabela do not, unless flooding in Capatan Bridge blocks direct access to downtown Tuguegarao. It also has an extensive and untouched coastline along the Pacific Ocean, but there is no road access and the area is sparsely populated. The only access is through irregular passenger ferries from the coastal towns of Isabela province or from Santa Ana.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text:
Many tricycles ply around the city which transports passengers to different points within the city. Tuguegarao's tricycle drivers are infamous even among locals for overcharging and haggling way beyond the official P20 minimum rate, with fares running to the hundreds of pesos not unheard of. The calesa (horse-drawn carriage) is also an available mode of transport in the city.

Since the 2010s, traffic jams have become a major problem in the city due to inadequate infrastructure and an explosion in the number of vehicles. Known areas of gridlock during rush hour are Bonifacio Street (Calle Comercio), Tanza Junction, Caritan and Balzain Junctions, Diversion Road, Ugac and Buntun Highways leading to Buntun Bridge, the section of the Maharlika Highway from Tanza to Carig, and the approach to Capatan Bridge from Libag to the city center.

chunks.name: Buntun Bridge
chunks.text:
One of the longest bridges in the country at 1.124 km. It is 2.5 km from the city proper and offers an unobstructed view of the Cagayan River. It connects Tuguegarao with western Cagayan, Kalinga, Apayao and western Isabela.
address: Buntun Highway, Buntun

chunks.name: Sts. Peter and Paul Metropolitan Cathedral
chunks.text:
The seat of the Archdiocese of Tuguegarao. The church with the belfry is the biggest Spanish colonial church in Cagayan Valley built by the Dominicans. It was constructed from 1761 to 1767 under the supervision of Fr. Antonio Lobato, OP. The cathedral suffered massive destruction in World War II losing its pipe organ, three wooden retablos, pulpit, wooden choir loft and the painted wooden ceiling all of which were from the early 18th century. The complex was rebuilt by Msgr. Bishop Constance Jurgens who is now entombed inside the church. The Cathedral is also said to be one of the beautiful structures that stood in the land and because of that impression, its portrait can also be seen in Vatican City. The traditional ringing of the cathedral bells for the Angelus and during Mass is still being practiced today. Its belfry is visible from a distance of 15 km.
address: Rizal Street, Barangay Centro 10

chunks.name: St. Hyacinth Church
chunks.text:
An elevated historic chapel established in 1604, 100 years older than the Sts. Peter and Paul Cathedral. American soldiers during the Philippine-American War used it as headquarters in 1899. St Hyacinth is the patron saint of the city whose feast is celebrated every August 15 coinciding with the Pav-vurulun Festival. The oldest brick structure in the city is the first parochial building built by the Dominican fathers in Tuguegarao. The current structure is the latest in a process of rebuilding beginning in 1724, in 1892 after it was destroyed by an earthquake and reconstruction after World War II. The chapel was not heavily damaged during the war and as a result retains its original wooden retablo which dates to the 18th century.
address: Mabini Street corner College Avenue, Barangay Centro 8

chunks.name: Cagayan Provincial Museum and Historical Research Center
chunks.text:

The museum houses extensive data on the discovery of Callao Man by the National Museum of the Philippines. Since 2023, it is housed in the old provincial jail, which in turn used to be the Casa Tribunal de Cagayan that was built in 1877.

chunks.name: St. Paul University Philippines
chunks.text:
It was founded by the Sisters of St. Paul of Chartres in 1907, who came to Cagayan upon the invitation of Bishop Dennis Dougherty. The school had its operation in a Spanish Convento, adjoining the Cathedral of Tuguegarao. The institution transferred to its present location in 1934 after it was acquired from the Dominican Order. The entire building complex became hospital and garrison of the Japanese forces during World War II and was bombed by the combined American and Filipino ground troops during the liberation in 1945. The institution became the first Catholic University in Cagayan Valley in 1982.

chunks.name: Do / Festivals
chunks.text:
Pav-vurulun Festival: - week-long, ends in 16 August (annually). Pav-vurulun is an Ibanag word which means get-together or a sense of belonging. It is in this context that the city annually celebrates its patronal fiesta in honor of St. Hyacinth, the patron saint of the city. It gathers Tuguegaraoeños to a week-long festivities culminating with a mass and procession of the patron saint on August 16. The week-long celebration is a festival of activities marked by parades, beauty contests, Pancit Batil-Patung eating contest, street dancing competition, music festival, sports fest, and trade fairs among others.

It is now called the Pavvurulun Afi Festival, a fire-themed festival. Afi is an Ibanag word which means fire, signifying the city's etymology. A highlight of the celebration was the lighting of bamboo torches by more than 3,000 college students from Cagayan State University as part of the kick-off activities. The organizers used citronella oil instead of kerosene, as a safety precaution, to ignite the torches.

chunks.name: Tumauini
chunks.text: Tumauini is a municipality in Isabela. It is to the north of the provincial capital, Ilagan.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Tumauini was officially established by the Spanish in the 18th century, although a mission existed in what is now Barangay Pilitan from 1598 until its destruction in an uprising in 1621. It briefly became a temporary capital of the newly-established province of Isabela in the 1850s before it moved to neighboring Ilagan.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
Tumauini is along the Maharlika Highway to Tuguegarao, and there are buses passing here generally every hour all day. The main bus stops are at XentroMall and Shell Gas Station, where a junction leads to Delfin Albano.

Tumauini is also serviced by passenger vans plying the Tuguegarao-Santiago City route. The main van stops are shared with the bus stops above.

Secondary provincial roads connect Tumauini with Ilagan and Mallig (and hence to Roxas) via Delfin Albano.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: Tricycles are the main form of transport. Fares start at P20. To reach the barangays west of the Cagayan River (Paragu and Pilitan), make a detour through Delfin Albano.

chunks.name: Tumauini Church
chunks.text:
One of the oldest churches in Isabela and a designated national treasure. It contains the only cylindrical bell tower in the Philippines. Its striking red brick facade has intricate carvings and symbols, including an inscription of its construction date of 1784. The church is being nominated for inclusion as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

chunks.name: Umingan
chunks.text: Umingan (pronounced "oo-meeng-gan") is a town in Pangasinan. It is a rising eco-tourism destination ideal for nature lovers and adventurers seeking a quiet countryside escape. There are waterfalls and hot springs nearby.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
Located at the foot of the Caraballo Mountains, it is at the southeasternmost part of Pangasinan. It borders the Nueva Ecija towns of Lupao on the east and Cuyapo on the south, and Balungao in Pangasinan on the west.

. Most of the town's population are descendants of the Ilocanos.

Buses heading to Cagayan Valley pass by Umingan from Rosales on their way to San Jose in Nueva Ecija.

chunks.text: Uyugan is a municipality of Batanes province in the northern Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text: Uyugan is in the southeastern part of Batan Island, the main island in the Batanes archipelago. Being the nearest place to Luzon, it became the first place in Batanes to be conquered by the Spanish in the 17th and 18th centuries.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
The best time to visit is during the dry season between March and June, when the winds and waves are calm. Otherwise, expect frequent cancellations at the last minute.

Uyugan is connected to the rest of Batan Island through a scenic highway system, with jeepneys and tricycles running between the town and the provincial capital Basco.

chunks.name: Vigan
chunks.text: Vigan is a city in Ilocos Sur, Northern Luzon. Its Spanish colonial influence in local architecture and old-world charm make it a unique city in the Philippines.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text:
The area of Vigan was once a settlement of traders from Fujian Province, China. At the time of Spanish colonization, the Chinese settlers, whose language was Southern Fujianese (Minnan, referred to as "Hokkien" by most Filipinos), referred to the area as "Bee Gan" (Chinese: 美岸; pinyin: Měi'àn, pe̍h-ōe-jī: Bí'gān), which means "Beautiful Shore." Since the Castillian and Basque Spanish conquistadors interchanged V and the B to refer to the B sound, they spelled the Hokkien Chinese name "Bee Gan" as "Vigan", which is the name used to this day.

In pre-colonial times, Vigan was an important trading post for Chinese merchants trading gold, beeswax and other products from the central Cordilleras for exotic Asian goods. Many Chinese traders settled in the mestizo district, marrying locals and starting new bloodlines.

Vigan was captured and settled by the Spanish in 1572, and grew to become a center of Spanish political and religious power in the north of Luzon. In 1758 Vigan became the seat of the Diocese of Nueva Segovia.

The town was also a hotbed of anti-Spanish politics. Diego Silang was perhaps the most notable resistance leader, but was assassinated by his friends (on commission from the Spanish) in May 1763. Undeterred, Silang's wife, Maria Josefa Gabriela Silang, assumed leadership of the uprising but was later captured by the Spanish and publicly hanged on September 20, 1763.

chunks.name: Understand / History
chunks.text: Local legend has it that Vigan got its name from a simple communication breakdown. A Spaniard walking along the Metizo River apparently met a local and asked what the city was named. Not understanding what he was being asked, but seeing that the Spaniard seemed to be pointing to a tree, replied "Bigaa Apo" (a giant Taro plant that was common in the area). It is from the word "Bigaa" that Vigan is said to have derived its name.

chunks.name: Understand / Orientation
chunks.text:
Vigan is a relatively small city with two hearts: the recreational and shopping area around the adjacent Plaza Salcedo and Plaza Burgos in the north, and the commercial centre around the public market in the south. The mestizo district is focused along Plaridel and Mena Crisologo Streets, running south from Plaza Burgos towards the cemetery.

There is a helpful and friendly provincial tourist information office south west of Plaza Burgos (next to Cafe Leona) that can dispense information on Vigan and the rest of Ilocos Sur. Banks with ATMs accepting foreign credit cards are located around the recreational and shopping areas and at Quezon Avenue, as are internet cafes with access that charge ₱20 per hour. Some restaurants offer Wi-Fi access.

, unlike many Philippine cities with a minimum of at least 100,000 population. This is however bolstered by the presence of neighboring towns that form a de facto urban conurbation around the city, which includes Bantay, Santa Catalina, San Vicente and Caoayan.

chunks.name: Dominion bus lines
chunks.text:
From Quezon City to Vigan at several times of day.
price: ₱580

chunks.name: Get in / By bus or car
chunks.text: It's 7-10 hours' drive along the scenic MacArthur Highway or Manila North Road from Manila or Quezon City to Vigan. Partas Bus Co., Dominion Bus Lines, Viron Transit, and St. Joseph/Aniceto Transit have regular trips to Vigan. Bus lines like Philippine Rabbit Bus Line, Farinas Transit, Maria de Leon, Florida, and RCJ Transit have regular trips plying the Manila-Laoag route, which passes by Vigan.

chunks.name: Mindoro Airport
chunks.text:
Vigan is not served by any airlines as of September 2023.
address: Barangay Mindoro

chunks.name: Get in / By plane
chunks.text: Alternately, you could go to Laoag's International Airport (1.5 hours by car). Philippine Airlines flies dally from Laoag and Manila

chunks.name: Get in / By boat
chunks.text: The nearest cruise ship terminal is in Salomague Port in Cabugao, 30 km to the north.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: A fun throwback to colonial days are the calesa horse-drawn carriages that still clip-clop through Vigan's streets. Rates for calesa rides should be the same as those for the many tricycles (₱8-10 within the city limits) that will undoubtedly by vying for your custom. But you could also hire a private calesa for around ₱150 per hour. Unless you're absolutely sure you have a tour guide that will give you in depth information about the sites you're visiting, A whole day calesa adventure for about ₱1000 (roughly 6-7 hours) would be advisable. You can take your time visiting the sites and not being rushed by a guide, as well as picking and choosing the areas you want to visit.

chunks.name: Mestizo District
chunks.text: offers a wonderful glimpse into the Philippines' colonial past. The ancestral houses were mostly built by Chinese traders using a mixture of local, Asian and Spanish architectural styles. Movie fans recognize the streets from the movie Born on the Fourth of July. If someone looks closely, there are still evidence left from the shooting, e.g. signs in Spanish but hastily and thinly painted over with white paint.

chunks.name: St. Paul's Metropolitan Cathedral
chunks.text:
The seat of the Archdiocese of Nueva Segovia and built by the Augustinians around 1790, this cathedral features a unique design intended to minimize earthquake damage, called "earthquake baroque". Look out for the brass communion handrails forged in China, complete with Chinese characters scrawled by its ancient installers (if you look closely). The eight-sided bell tower is just south of the cathedral. Its position was actually the safety measure of the earthquake baroque style: it was built separately from the church so that it would not topple into the church in the event of an earthquake. Its eight-sided design reflects its Chinese feng-shui influences. If you look closely inside the cathedral, you can find the tombstone of the great Ilocano poet Leona Florentino (in the column near the entrance facing Plaza Burgos).
price: Admission free; address: Nueva Segovia corner Burgos Streets

chunks.name: Plaza Salcedo (Luneta Park Musical Dancing Fountain)
chunks.text:
west of the cathedral features a 17th-century monument to Juan de Salcedo, and was also the site of resistance leader Gabriela Silang's public hanging in 1763. Also within the site at the lagoon is the Vigan Dancing Fountain. This Korean-engineered attraction is the first of its kind in the country, and rivals the Bellagio Water Fountains in Las Vegas, Nevada.
hours: 7AM–7:30PM; price: Free; address: Quezon Avenue corner Burgos Street

chunks.name: National Museum/Padre Burgos House
chunks.text:
also known as the Ayala Museum, this showcases the memorabilia of martyred priest Jose Burgos. Behind the house is the national museum (formerly the Ilocos Sur Provincial Jail), housing other ethnic and Ilocano artifacts such as artifacts, weapons, kitchen utensils, basketry, costumes, jewellery and Burgos memorabilia. There are also some dioramas showing important events in the history of Ilocos Sur, and a mini library. It just so happens to be where the Philippines' first Ilocano president, Elpidio Quirino, was born, his father having been a jail warden.
hours: 9AM-6PM; price: Free; donation optional

chunks.name: Plaza Burgos
chunks.text: is a favorite hang out for locals and is also used for staging major public events. It has also food stalls selling local snacks, especially the empanada. It is next to Vigan Cathedral and dedicated to the memory of Father Jose Burgos. Depending on the weather, the streets surrounding it (except for the street adjacent to the Empanadaan) are closed off to motorized traffic every Saturday and Sunday to allow people to walk the streets freely. It is a popular skateboarding venue among the locals.

chunks.name: Crisologo Museum
chunks.text: used to be the home of assassinated Congressman Floro Crisologo and wife Carmeling, former governor of Ilocos Sur. It contains Crisologo memorabilia.

chunks.name: Syquia Mansion
chunks.text:
Vigan residence of President Elpidio Quirino, who married a member of the Syquia family. There are memorabilia inside the residence, including a campaign portrait of Quirino.
address: Quirino Boulevard

chunks.name: Calle Crisologo
chunks.text: It is what Vigan City is known for — streets lined with Spanish Era ancestral houses (with ancient tile roofs, massive hardwood floors, balustrades and azoteas in varying Spanish, Mexican, and Chinese architectural styles) and cobblestone streets, which led to Vigan's inscription in the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Tourists can buy souvenirs or even ride a calesa (horse-drawn buggy). This street is also known as Vigan Heritage Village.

chunks.name: Barangay Pagpartian
chunks.text: Where the great conquistador Juan de Salcedo landed when he arrived in Vigan through the Mestizo River. Also the site of the city slaughterhouse, built during the Spanish Era (for which the barangay is named).

chunks.name: Hidden Garden
chunks.text: A wonderland of greenery, with a mini-snack bar nestled in the middle.

chunks.name: Quema House
chunks.text: The residence of the Quema family, considered by sociologist Fernando Zialcita as most representative of 18th-century Philippine architectural style.

chunks.name: Mindoro Beach
chunks.text: The only seaside tourist spot in the city, just adjacent to Vigan Airport.

chunks.name: Simbaan A Bassit
chunks.text:
This cemetery chapel found at the southern end of Quezon Avenue has a bell-gable design, the only one of its kind in the Ilocos Region. The chapel's name is an Ilocano term meaning "small church."
address: Quezon Avenue

chunks.name: Donato House
chunks.text:
Ancestral house.
address: De Los Reyes Street

chunks.name: Museo Nueva Segovia
chunks.text:
Just adjacent to the Cathedral is the Archbishop's Palace of the Archdiocese of Nueva Segovia, which dates from the 16th century during the Spanish era - the oldest archbishop's residence still in use in the Philippines. It was completed in 1793 after seven years of construction. It features sliding capiz windows and cut-out decorations with floral motifs. It has a back entrance that leads to the nearby Govantes Dike. The palace has a collection of priceless ecclesiastical artifacts and relics from other Ilocos churches.
hours: 8:30AM–4PM; address: Bishop's Palace, N. Segovia Street

chunks.name: Baluarte Resort and Mini Zoo
chunks.text:
A zoo founded by local politician and businessman Chavit Singson, featuring the usual animals as well as hunting trophies from his safaris in Africa.
address: Quirino Boulevard, Tamag

chunks.name: See
chunks.text:
The Historic Town of Vigan is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Govantes Dike is a body of water connected to the Archbishop's Palace which was once a docking port for water craft. It is now a place for boating, similar to the lake in Burnham Park in Baguio.

chunks.name: Parish of Saint Augustine of Hippo
chunks.text:

address: Real Street, Barangay 5, Bantay

chunks.name: Bantay Watchtower
chunks.text:
The belfry of Bantay Church, built during the Spanish era on a hilltop and physically separated from its church as part of its double function as a lookout for pirates and foreign invaders from the South China Sea. The site was declared a National Cultural Treasure by the Philippine government in 2015. Access to the site has been restricted since an earthquake in 2022 that severely damaged the structure.
address: Barangay I, Bantay

chunks.name: Our Lady of Hope Parish Church
chunks.text:

address: Don Lorenzo Querubin, Caoayan

chunks.name: Archdiocesan Shrine of Saint Vincent Ferrer
chunks.text:
San Vicente's main Roman Catholic Church, built in the Baroque style during the Spanish era in 1795. The site, along with the adjacent town plaza, municipal hall, and a building of the San Vicente Integrated School, which also dates back to the Spanish period, was declared a National Cultural Treasure by the Philippine government in 2020.
address: Bantay-San Vicente Road, Poblacion, San Vicente

chunks.name: Saint Catherine of Alexandria Parish Church

address: Vigan-Santa Catalina Road, Poblacion, Santa Catalina

chunks.name: New Quirino Bridge
chunks.text:
A two-lane bridge over the Abra River Gorge marking the boundary between Bantay and Santa to the south. At both ends of the bridge are viewing platforms with panoramic vistas of the area, including the old arch bridge east of the river, which has now lost much of its span following typhoons and flooding.
address: Manila North Road, Banaoang, Bantay

chunks.name: Vigan City Fiesta
chunks.text: The Bigueños celebrate the Longganisa Festival every January 22 in accordance to the cityhood of Vigan. With a colorful street dancing competition along the Calle Crisologo, this festival features one of the city's products, the very well-known Vigan longganisa. On the 25th, Vigan celebrates its town fiesta in honor to its patron saint, Saint Paul.

chunks.name: Viva Vigan! 'Binatbatan' Festival of the Arts
chunks.text: Every first week of May, Vigan plays host to visitors for this festival featuring painting and product exhibits, a calesa parade, and other cultural activities.

chunks.name: Semana Santa
chunks.text: St. Paul’s Metropolitan Cathedral is the venue of religious rites during Holy Week. The Good Friday procession features decorated carrozas bearing life-size statues of Spanish vintage. On Easter Sunday, the dawn celebration depicting the Resurrection of Christ, called "Sabet", is a scene to behold.

chunks.name: Raniag Festival

address: Playa de Oro Road, Mindoro

chunks.text:
Vigan is famous for its burnay jars that have been used as storage material for various wares since the precolonial era. This venue makes these jars, which are made of carabao-kneaded clay and fire-blasted in a huge kiln and allows visitors to try their hand in making their own jars.
address: Gomez Street

chunks.text: A barangay of Vigan known for its concentration of shops and manufacturers, usually old women, weaving the traditional Ilocano Abel textiles.

Although most of the antiques are only reproductions, you'll still enjoy browsing odd items, religious paraphernalia (look out for the toddler Jesus figurines) and some unique foods. You can also buy hand-rolled cigars, sold in packs of three.

You can buy native handwoven abel cloth at the Vigan Public Market, as well as delicacies like longganisa (native pork sausages) and bagnet (deep-fried crispy pork) at its Meat Section.

chunks.name: Visayas
chunks.text: The Visayas are a major island and cultural grouping in the midsection of the Philippines. Nearly every part of the region has some fine beaches along its coasts, some fine diving areas including many coral reefs teeming with life, and some interesting historic buildings, mostly from the Spanish colonial period (1560s-1890s), in the cities and some towns. Most of the larger islands have mountains near the center, most of them volcanic in origin though few are active now.

chunks.name: Understand
chunks.text:
The history goes back to prehistoric times; the largest migration was of Austronesian people, who are the ancestors of most modern Filipinos and related peoples, such as Indonesians, Malaysians, Micronesians and Polynesians. There are several different theories which differ on the details, but all agree that the migration took place several thousand years BCE.

The Portuguese adventurer Ferdinand Magellan led a Spanish expedition that made the first circumnavigation of the earth in the 1520s, and visited the Visayas. Limasawa in Southern Leyte, is where the first Christian mass in the Philippines was held. Magellan himself did not complete the trip; he was killed while fighting a Visayan warrior-ruler named Lapu-Lapu on Mactan Island, Cebu Province.

chunks.name: Get in
chunks.text:
The region's main air hub is Mactan-Cebu International Airport. It has domestic flights to most airports in the Philippines, international flights to many in the Asia/Pacific region, and a few to places beyond that. Other airports with some international flights are Iloilo, Kalibo and Panglao.

There are many flights from Manila to most major cities in the Visayas — Cebu, Tagbilaran, Tacloban, Kalibo, Iloilo, Bacolod and Dumaguete — mostly on Air Asia, Cebu Pacific or Philippine Airlines. Some of these also have flights from Cebu, but many travellers use buses or ferries instead. A few have flights from CDO/Iligan airport or Clark.

The port in Cebu City is the main hub for sea travel. It has boats to many destinations in the Visayas, several in Mindanao, and Manila. Other port cities such as Dumaguete and Iloilo also have many ferries.

chunks.name: Get around
chunks.text: There are ferries nearly anywhere in the Visayas, with the port in Cebu City as the main hub and smaller ports all over the region. There are also lots of buses, many of which ride ferries for parts of their routes. See the "Get in" sections of destination articles for details.
